- [ ] Song sheets

**Supplies:**
- [ ] Extra menorahs to lend/give
- [ ] Extra candles/oil
- [ ] Matches/lighters
- [ ] Menorah kits assembled

**Outreach:**
- [ ] Database segmented (active/inactive)
- [ ] Phone call list for personal touches
- [ ] Follow-up schedule planned
- [ ] Daily content calendar

---

## Personalization Tips

### Make It Your Own

**Local Customization:**
- Use exact sunset times for your city
- Reference local landmarks
- Include local Chabad contact info
- Add your personal greeting style

**Relationship-Based:**
- VIPs get personal phone calls
- Regular attendees get personal emails
- General community gets broadcasts
- New contacts get extra resources

**Language Options:**
- Provide in community languages
- Russian, French, Hebrew, etc.
- Show inclusivity
- Reach broader audience

---

## Final Thoughts

**Purpose of These Instructions:**

Simple, clear guidance that removes all barriers to performing the mitzvah. When people receive this, they should have:
- ✅ Exact timing
- ✅ Step-by-step process
- ✅ Blessing transliterations
- ✅ Your contact info for questions
- ✅ Confidence they can do it

**Philosophy:**
> "Don't assume they know. Don't assume they remember. Make it so easy that the only barrier is forgetting to read your message."

**Result:**
More families lighting, more consistently, throughout all eight nights. That's the goal.

**Use this template** as the basis for your daily Chanukah outreach messages, adapted for your community's needs and communication style.

# [Misc > For Writer > _5 Chanukah > General] Chanukah Heroines - Yehudit & Chana

## Women's Weekly Roundtable Class

**Series:** Links in a Golden Chain - Portraits of Biblical and Talmudic Women

**Source:** www.ChabadPotomac.com

---

## Discussion Questions

**Opening Reflection:**
- What level of responsibility do I feel for my community?
- To what extent would I go to serve my community?

**Closing Reflection:**
- Is there something more valuable than staying alive?
- Are we willing to exhibit self-sacrifice for Judaism?

---

# Part I: Yehudit's Story

## Historical Context

**Timeline Uncertainty:**
The story of Yehudit is not clearly dated. First appeared in an ancient book named after the heroine, originally written in Hebrew but the original text was lost. Only a Greek translation remained, and not a very accurate one.

**Possible Dating:**
According to one version, it happened during the time of the Maccabean revolt against Syrian oppression. Yehudit may have been a daughter of Yochanan the high priest, father of the Hasmonean family.

**Enduring Impact:**
> "The heroic deed of Yehudit has inspired faith and courage in the hearts of Jews throughout the ages."

---

## The Siege of Bethulia

### The Enemy Commander

**Holofernes:**
- Mighty Syrian-Greek general
- Head of a huge army
- Notorious for cruelty in suppressing rebellions
- Showed no mercy to men, women and children
- Determined to crush Bethulia's rebellion

**The Conflict:**
- Town of Bethulia in Judea under siege
- Inhabitants refused Syrian rule
- Men fought bravely against superior forces

---

### The Starvation Strategy

**Holofernes's Plan:**
- Couldn't take fortified town by force
- Decided to starve inhabitants into submission
- Cut off food and water supply
- Town brought to verge of surrender

**The Crisis:**
- People gathered in marketplace
- Demanded surrender rather than death by starvation
- Uzziah (defense commander) and elders tried to calm them
- Final plea: "Give us five more days. If no salvation comes by the end of five days, we will surrender. Just five more days..."
- Reluctantly, people agreed

---

## Yehudit Steps Forward

### Who Was Yehudit?

**Background:**
- Noble daughter of Yochanan the high priest
- Young widow
- Lost beloved husband Menashe several years prior
- Devoted time to prayer and acts of charity

**Character:**
- Blessed with extraordinary charm, grace and beauty
- Particularly respected for:
  - Devoutness
  - Modesty
  - Lovingkindness

---

### Her Challenge to the Leaders

**Yehudit's Words:**
> "Why do you test G-d, giving Him only five days in which to send us His help? If you truly have faith in G-d, you must never give up your trust in Him. Besides, don't you know that surrender to Holofernes is worse than death?!"

**Leadership's Response:**
> "You are quite right, daughter, but what can we do? Only a downpour of rain that would fill our empty cisterns could save our people, but it is not the rainy season. We are all suffering the pangs of hunger and thirst. Pray for us, Yehudit, and maybe G-d will accept your prayers..."

**Yehudit's Reply:**
> "We must all continue to pray, and never despair of G-d's help. But I have also thought of a plan. I ask your permission to leave town together with my maid. I want to go to Holofernes..."

---

### The Risky Mission

**Leaders' Shock:**
> "Do you know what you are saying, Yehudit? Would you sacrifice your life and honor on the slim chance that you might soften Holofernes's heart? We cannot allow you to make such a sacrifice for us."

**Yehudit's Biblical Precedent:**
> "It has happened before that G-d sent His salvation through a woman. Yael, the wife of Heber, was her name, as you well know. It was into her hands that G-d delivered the cruel Sisera..."

**Resolution:**
- Uzziah and elders tried to discourage her
- She insisted she be allowed to try
- Finally, they agreed

---

## Entering the Enemy Camp

### The Journey

**Preparation:**
- Dressed in her best clothes (not worn since husband passed away)
- Delicate veil all but hid beautiful face
- Accompanied by faithful maid
- Basket with rolls, cheese and several bottles of old wine
- Sun beginning to set behind green mountains
- Lips whispering prayers to G-d

**Encounter with Sentries:**
> "We have an important message for your commander, the brave Holofernes. Take us to him at once."

---

### Meeting Holofernes

**Her Cover Story:**
> "I am but a plain widow from Bethulia. Yehudit is my name. I came to tell you how to capture the town, in the hope that you will deal mercifully with its inhabitants..."

**The Deception:**
- Claimed life in besieged town unbearable
- Said she bribed watchmen to let her out
- Praised his bravery and mighty deeds
- Described desperate situation in town
- Key claim: "Their faith in G-d remained strong, and so long as they had faith, they would not surrender"
- Critical prediction: When kosher food runs out, they'll eat unkosher food, "and then G-d's anger would be turned against them, and the town would fall"

---

### Winning His Trust

**Holofernes's Question:**
> "But how will I know when the defenders of the citadel will begin to eat unkosher food, as you say, so that I can then storm the walls and capture the city?"

**Yehudit's Solution:**
> "I had thought of that. I have arranged with the watchmen at the city's gates that I would come to the gate every evening to exchange information: I will tell them what's doing here, and they will tell me what's doing there."

**Holofernes's Response:**
- Completely captivated by her
- Promised: "If you are telling me the truth, and will indeed help me capture the city, you will be my wife!"
- Gave orders: Complete freedom for her and maid to walk through camp
- Anyone molesting them would be put to death immediately
- Comfortable tent prepared next to his

---

## The Setup

### Daily Routine Established

**Freedom of Movement:**
- Two veiled women walked leisurely through camp any time of day or evening
- Everyone gave them wide berth (fearful of commander's orders)
- Soon attracted little attention
- Could walk to city gates after dark unnoticed

**Messages to City:**
> "Tell Uzziah that, thank G-d, everything is shaping up according to plan. With G-d's help, we shall prevail over our enemy. Keep your trust strong in G-d; do not lose hope for a moment!"

**Second Evening:**
- Repeated same message
- Added that she'd won Holofernes's complete confidence

---

### The Waiting Game

**Holofernes's Impatience:**
- Spent most time drinking
- When not completely drunk, sent for Yehudit
- She always came with her maid
- By third day, getting impatient

**His Complaint:**
> "Well, gracious Yehudit, what intelligence do you bring me today? My men are getting impatient and demoralized doing nothing; they cannot wait to capture the city and have their fun..."

**Yehudit's Report:**
> "I have very good news, general. There is not a scrap of kosher food left in the city now. In a day or two, famine will drive them to eat their cats and dogs and mules. Then G-d will deliver them into your hands!"

**Holofernes's Invitation:**
> "Wonderful, wonderful! This surely calls for a celebration. Tonight we'll have a party, just you and I. I shall expect you as my honored guest."

---

## The Climactic Night

### The Feast

**Setup:**
- Table laden with various delicacies
- General delighted to welcome her
- Bade her partake of feast

**Yehudit's Strategy:**
- Said she brought her own food and wine
- Prepared especially for the occasion
- "My goat cheese is famous in all of Bethulia, I'm sure you'll like it, General"
- Strong, undiluted wine

**The Execution:**
- She fed him cheese, chunk after chunk
- He washed it down with wine
- Before long: sprawled on ground, dead drunk

---

### Yehudit's Prayer

**Her Words to G-d:**
> "Answer me, O L-rd, as You answered Yael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, when you delivered the wicked general Sisera into her hands. Strengthen me this once, that I may bring Your deliverance to my people whom this cruel man vowed to destroy, and let the nations know that You have not forsaken us..."

---

### The Deed

**The Act:**
- Unsheathed Holofernes's heavy sword
- Took aim at his neck
- Brought sword down with all her might
- Sat for moment to compose herself
- Wrapped general's head in rags
- Concealed under shawl
- Calmly walked out to her own tent

**Escape:**
> "Come quickly, but let's not arouse suspicion."

- Two veiled women walked leisurely as usual
- Reached city gates
- "Take me to Uzziah at once"

---

## Victory

### Presenting the Prize

**Uzziah's Reaction:**
Could not believe his eyes at the gruesome prize.

**Yehudit's Command:**
> "There is no time to lose. Prepare your men for a surprise attack at dawn. The enemy's camp is not prepared for it. When they run to their commander's tent, they will find his headless body, and they will flee for their lives..."

**The Outcome:**
> "This is precisely what happened."

- Enemy fled in confusion and terror
- Left much booty behind
- Wonderful victory
- Saved by G-d-fearing and brave daughter of Yochanan the high priest

---

## Linking Past to Present

**Key Insight:**
Yehudit put her life on the line (both spiritually and physically) to save her community. While fighting the war was traditionally men's work, when necessary, a woman stepped forward to do what needed to be done.

---

# Part II: Women and Chanukah

## Halachic Sources

### 1. Women's Obligation in Mitzvah

**Source:** Talmud Shabbat 23a

> "Women are obligated to kindle the Chanukah lights, for they too, were included in the miracle."

---

### 2. Custom to Eat Cheese

**Source:** Shulchan Aruch Orach Chaim 670

> "There are those who say that we have the custom to eat cheese on Chanukah to commemorate the miracle when Yehudit fed cheese to the enemy."

---

### 3. Women Refrain from Work

**Source:** Me'Am Loez, Bamidbar, page 98

> "It is customary for women to refrain from work while the candles are burning... because another miracle happened then by virtue of a woman."

---

### 4. Extended Explanation

**Source:** Kitzur Shulchan Aruch, Laws of Chanukah 139:3

**Work Permitted on Chanukah:**
Work is permitted on Chanukah. Women, however, follow the custom of refraining from work during the time the Chanukah candles are burning at home. They should continue this custom without any leniency.

**Why Women's Greater Stringency:**

**Reason 1 - Harsher Decrees:**
> "The Greek's decrees were harsher for the women. They had decreed that any Jewish virgin who is getting married, must first have sexual relations with the Greek governor."

**Reason 2 - Miracle Through a Woman:**
The extended version of Yehudit's story:
- Daughter of Yochanan, the High Priest
- Very beautiful
- Enemy ruler proposed cohabitation
- She told him she would accede
- Fed him dishes of cheese to make him thirsty
- He drank much wine and became intoxicated
- While asleep, she cut off his head
- Brought it to Jerusalem
- Greek leader and army fled when they saw ruler slain

**Commemorative Custom:**
> "To commemorate this miracle, there are some who follow the custom of eating dairy dishes on Chanukah."

---

# Part III: Chana and Her Seven Sons

## The Story of Ultimate Sacrifice

### The Persecution

**Antiochus's Campaign:**
- Determined to enforce vicious edicts
- Effectively destroying Jewish attachment to Torah
- Forbade all religious laws
- Anyone with Torah would be executed
- Circumcision, kosher food, Shabbat outlawed
- All vestiges of Judaism forbidden

**Phillip's Enforcement:**
- Appointed governor of Judea
- Set out to ruthlessly enforce edicts
- Began with arrest of notable sage Elazar (High Priest)
- Elazar chose martyrdom over submission

---

### The Arrest

**The Family:**
Chana and her seven sons arrested, bound, brought before the king.

---

## The First Son

**Antiochus's Attempt:**
Tried to convince eldest boy to abandon Torah.

**The Youth's Response:**
> "Why do you bother with this long speech, trying to inflict your abominable religion upon us? We are ready to welcome death for the sake of our holy Torah!"

**The King's Reaction:**
- Furious
- Ordered boy's death
- Soldiers tortured the boy
- Forced mother and six brothers to watch
- King sure sight would intimidate prisoners

**Actual Result:**
> "Instead, the martyrdom spurred the family to a deep resolve to accept their fate and to sanctify G-d's name."

---

## The Second Son

**The Plea:**
Even king's retinue begged boy to obey.

**The Response:**
> "Do what you will with me. I am no less than my brother in devotion to G-d."

**His Final Words:**
> "Woe to you, pitiless tyrant! Our souls go to G-d. And when G-d will awaken the dead and His martyred servants, we will live. But you--your soul will dwell in a place of eternal abhorrence!"

---

## The Third, Fourth, Fifth, and Sixth Sons

**Third Brother:**
Unflinchingly suffered same fate.

**Fourth Brother:**
Echoed his brothers' exhortations, faced brutal death with firm resolve.

**Fifth Brother's Words:**
> "Don't suppose that G-d has handed us over to you to exalt you or because He hates us. It is because He loves us and has granted us this honor. G-d will take His vengeance upon you and your progeny."

**Sixth Brother:**
Same end as brothers who preceded him. Words bespoke deep faith that G-d would ultimately requite the suffering of His servants.

**Chana's Role:**
> "Throughout this horrible sequence Chana stood by her sons, giving them strength and encouragement."

---

## The Seventh Son

### The King's Final Attempt

**The Offer:**
- Only youngest child remained
- King offered gold and silver
- Seven-year-old displayed same courage
- Taunted king to carry out threats

**The King's Disbelief:**
Couldn't believe such words from mere child. Called out to Chana.

---

### Chana's Counsel to Her Son

**The Pretense:**
- Stood before murderer of her children
- King: "Woman, have compassion upon this child. Persuade him to do my will so that you will have at least one surviving child and you too will live."
- She pretended to agree
- Asked to speak with son

**Her True Message:**
> "My son, I carried you in my body for nine months, I nursed you for two years and I have fed you until today. I have taught you to fear G-d and uphold His Torah. See the heaven and the earth, the sea and the land, fire, water, wind and every other creation. Know that they were all created by G-d's word. He created man to serve Him and He will reward man for his deeds."

**About the King:**
> "The king knows he is condemned before G-d. He thinks that if he convinces you, G-d will have mercy on him."

**About Life and Death:**
> "G-d controls your life's breath and can take your soul whenever He desires. If only I could see the greatness of your glorious place where we would be illuminated with G-d's light and rejoice and exult together."

**To the King:**
> "I was unable to prevail upon him."

---

### The Child's Response

**His Words:**
> "Whom are you seeking to overpower with your words and enticements? I laugh at your foolishness. I believe in the Torah and in G-d Whom you blaspheme. You will remain an abomination upon all mankind, loathsome and far from G-d."

**The King's Final Test:**
According to the Talmud, Antiochus gave boy chance to save himself by ostensibly bowing down to retrieve his signet ring. The boy refused.

---

### Chana's Final Moments

**The Last Kiss:**
As they removed him, Chana begged to kiss him one last time.

**Her Words:**
> "My children, tell your ancestor Abraham, 'You bound only one son upon an altar, but I bound seven.'"

**The Execution:**
Antiochus ordered child be tortured even more than his brothers.

**Chana's Death:**
- Left surrounded by bodies of her sons
- Prayer exalting G-d on her lips
- Threw herself from a roof
- Rested beside her martyred sons

---

# Discussion Points for Class

## Yehudit's Story

**Themes:**
1. **Faith and Action** - "We must all continue to pray, and never despair... But I have also thought of a plan"
2. **Personal Risk for Community** - Put life and honor on line
3. **Strategic Thinking** - Carefully planned approach
4. **Precedent** - Referenced Yael as biblical model
5. **Divine Partnership** - Prayed at critical moment, then acted

**Questions:**
- What enabled Yehudit to take such a risk?
- How did she balance trust in G-d with practical action?
- What can we learn about community responsibility?

---

## Chana's Story

**Themes:**
1. **Spiritual Courage** - Not just physical bravery
2. **Mother's Role** - Strengthening children's resolve
3. **Kiddush Hashem** - Sanctifying G-d's name
4. **Comparison to Akeidah** - "You bound one, I bound seven"
5. **Eternal Perspective** - Focus on world to come

**Questions:**
- How could Chana encourage her children toward death?
- What does this teach about priorities in life?
- How do we apply this to our challenges (obviously much smaller)?

---

## Women's Role in Chanukah

**Themes:**
1. **Equal Obligation** - Women obligated in mitzvah
2. **Recognition** - Special customs commemorating women's role
3. **Stringency** - Women take on extra observance
4. **Historical Memory** - Keeping story alive through practice

**Questions:**
- Why are women's Chanukah customs stricter?
- What does this teach about women's spiritual power?
- How can we honor these heroines today?

---

## Universal Applications

**For Everyone:**
1. How far would you go for your community?
2. What role does faith play in courageous action?
3. How do we teach our children proper priorities?
4. What would we be willing to sacrifice for Judaism?
5. How do we maintain identity under pressure?

---

# Teaching This Material

## Class Structure Suggestions

**Opening (10 minutes):**
- Discussion questions
- Personal sharing about community responsibility

**Yehudit's Story (25 minutes):**
- Tell story dramatically
- Highlight key moments
- Draw out themes

**Women and Chanukah (10 minutes):**
- Present halachic sources
- Explain customs
- Connect to story

**Chana's Story (25 minutes):**
- Tell with sensitivity
- Emphasize spiritual heroism
- Mother's strength

**Closing Discussion (15 minutes):**
- Return to opening questions
- Personal applications
- Action items

---

## Key Takeaways

**For Participants:**

1. **Women's centrality** to Chanukah story and mitzvah
2. **Courage comes in many forms** - strategic, physical, spiritual
3. **Community responsibility** - willingness to sacrifice for klal
4. **Faith and action** - trust G-d and make a plan
5. **Legacy** - how we're remembered through customs and stories

**For Teachers:**

1. These stories inspire across generations
2. Women relate deeply to female heroines
3. Discussion questions make it personal
4. Halachic sources ground it in practice
5. Balance inspiration with practical application

---

## Additional Resources

**For Further Study:**
- Full Book of Judith (in Apocrypha)
- Talmudic passages on Chana's sons
- Chassidic discourses on women and Chanukah
- Historical context of Greek persecution
- Halachic details of women's Chanukah observance

**Discussion Prompts:**
- Modern parallels to these stories
- Women's leadership in Jewish history
- Mesiras nefesh (self-sacrifice) in contemporary life
- Teaching children about priorities
- Community vs. individual needs

---

**Bottom Line:**
These stories of Yehudit and Chana teach us that when the moment calls for extraordinary courage and sacrifice, Jewish women have always stepped forward. Their heroism is commemorated in our Chanukah customs, reminding us that miracles often come through unexpected channels, and that dedication to Torah and community can demand everything we have.


---
**End of Document 54**

# [Misc > For Writer > _5 Chanukah > General] Women of the Chanukah Story

## Women's Class Material

**Author:** [REDACTED-NAME], Leeds, UK
**Based on classes by:** [REDACTED-NAME]

**Note:** This file contains similar content to File 054 (Chanukah Heroines) and File 059 (Feminine Side of Chanukah). This version includes additional narrative framing and teaching approaches.

---

## Opening: The Wedding That Changed History

### The Dramatic Scene

**Setting:** Jerusalem, a prominent family wedding during Greek occupation

**The Event:**
- Hall was packed
- Wedding of daughter of one of Jerusalem's most prominent families
- Family: Leaders in quiet, non-violent rebellion against Greeks
- Respected and loved throughout Land of Israel
- Priests in the Temple, looked up to for generations

**The Shocking Moment:**
> "Amidst the elegant flowers, soft music, and the conversations of the guests, the bride suddenly stood up, walked to the center of the room, placed her hand on her chest, and tore open her gown."

---

### The Bride's Challenge

**Brothers' Reaction:**
- Shocked, angry, embarrassed
- Rose to drag her from room

**Her Words:**
> "You who are so zealous that you would kill me, are not zealous enough to protect me from the hands of the Greek governor who will come here to assault me tonight."

**Her Biblical Precedent:**
> "Did you not learn from Shimon and Levi, the brothers of Dinah, who, though only two men, killed the entire city of Shechem for her sake? Place your faith in the One Above, and He will help you."

**The Response:**
- Five brothers declared willingness to go to war
- Answered by voice from Holy of Holies promising victory

---

## Historical Context: The Greek Persecution

### Early Greek Rule

**Alexander the Great:**
- Initially treated Jews with greater respect than other conquered peoples
- Had seen High Priest Shimon the Righteous in a dream
- When Shimon met approaching army, Alexander knelt before him
- Pledged never to harm Jerusalem or Holy Temple

### The Deterioration

**After Alexander and Shimon:**
- Years passed, both leaders died
- Some Jews became infatuated with Greek culture
- The more they imitated Greeks, the less respect Greeks had for Jews
- Greeks began to mock Judaism and enact laws against it

---

### Escalating Persecution

**Phase 1: Synagogues and Schools**
- Greeks locked them up
- Jews' Response: Prayed and studied in homes

**Phase 2: Declaration Against G-d**
- Law: All Jews must write on livestock horns and doors that they had no portion in G-d of Israel
- Jews' Response: Sold livestock, removed doors from homes

**Phase 3: Circumcision Ban**
- Greeks outlawed brit milah
- Jews' Response: Made secret signs, announced ceremonies covertly, guests risked lives to attend

**Phase 4: Core Observances**
- Outlawed: Shabbat, New Moon celebration, Torah study
- Jews' Response: Hid in caves, continued observing all three

**Phase 5: Assault on Women**
- Greek soldiers started assaulting Jewish women
- Governor decreed jus primae noctis ("first night rights")
- Governor would kidnap and assault every bride on wedding night
- Common decree in ancient cultures, but devastating to Jewish sanctity

**The Breaking Point:**
> "And then the Jews went to war."

---

## Understanding the Victory

### Multiple Levels of Victory

**What We Celebrate:**
1. Victory of few over many
2. Victory of light over darkness
3. Victory of Jewish continuity
4. Defiance of all who sought to wipe out Judaism and Jewish history

### The Critical Role of Women

**The Pattern:**
> "The Jewish people—men and women—defied every Greek law with enormous self-sacrifice, yet it was largely by and for the sake of Jewish women that the Maccabees were led to declare war."

**The Decisive Moment:**
> "The decisive moment occurred when one Jewish woman looked her brothers in the eye and told them, 'You cannot let this happen to me.'"

**What the War Was For:**
- Holiness of Bet Hamikdash
- Holiness of Torah
- **Holiness of every human being**

---

## The Miracle We Commemorate

**Among Many Miracles:**
- Military victory
- Finding the oil
- Oil lasting eight days
- **AND:** Acknowledgment of every woman's sanctity and right to personal safety and dignity

> "It's a detail well worth remembering."

---

## Halachic Sources: Women's Obligation

### 1. Talmudic Statement

**Source:** Talmud Shabbat 23a

**Rabbi Yehoshua Ben Levi said:**
> "Women are obligated in the kindling of the Chanukah light, for they, too, were involved in that miracle."

---

### 2. Notable Exception

**Source:** Tosfot to Pesachim 29a

**Principle:**
> "Even though this is a positive commandment that is bound by time and women are generally exempt from performing such Mitzvot—even those that are of Rabbinic origin."

**Significance:** Women are obligated despite typical exemption from time-bound mitzvot

---

## Why Women Are Obligated: Three Reasons

### Reason 1: Specific Persecution

**The Decrees:**
- Greeks made many decrees against all Jews
- No kosher food, no Shabbos, no circumcision
- **But even more specifically targeted Jewish women**

**Jus Primae Noctis:**
> "The Greeks decreed that every Jewish bride would be violated on her wedding night by first submitting to the local Greek commander."

**The Salvation:**
> "So when the salvation and the miracles of Chanukah finally came about, it was a salvation for all Jews but the women in particular experienced a very personal freedom from being assaulted by the Greeks."

---

### Reason 2: Miracle Through a Woman - Yehudis

**The Hero:**
- Woman named Yehudis (Judith)
- Bravely killed Greek general Holofernes (Helifornus)
- Victory was turning point for Jews in battle against Greek army

**Why We Eat Dairy:**
> "Side note: This is why many have the custom of eating dairy foods on Chanukah."

---

### Reason 3: Matityahu's Daughter

**Another Woman:**
- Daughter of Matityahu (who led Jewish army to victory)
- Not as well known
- Had significant impact on victory and war

**Her Story:** (The wedding scene from the opening)

---

## Women's Deeper Connection

**Summary:**
> "Women thus have a stronger connection to Chanukah than the men since a) women were singled out in the Greek prosecution and b) since the miracle happened through her."

**The Attack:**
> "Through the violation of Jewish women, the Greeks were personally attacking the Jewish woman's purity and integrity."

**The Victory:**
> "Furthermore, the salvation came about through a woman and its victory is all the more meaningful for her."

---

## Halachic Expression of This Connection

### Women's Work Restriction

**General Rule:**
Work is permitted on Chanukah.

**Women's Custom:**
> "Code of Jewish Law tells us that women, however, follow the custom of refraining from work during the time the Chanukah candles are burning at home."

**Why Women Are More Strict:**
> "Women's refraining from work reflects their ability to absorb the spiritual light and holiness of the holiday, thus causing them to react in a similar manner as Shabbat and Yom Tov during which work is forbidden due to the immense degree of spirituality."

---

# The Stories in Detail

**(Detailed stories of Yehudit and Chana appear here - see File 054 for complete versions)**

**Note:** This document contains the same detailed stories as File 054 (Chanukah Heroines class). The stories of Yehudit and Chana appear here in similar detail. For the full annotated versions with discussion questions and teaching notes, see File 054.

---

## Key Story Elements Included

### Yehudit's Story
- Siege of Betulia by Holofernes
- Yehudit's challenge to town leaders
- Her dangerous mission to enemy camp
- Feeding Holofernes cheese and wine
- Beheading the general
- Surprise victory

### Chana's Story
- Antiochus's persecution
- Arrest of Chana and seven sons
- Each son's martyrdom
- Chana's encouragement to her children
- Her comparison to Akeidat Yitzchak
- Her own martyrdom

---

## Teaching This Material

### Class Structure

**Opening (10 min):**
- Dramatic wedding scene
- Sets emotional tone
- Establishes women's centrality

**Historical Context (15 min):**
- Greek persecution timeline
- Escalating oppression
- Jewish resistance
- Breaking point

**Halachic Discussion (10 min):**
- Women's obligation in mitzvah
- Reasons for obligation
- Work restriction custom

**Yehudit's Story (20 min):**
- Full narrative
- Heroism and strategy
- Turning point in war

**Chana's Story (20 min):**
- Ultimate self-sacrifice
- Mother's strength
- Spiritual courage

**Closing (10 min):**
- Women's role in miracles
- Modern applications
- Personal takeaways

---

## Key Themes

### For Discussion

1. **Women's Sanctity**
   - Personal safety and dignity
   - Central to war's purpose
   - Remembered in mitzvah

2. **Strategic Heroism**
   - Yehudit's calculated plan
   - Using enemy's weakness
   - Courage meets wisdom

3. **Spiritual Courage**
   - Chana's faith
   - Encouraging children
   - Eternal perspective

4. **Escalating Response**
   - Jews resisted each decree
   - Creative solutions
   - Final line: assault on women

5. **Holiness as Battleground**
   - Physical safety
   - Spiritual integrity
   - Identity preservation

---

## Modern Applications

### Questions for Participants

**Personal Sanctity:**
- How do we honor women's dignity today?
- What are modern threats to Jewish women's safety?
- How do we respond to assaults on our values?

**Courage:**
- When have you stood up for Jewish values?
- What risks are you willing to take?
- How do you encourage others?

**Strategy:**
- Can we be both wise and courageous?
- How do we choose our battles?
- When to resist, when to find creative solutions?

**Community:**
- What role do women play in our community?
- How do we support each other?
- Are we willing to fight for each other?

---

## Additional Teaching Resources

### Supplementary Materials

**Videos:**
- Animated versions of stories
- Rebbe's talks on women and Chanukah
- Contemporary women sharing stories

**Handouts:**
- Timeline of Greek persecution
- Halachic sources sheet
- Modern parallel situations
- Action items for participants

**Activities:**
- Role-play wedding scene
- Discuss creative resistance strategies
- Personal story sharing
- Commitment to action

---

## Closing Message

**Core Teaching:**
This is not just ancient history. The Chanukah story teaches us that:
1. Women's dignity is worth fighting for
2. Courage can come in many forms
3. One person can change history
4. Our obligations reflect our role in miracles
5. Spiritual light requires personal sacrifice

**Call to Action:**
How will YOU be a Yehudit in your life? What will you stand up for? Who will you protect? What Jewish values are worth fighting for?

**Remember:**
> "Among the many miracles we acknowledge and commemorate as we kindle the lights of the menorah, we also acknowledge the simple truth of every woman's sanctity and her right to personal safety and dignity. It's a detail well worth remembering."

---

## For Teachers

**This version works well for:**
- Women's circles
- Seminary classes
- Mother-daughter programs
- Larger community classes

**Strengths:**
- Dramatic opening engages immediately
- Historical progression is clear
- Halachic sources are accessible
- Stories are detailed but manageable
- Modern applications are implied throughout

**Teaching Tips:**
- Start with wedding scene - don't give away ending
- Let shock and emotion build
- Use timeline to show escalation
- Pause before revealing that women were breaking point
- Emphasize that this isn't just women's issue - it's everyone's
- End with personal challenge

**Time Management:**
- Full class: 90 minutes
- Short version: Focus on wedding scene, halachic sources, and one hero story (45 min)
- Multiple sessions: One session per major section

---

**Bottom Line:**
Women weren't just involved in the Chanukah miracle - they were central to it. The war began because of what was threatened, the victory came through women's courage, and our observance acknowledges their essential role. This isn't a side note to Chanukah - it's the heart of the story.

# [Misc > For Writer > _5 Chanukah > General] Chanukah Class - 8 Candles, 8 Lessons

## Eight Lessons from the Chanukah Lights

**Format:** Short, quotable lessons with explanations - perfect for brief divrei Torah or social media posts

---

## Lesson #1: Light Dispels Darkness

### The Core Principle

> "Darkness, no matter how ominous and intimidating, is not a thing or force: it is merely the absence of light. So light need not combat and overpower darkness in order to displace it -- where light is, darkness is not. A thimbleful of light will therefore banish a roomful of darkness."

### Application to Good and Evil

> "The same is true of good and evil: evil is not a thing or force, but merely the absence or concealment of good. One need not 'defeat' the evil in the world; one need only bring to light its inherent goodness."

---

### Supporting Quotes

**Eleanor Roosevelt:**
> "It is better to light a candle than curse the darkness."

**Mahatma Gandhi:**
> "Be the change you want to see in the world."

---

### Biblical Foundation

**Creation Story:**
> "Darkness was not a creation – Veha'aretz hayasoh uvavohu vechoshech al pnei sehom. And in the next posuk – Vayehi or."

**The Point:**
Darkness existed as default. Light was created. Light is active; darkness is passive. We don't fight darkness - we bring light.

---

### Practical Application

**Agricultural Metaphor:**
> "You only need one tiny seed - for a tall tree, with many fruits and seeds to grow."

**Takeaway:**
- Don't focus on combating evil
- Focus on bringing good
- One small act of kindness can multiply
- Start where you are with what you have

---

## Lesson #2: Never Be Satisfied - Keep Growing

### The Pattern of Adding

> "Each night of Chanukah we add a light. This teaches us that we must avoid self-satisfaction in spiritual matters. If we are given another day--it is to accomplish something positive we have not yet achieved."

---

### The $86,400 Parable

**The Game:**
Every morning, you get $86,400 deposited into your bank account for your use.

**Rule #1:**
Everything that you didn't spend is taken away at the end of the day. You can't transfer it or save it. It simply disappears.

**Rule #2:**
This game can end whenever; at any time it can say, the game is over. The account can close and you will not receive a new one.

**Rule #3:**
Tomorrow morning, another $86,400 will be deposited into your bank account.

---

### The Question

> "What would you personally do? You would buy anything and everything you wanted? Not only for yourself, but for all people you love? Even for people you don't know, because you couldn't possibly spend it all on yourself? You would try to spend every cent, and use it all?"

---

### The Revelation

**The Reality:**
> "Each morning we awaken to receive 86,400 seconds as a gift of life, and when we go to sleep at night, any remaining time is NOT credited to us. What we haven't lived up that day is forever lost. Yesterday is forever gone. Each morning the account is refilled, but the bank can dissolve your account at any time… without warning."

**The Challenge:**
> "So, what will YOU do with your 86,400 seconds? Aren't they worth so much more than the same amount in dollars? Enjoy every second of your life, because time races by so much quicker than you think. So take care of yourself, be happy, love deeply, and enjoy life."

---

## Lesson #3: Share Your Light - Don't Be Spiritually Selfish

### Placement of Menorah

> "We kindle the Chanukah lights by a door or a window--exits to our home. It is not enough to light up our own lives; we must share what we know to be good with others. Spiritual selfishness is the worst kind of all."

---

### Temple Windows

**Design Detail:**
Menorah in the Temple - windows illuminating outward.

**Unlike regular windows:**
- Most ancient buildings: windows narrow outward (for defense, light comes IN)
- Temple windows: narrow inward, wide outward (light goes OUT)
- Pirsumei nisa - publicizing the miracle

---

### The Tzaddik in the Pelz

**Yiddish Story:**
A righteous man (tzaddik) sits in his warm fur coat (pelz) complaining about how cold it is in the synagogue.

**Rabbi's Response:**
Instead of wearing a coat to keep yourself warm, why not create a fire that warms everyone?

**Lesson:**
Don't just insulate yourself - create warmth that others can share.

---

## Lesson #4: Address Your Own Darkness First

### Timing of Lighting

> "We kindle the Chanukah lights only when it becomes dark in our spot of the globe. We must devote our efforts to the particular darkness we see in our lives and communities. If there is a darkness in our 'place,' there is where we must bring our light."

---

### The Challenge of Distance

**Easy vs. Hard:**
> "Sometimes it is easier to support a cause far away – hunger in Africa, etc than the homeless man in the corner. It is easier to address problems and issues that you are not involved in."

**The Priority:**
> "Aniyay ircha kodmim. Help those around you, your own family, your neighbor, etc."

**Translation:** The poor of your city come first.

---

### Why Distance is Easier

- Less personal involvement
- No ongoing relationship required
- No need to confront your own discomfort
- Can feel good without getting messy
- One-time donation vs. ongoing commitment

**The Torah Way:**
Deal with the darkness in your own sphere first. Your family, your neighbors, your community.

---

## Lesson #5: Body, Soul, and Torah Working Together

### The Foundation

**Proverbs 20:27:**
> "The soul of man is a lamp of G-d."

**The Principle:**
> "Man is a complex conglomeration of heaven and earth, spirit and matter, fire and wick."

---

### Three Elements of the Lamp

**Like the lamp, man has three elements:**

1. **The Wick** = Body
2. **The Flame** = Soul
3. **The Oil** = Torah

---

### The Soul (Flame)

**Character:**
> "His soul, like the flame, is aflame with yearning and inspiration. It burns brightly within him, inspiring him to connect to his Creator. It desires fiercely to break the bonds of this physical world, to transcend the barriers of a material existence and unite with its Maker."

**Movement:**
- Flames always reach upward
- Wants to break free from physical
- Yearns to unite with Source
- BUT: also falls back down to illuminate this world

**Purpose:**
> "When allowed full expression, the soul encourages man to seek spiritual pursuits, to almost tear itself free from the gravity of physical reality that grounds it. Yet, like the flame of the candle, after the soul performs its celestial dance it also falls back, returning to illuminate this world and leave its mark on physical reality."

**The Paradox:**
> "By cleaving to the ultimate Source, the soul would be encompassed within it. Only as it exists within a seemingly distinct being can the soul accomplish the very purpose of its descent."

---

### The Body (Wick)

**Character:**
> "The body of man, like the wick of the candle, is both grounded and physical. With its many limitations, many real needs and desires, the body entraps and enslaves the soul within it."

**But Also Enables:**
> "Yet, while imposing its restrictions, the body also houses the soul and provides an outlet for its unique expression. The soul can only feel, perceive and savor reality through the body's senses; it can only move about freely with the body's limbs; and it can only think and analyze with the body's mind. The body's very groundedness, then, provides a means and opportunity for the soul's relationship with creation."

**The Necessity:**
Without a wick, the flame cannot exist in this world. Without a body, the soul cannot accomplish its mission.

---

### The Torah (Oil)

**Character:**
> "Torah, like the oil of the lamp, is the source for man's ideals, providing the direction for a meaningful life that connects him with his Creator. Mitzvot ignite man's potential, showing him in a concrete way how to utilize his abilities and talents for a G-dly end."

**Qualities:**
> "Enlightening, pure and clear, like the oil, the Torah and its mitzvot direct the potential in man to its ultimate purpose."

---

### Becoming a Lamp of G-d

**Ecclesiastes 3:21:**
> "The spirit of man gravitates upward."

**The Formula:**
> "When man is true to the yearnings of his soul, directs them with the wisdom and enlightenment of Torah, puts them into practice by fulfilling the mitzvot with the faculties and limbs of his body, he generates light and becomes 'a lamp of G-d.'"

**All Three Required:**
- Soul provides yearning
- Torah provides direction
- Body provides action
- Together: Light

---

## Lesson #6: Float Above, Permeate Within (Like Oil)

### Oil's Paradox

> "Oil is a strange substance with two very opposite properties. On one hand, it always floats to the top. No matter how hard you try, it just won't mix with other liquids. Yet, at the same time, when oil goes somewhere, it goes all the way through. It's this sort of saturation that makes oil-based stains so tough to remove. So it both floats above and permeates within. Go figure!"

---

### Jews Are Like Oil

**Property #1: We Float Above (Stay Distinct)**

> "On one hand, we are quite different from those around us. We must treasure our distinct identity, being proud to look and act like Jews do. We are the ancient tribe that never assimilated, that's here today just as we were three and a half thousand years ago."

**Gentile Perspective:**
> "And how do others view this? Look for yourself: Gentiles respect Jews who respect themselves--and are embarrassed of Jews who are embarrassed of themselves."

**The Lesson:**
Maintain Jewish identity proudly. Don't blend in to the point of disappearing.

---

**Property #2: We Permeate Within (Spread Influence)**

> "Yet at the same time, we mix freely among the peoples of the world. You'd think a tribe like ours would stick to Israel and parts of Brooklyn. But that just isn't so. For the Jews are 'a light onto nations.' We are all ambassadors of G-d sent here on a mission to bring holiness and goodness to all those around us. We are role models whose good deeds are to rub off upon others."

**The Balance:**
- Distinct identity (oil floats)
- Widespread influence (oil permeates)
- Both simultaneously

---

### The Process: Squeezing the Olive

**To Produce Oil:**
> "Additionally, in order to produce oil, you have to squeeze the olive. Sometimes challenges and obstacles bring forth strength, and causes one to shine."

**Application:**
- Pressure reveals essence
- Hardship brings out best
- Challenges = opportunities for growth
- Your brightest light may come from your hardest times

---

## Lesson #7: Sharing Doesn't Diminish You

### The Principle

**Buddha Quote:**
> "Thousands of candles can be lit from a single one, and its life will not be shortened. Happiness never decreases by being shared."

---

### What This Applies To

**Not Just Candles:**
- Knowledge
- Acts of kindness
- Wisdom
- Love
- Joy
- Inspiration
- Teaching
- Support

**The Paradox:**
> "Not only do they not take anything away from you, you get so much from it. To give is to get."

---

### Examples

**Knowledge:**
When you teach someone, you don't lose what you know. In fact, teaching deepens your own understanding.

**Kindness:**
Helping others doesn't deplete your capacity for goodness. It increases it.

**Happiness:**
Sharing joy with others multiplies rather than divides it.

**The Formula:**
- Material goods: Giving = having less
- Spiritual goods: Giving = having more

---

## Lesson #8: Light a Candle for the Children

### The Song

**Benny Friedman:**
> "Light a candle for the Maccabee children, whose right to exist was denied."

---

### The Dedication

**Remember:**
- Those who fought for our right to be Jewish
- Those who died for our ability to practice
- Those who refused to assimilate
- Those who kept the flame alive

**Our Responsibility:**
- Keep their legacy burning
- Pass it to next generation
- Never take our freedom for granted
- Light candles for our own children's future

---

## Using These Lessons

### Class Formats

**One Night, Eight Lessons:**
- 5-7 minutes per lesson
- Go through all eight in one class
- Print as handout
- Great for community event

**Eight Classes:**
- One lesson per session
- Deep dive into each topic
- Discussion and personal applications
- Perfect for weekly series

**Social Media Series:**
- One post per night of Chanukah
- Pair lesson with that night's candle
- Include quote and short explanation
- Encourage shares and comments

**Family Discussion:**
- One lesson per night at menorah lighting
- Age-appropriate examples
- Personal stories
- What does this mean for us?

---

### Key Takeaways

1. **Don't fight darkness - bring light**
2. **Never stop growing - add every day**
3. **Share your light - illuminate others**
4. **Fix your own world first**
5. **Body, soul, Torah - all working together**
6. **Be distinct yet influential**
7. **Giving multiplies your own light**
8. **Remember those who kept the flame alive**

---

## For Teachers

**Strengths of This Material:**
- Short, punchy lessons
- Memorable quotes
- Diverse sources (Torah, Eleanor Roosevelt, Buddha, Gandhi)
- Multiple applications
- Works for all ages
- Flexible format

**How to Adapt:**
- Add personal stories to each lesson
- Include interactive elements
- Relate to current events
- Create visual aids
- Develop discussion questions
- Assign action items

**Perfect For:**
- Quick divrei Torah
- Family programs
- Youth groups
- Social media content
- Newsletter articles
- Before menorah lighting

---

**Bottom Line:**
Eight simple but profound lessons that transform Chanukah from historical event to personal guide for living with light, growth, generosity, and purpose.

## Class Outline with Rebbe Story

**Note:** Document appears incomplete - contains opening sections and discussion framework

## Opening Story: The Rebbe and Jewish Prisoners

**Context:** Story about the Rebbe ensuring Jewish prisoners in South Africa could light the menorah

**Theme:** No Jew should be left in darkness, no matter where they are or what their circumstances

**(Full story details not included in source document)**

---

## Night #1: The Right to Believe in G-d

### The Core Question

**What We're Fighting For:**
> "Fight for G-dliness, the right to believe in things that can be felt even if they can't be seen, touched or heard."

---

### The Modern Challenge

**The Question Everyone Asks:**
> "So what would you answer when asked- Why G-d? Why Judaism? Why can't I just be a good person?"

**Why This is Valid:**
> "Now more than ever, it's such a valid question to ask. Our kids can volunteer in so many organizations, we can marry good respectful people, be a fair boss, align ourselves politically with people who fight for the rights of others- so who needs G-d in all of that?"

---

**Discussion Prompt:**
> "Go around and gather answers"

---

### Historical Context: The Greek Challenge

**Before the Greeks:**
> "For many years Jews more enlightened than society around them, suddenly pops up this cultured learned, body caring for/ worshiping, clean people known as the Greeks and Hellenistic culture and the confusion and temptation sets in. Until now there really wasn't much of an appealing choice."

**The New Temptation:**
For many years, Hellenism offered:
- The Olympics
- Greek Gods
- Worship of intellect
- Worship of the body
- Culture and sophistication

**Initially Free Choice:**
> "For many years Hellenism, the Olympics, Greek Gods, the intellect, the worship of the body etc was simply laid out in front of the Jews in a tempting way but you had free choice to do what you want. And many Jews did assimilate."

---

### The Turning Point: Forced Assimilation

**After Years of Temptation:**
> "After quite some years of the Greek culture laid out temptingly before the Jews but not forced upon them finally king Antiochus put his foot down and forced obedience."

**The Decrees:**
- No more kosher
- No more brit milah
- No Shabbos
- Otherwise you would die

**The Pattern:**
> "Specifically the laws that we do because Hashem said so, not because they made sense to Greek culture."

---

### The Stories of Resistance

**Mentioned:**
1. **Chana and her seven sons** - Ultimate martyrdom
2. **Yehudis** - Strategic victory
3. **Maccabees formed** - Military resistance

**The Victory:**
Jews won, came to rededicate the temple.

---

## The Oil: Why That's the Focus

### The Discovery

**The Situation:**
> "While there was LOTS of oil to be found, But it was the pure oil with the seal of the high priest that was not, Until G-d miraculously had them find it and then had it burn for 8 days when there was enough for 1."

---

### How the Talmud Summarizes Chanukah

**Talmud, Shabbat 21b:**
> "What is Chanukah? ... When the Greeks entered the Sanctuary, they contaminated all its oil. Then, when the royal Hashmonean family overpowered and was victorious over [the Greeks], they searched and found only a single cruse of pure oil that was sealed with the seal of the kohen gadol (high priest)-enough to light the menorah for a single day. A miracle occurred, and they lit the menorah with this oil for eight days. The following year, they established these [eight days] as days of festivity and praise and thanksgiving for G-d."

---

### The Puzzling Focus

**Wait, What?**
> "Wait, that's chanukah?? Not the fact this group of kohanim, Maccabees won against the most sophisticated army in the world?! Not that Yehudis, a women single handedly shut down one of the fiercest generals and the war took a tremendous positive turn?"

**The Question:**
> "Chanukah is about the oil??? Note that the focus of our celebration is all about oil- menorah, latkes. True we mention the military victory in Chanukah prayers, but still. It totally takes a back seat. Why? Why Was the fight and the victory mainly about oil?"

---

## What the Greeks Had Against Us

### Not Physical Destruction

**The Greek Approach:**
> "The Greeks did not endeavor to physically destroy the Jewish people, or even to deprive them of their religion and way of life; they merely wished to Hellenize them -- to enlighten their lives with the culture and philosophy of Greece."

**Their Message:**
> "Keep your books of wisdom, they said to the Jew, keep your laws and customs, but enrich them with our wisdom, adorn them with our art, blend them into our lifestyle."

**The Offer:**
- Worship your G-d in your temple
- But also worship the human body in the sports stadium we'll build
- Study your Torah
- But integrate it with principles of our philosophy and aesthetics of our literature

**The Evolution:**
> "Eventually, It led to our lives being in danger so we had to fight back but for many years they only had issue with what oil represents- the little cruise of G-dliness within each of us – the spiritual flame that flickers, the G-d given aspect of Torah."

---

### What They Accepted vs. Rejected

**The Greeks Were Fine With:**
- Don't murder ✓
- Honor your parents ✓
- Day of rest ✓

**The Greeks Opposed:**
> "So laws like don't murder, honor your parents. No prob. Even having a day of rest worked for the Greeks. But why be s..."

**(Document appears incomplete here)**

---

### The Real Battle: The Spark of G-dliness

**What Oil Represents:**
> "The little cruise of G-dliness within each of us – the spiritual flame that flickers, the G-d given aspect of Torah."

**Why This Matters:**
The Greeks wanted to extinguish:
- The inexplicable
- The beyond-reason
- The purely G-dly
- The choiceless connection
- The soul's essence

**This is Why Oil is the Focus:**
- Oil = pure G-dliness
- Sealed oil = untouched by contamination
- One cruse = enough for Jewish identity to survive
- Eight days = beyond natural (seven is natural cycle)
- The miracle wasn't just military - it was spiritual preservation

---

## Discussion Framework

### For Class Use

**Opening Questions:**
1. Why G-d? (Go around the room)
2. Can't I just be a good person without religion?
3. What makes Judaism different from ethics?

**Historical Progression:**
1. Jews as light in primitive world
2. Greeks as first sophisticated alternative
3. Temptation of free choice
4. Forced compliance
5. Resistance and victory

**The Oil Question:**
1. Why focus on oil miracle?
2. What does oil represent?
3. What were Greeks really after?
4. Why does that matter today?

**Personal Application:**
1. What's your "oil"?
2. What tries to contaminate it?
3. How do you keep it pure?
4. Where's your one sealed cruse?

---

## For Teachers

**This Outline Works For:**
- Adult education
- Teen discussions
- University Hillel
- Professional groups
- Interfaith dialogue preparation
- Anyone questioning "why Judaism?"

**Strengths:**
- Addresses modern skepticism
- Historical progression clear
- Oil symbolism explained
- Greeks as sophisticated (not primitive) enemy
- Focuses on ideas, not just events

**How to Complete:**
Document appears to cut off mid-thought. Teachers should:
1. Expand on "why be s..." question
2. Complete analysis of rational vs. supra-rational commandments
3. Develop modern parallels (secular humanism, ethical culture movements)
4. Add personal stories
5. Create action items

**Key Point to Develop:**
Greeks opposed specifically chukim (supra-rational commandments) because these represent pure G-dliness beyond human comprehension. That's why oil matters - it represents the inexplicable, essential connection to G-d that can't be rationalized or compromised.

---

## Additional Sections to Add

### The Rebbe Story
- Full narrative of South Africa prisoners
- How Rebbe ensured menorah lighting
- Message about reaching every Jew
- No one left in darkness

### Modern Greek Culture
- Secular humanism
- "Spiritual but not religious"
- Ethics without G-d
- Can we be good without religion?
- The limits of rationalism

### The Eight Nights
- Continue framework for other 7 nights
- One theme per night
- Build on oil symbolism
- Progressive deepening

### Practical Applications
- How to answer "why G-d" question
- Discussing religion with skeptics
- Finding your pure oil
- Keeping spiritual flame alive

---

**Bottom Line:**
The battle wasn't just political or military - it was philosophical and spiritual. Greeks wanted to remove the G-dly essence from Judaism, keeping only what made rational sense. The oil represents our refusal to compromise on the inexplicable, essential, supra-rational connection to G-d. That's why we celebrate the oil.

# [Misc > For Writer > _5 Chanukah > General] The Feminine Side of Chanukah

## Chabad Women's Circle - Winter Wellness

**Note:** This document covers similar content to Files 054 and 056 (Chanukah Heroines and Women of Chanukah Story) but in condensed format - perfect for shorter classes or handouts.

---

## Women's Obligation in Chanukah

### 1. The Talmudic Source

**Talmud Shabbat 23a:**
> "Rabbi Yehoshua Ben Levi said; Women are obligated in the kindling of the Chanukah light, for they, too, were involved in that miracle."

---

### 2. The Exceptional Nature

**Tosfot to Pesachim 29a:**
> "Even though this is a positive commandment that is bound by time and women are generally exempt from performing such Mitzvot-even those that are of Rabbinic origin."

**Significance:**
This obligation is unusual - women are typically exempt from time-bound mitzvot, yet here they are obligated.

---

## Why Are Women Obligated?

### Reason #1: Women Were Specifically Targeted

**The Greek Decrees:**
- Many decrees against all Jews:
  - No Kosher
  - No Shabbos
  - No Circumcision
- **But even more specifically targeted Jewish women**

**The Jus Primae Noctis Decree:**
> "The Greeks decreed that every Jewish bride would be violated on her wedding night by first submitting to the local Greek commander."

**The Salvation:**
> "So when the salvation and the miracles of Chanukah finally came about, it was a salvation for all Jews but the women in particular experienced a very personal freedom from being assaulted by the Greeks."

---

### Reason #2: The Miracle Happened Through a Woman

**Yehudis's Story:**

**Who She Was:**
- Daughter of Yochanan the Kohain Gadol (High Priest)
- Extremely beautiful

**What She Did:**
1. Greek general greatly desired her
2. She pretended to give herself to him
3. Fed him cheese dishes until he became very thirsty
4. Gave him wine to quench his thirst
5. He drank until drunk and fell asleep
6. She beheaded him
7. Brought his head to Jerusalem
8. Enemy commanders saw what happened, got scared, and fled

**The Impact:**
> "This victory was the turning point for the Jews in the battle against the Greek army."

**Side Note:**
> "(Side note: This is why many have the custom of eating dairy foods on Chanukah.)"

---

### Reason #3: Another Heroine - Matityahu's Daughter

**The Story:**

**The Wedding:**
At her own wedding, she ripped off her gown.

**Brothers' Reaction:**
- Macabees completely embarrassed
- Became outraged
- Wanted to kill her for immodesty

**Her Challenge:**
> "She then reprimanded them by asking them why they were so zealous that they would kill her for violating her modesty, yet they weren't so zealous enough to protect her from the hands of the governor who would come to assault and violate her that same night."

**The Result:**
> "Her words were what aroused the 5 brothers to go to war and to battle the Greeks."

**Source:** Midrash Maaseh Chanukah, Otzar Meforshim Vol.1

---

### Additional Heroism: Women During Circumcisions

**The Context:**
Circumcision was outlawed under penalty of death. Many men fled into hiding.

**What the Women Did:**
> "If a child was born to the wife of one of those who had fled into hiding, the mother would circumcise the child on the 8th day. She would go upon the wall of Jerusalem carrying her child. She would hurl herself and her child from the wall-thereby saying to her husband, and all her brothers who had gone into hiding to escape the war:"

**Her Message:**
> "If you will not go out to wage war against your enemies, you will have neither children nor wives, and your end will be total annihilation. We will observe what is holy to us, not in hiding, but publicly, before the eyes of all. If you intend to save us, emerge from your caves, and wage war against the enemy till you destroy him. G-d will be with you!"

**The Response:**
> "Thereupon Matityahu and his 5 sons arose like lions."

---

## Women's Deeper Connection to Chanukah

### The Summary

> "Women thus have a stronger connection to Chanukah than the men since a) women were singled out in the Greek prosecution and b) since the miracle happened through her."

---

### The Personal Nature of the Victory

**The Attack:**
> "Through the violation of Jewish women, the Greeks were personally attacking the Jewish woman's purity and integrity."

**The Victory:**
> "Furthermore, the salvation came about through a woman and its victory is all the more meaningful for her."

---

## Halachic Expression of Women's Connection

### Women's Custom Regarding Work

**General Rule:**
> "Work is permitted on Chanukah."

**Women's Exception:**
> "Women, however, follow the custom of refraining from work during the time the Chanukah candles are burning at home. (They should continue this custom) without any leniency."

**Source:** Code of Jewish Law

---

### Why Women Are More Stringent

**The Explanation:**
> "Women's refraining from work reflects their ability to absorb the spiritual light and holiness of the holiday, thus causing them to react in a similar manner as Shabbat and Yom Tov during which work is forbidden due to the immense degree of spirituality."

**The Implication:**
Women's souls are so attuned to the spiritual light of Chanukah that they naturally respond as if it were Shabbat or Yom Tov.

---

## Life's Lessons

### The Pattern of Jewish History

**The Principle:**
> "Women are the heroines of each of the major holidays. They were the ones to take action and bring about salvation for the entire Jewish People."

**Examples:**
- **Pesach:** Miriam, Yocheved, Serach bat Asher, midwives
- **Purim:** Esther
- **Chanukah:** Yehudis, Matityahu's daughter, circumcising mothers

---

### Our Responsibility

**The Challenge:**
> "We must follow their lead and do the same!"

**What This Means:**
1. Take initiative (don't wait for others)
2. Act courageously (even when it's risky)
3. Prioritize holiness (over comfort or safety)
4. Challenge men to rise to occasion (when necessary)
5. Bring salvation (be the change-maker)

---

## Discussion Questions

### For Women's Groups

**Personal Heroism:**
- When have you had to stand up for Jewish values?
- What risks have you taken for Judaism?
- Where do you find courage?

**Modern Applications:**
- What are today's threats to women's sanctity?
- How do we respond to cultural pressure?
- When should we challenge our community?

**Spiritual Connection:**
- Do you feel the spiritual intensity of Chanukah?
- How do you honor the work restriction custom?
- What does women's special role mean to you?

**Legacy:**
- What are you passing to your daughters?
- How do you teach about these heroines?
- What Jewish battles are worth fighting today?

---

## Using This Material

### Ideal Formats

**Short Class (30 minutes):**
- Three reasons for obligation
- Brief story summaries
- Work restriction custom
- Personal application

**Medium Class (60 minutes):**
- Full obligation discussion
- Detailed hero stories
- Halachic analysis
- Group discussion

**Series (3 sessions):**
1. **Session 1:** Halachic sources and reasons
2. **Session 2:** Hero stories in detail
3. **Session 3:** Modern applications and personal commitments

---

### Handout Format

**One-Page Version:**
- Talmudic source
- Three reasons (brief)
- Work restriction
- One quote from each heroine
- Life lesson
- Personal reflection question

**Multi-Page Version:**
- Full content as provided
- Discussion questions
- Additional sources
- Timeline of events
- Comparison chart (women's roles in different holidays)

---

## Key Talking Points

### For Presenters

**Opening:**
"Chanukah isn't just about the Maccabees. In fact, the war might never have happened without the courage of Jewish women."

**Middle:**
"Three types of women shaped this victory: those who were victims of persecution, those who took offensive action, and those who challenged men to fight."

**Closing:**
"Jewish history repeats this pattern: women as catalysts for redemption. That's not ancient history - it's our job description."

---

## Additional Resources

### For Further Study

**Sources to Explore:**
- Full Book of Judith (Apocrypha)
- Midrash Maaseh Chanukah
- Chassidic discourses on women and Chanukah
- Responsa on women's work restriction

**Related Topics:**
- Women's role in Exodus
- Esther and Purim
- Devorah and Yael
- Modern women leaders in Jewish life

---

## Practical Applications

### Action Items for Participants

**This Chanukah:**
1. Honor work restriction (or try it)
2. Share these stories with daughters
3. Light menorah with intention for women's role
4. Stand up for Jewish values in one situation
5. Challenge yourself to be courageous

**Long-Term:**
1. Study women's roles in Jewish history
2. Mentor younger women
3. Speak up in your community
4. Don't wait for others to act
5. Be the heroine of your own story

---

## For Teachers

**This Version is Perfect For:**
- Women's circles
- Mother-daughter programs
- Bat mitzvah prep
- Seminary classes
- Brief divrei Torah

**Strengths:**
- Concise but complete
- Multiple heroines
- Clear halachic connection
- Practical applications
- Empowering message

**How to Expand:**
- Add personal stories
- Include modern examples
- Develop discussion questions
- Create visual aids
- Provide source sheets

**Time Management:**
- Core content: 20 minutes
- With discussion: 45 minutes
- Full exploration: 90 minutes

---

**Bottom Line:**
Women weren't just present at the Chanukah miracle - they were the catalysts. They were specifically targeted, they took decisive action, and they challenged men to fight. Our obligation to light the menorah isn't honorary - it's recognition that we're the heroines of this story. And we're called to continue that legacy today.


---
**End of Document 58**

# [Misc > For Writer > _5 Chanukah > General] Yehudis Speech for Women's Event

## Sample Speech for Chanukah Women's Program

**Format:** Complete speech ready to deliver at women's Chanukah event

**Length:** Approximately 8-10 minutes

**Tone:** Warm, inclusive, inspiring

---

## Opening: Welcome and Joke

### The Greeting

> "Good evening everyone! If you can please find your seat, we'd love to start. Before I get started, I would like to stress a tremendous Thank You to …Thank you all for making this evening possible, and for giving the women in our community a time to learn, socialize, say a little l'chaim and get in to the Chanukah spirit!"

**[Insert names of sponsors, volunteers, organizers]**

---

### The Chanukah Stamp Joke

**Setup:**
> "Y'know, they tell a story… A woman goes to the post office to buy stamps for her Chanukah cards. She says to the clerk 'May I have 50 Chanukah stamps please.'"

**Punchline:**
> "'What denomination?' asks the clerk.
>
> The woman says 'Oy vey...my god, has it come to this?
> Okay, give me 6 orthodox, 12 conservative and 32 reform!'"

---

### The Message of Unity

> "Well, friends, I am proud that here in Chabad there are no labels. What matters is that we're Jewish, we're sisters, and we're celebrating Chanukah together."

---

## Body: The Greek Threat

### Transition

> "So, I'd like to share a thought on Chanukah. **PAUSE…**"

---

### Not Like Other Enemies

**The Distinction:**
> "The Greeks of the Chanukah story were not like the Nazis or the Arab terrorists, who go after Jewish blood just for the sake of killing Jews. The Greeks didn't actually want to kill the Jews."

**Their Offer:**
> "They came to the Jews with one request: become like us, so we can all live happily ever after..."

---

### The Greek Mindset

**Their Logic:**
> "And the Greeks thought the Jews would agree to become more like them! They figured, who in their right mind wouldn't want to join the wave of the future, and give up this musty, old-fashioned religion called Judaism?"

**Their Questions:**
- What did the Jews have against philosophy anyway?
- Or gladiators?
- Or idols?
- Or other things from Greek culture?
- Why would any enlightened human being have anything against progress?

---

### The Enforcement

**The Decrees:**
> "To accomplish this, the Greeks outlawed the observance of Shabbat, and circumcision, and Torah study."

---

### The Tragic Success

**Most Jews Assimilated:**
> "And, the Greeks weren't totally wrong. Most Jews were sucked in by the Greeks. These Jews started dressing like Greeks, thinking like Greeks and praying like Greeks. Within a generation or two, the descendants of these assimilated Jews were no longer members of the Jewish people."

---

## The Heroes

### The Maccabees

**Who They Were:**
> "The heroes of the Chanukah story, the Maccabees, were different. This was a single family that refused to give in. This family dared to take on the whole Syrian-Greek empire on behalf of the few Jews who courageously remained loyal to the Jewish tradition. They were led, of course, by Judah the Maccabee."

---

### The Forgotten Heroine

**The Introduction:**
> "But did you know that Judah the Maccabee had an aunt? A lone Maccabee-ette. She was a young widow named Yehudis, and she was as wise and pious as she was beautiful."

---

## Yehudis's Story

### The Siege

**The Situation:**
> "Yehudit lived in a village that bravely refused to give up the Torah and assimilate in order to live happily ever after. In response, the Greeks laid siege to the village, cutting off their food and water supply, until its residents were starving and dying of thirst. Reluctantly, the village leaders decided to submit to the Greek demands."

---

### One Woman's Courage

**Her Decision:**
> "But one brave woman felt otherwise. Yehudit dressed up in her most beautiful gown, put on her fanciest jewelry and her most expensive perfume, and risked her life as she set out for the military camp of the evil Greek governor, Holofernes."

**The Meeting:**
> "The governor noticed the beautiful Jewish woman and invited her for a private audience in his tent."

---

### The Victory

**Her Plan:**
> "Yehudit got the governor so drunk that he fell asleep. Instead of the romantic encounter Holofernes had counted on, Yehudit used the general's sword to behead him as he slept, setting the stage for a surprise military victory for the loyal Jews of her village."

---

## The Lesson

### Transition

> "**[Pause]**"

---

### What We Learn

**The Core Message:**
> "We can learn many lessons from Yehudit's story, but most importantly, this brave Jewish woman teaches us that being a good Jew is something that often requires courage and self-sacrifice."

---

### Modern Context

**Personal Reflection:**
> "The story of Yehudis reminds me, personally, that it is one thing to be a Jew in a place like Jerusalem, or Brooklyn, where there are three synagogues on your block and dozens of kosher restaurants within smelling distance. But it is quite another thing to be a Jew practicing his or her religion in a place where Judaism is considered exotic at best, and musty and old-fashioned at worst."

---

### Our Special Opportunity

**The Challenge:**
> "But, it is specifically in these places that we have a special opportunity to live up to Yehudit's legacy, and to bring the special light of Chanukah into the world. **PAUSE..**"

---

## Modern-Day Yehudits

### The Office

> "The Jew who raises questions when she turns down a slice of her coworker's famous baked ham at her office's annual X-mas party… **SHE is a modern-day Yehudit.**"

---

### The Window

> "The Jewish woman who raises eyebrows by putting a menorah in her window when all her friends have flickering lights outside their windows… **SHE is a modern-day Yehudit.**"

---

### The Classroom

> "The Jew who raises awareness by giving a presentation on Chanukah to children of diverse backgrounds in her son's first-grade classroom… **is a modern-day Yehudit.**"

---

### The Home

> "Or the mother who sits her children down, and patiently explains to them that they should be proud to be the only kids in their class without an x-mas tree, and that they are part of a nation that for 2000 years were willing to sacrifice their lives for their beliefs… **She is a modern-day Yehudit.**"

---

## Closing Story

### The College Menorah

**A Friend's Experience:**
> "A friend once shared with me that when she was a freshman in college, she walked by the 30-foot X-mas tree in the Student Union every day. Then, one day, she noticed a small paper menorah that one brave Jewish student hung up beside it."

---

### The Impact

**The Revelation:**
> "To this day, she said, I have no idea who that student was. But I can tell you one thing for sure. **That student's name was Yehudit.**"

---

## Final Words

> "Thank you, and happy Chanukah!"

---

## Speaker Notes

### Delivery Tips

**Pacing:**
- Start warm and welcoming
- Joke should be light and relatable
- Historical section: more serious tone
- Yehudis story: dramatic build-up
- Modern applications: personal and intimate
- College story: slow down, let it land
- Final line: pause before delivering

**Emphasis:**
- "SHE is a modern-day Yehudit" - strong emphasis each time
- Pauses matter - don't rush
- Make eye contact during modern examples
- Personal touch when talking about children

---

### Customization Points

**Personalize:**
- Add local sponsors' names in opening
- Include specific examples from your community
- Reference your own experiences
- Adapt X-mas party example to local context
- Add your own "modern Yehudit" examples

**Expand If Needed:**
- More details on Greek philosophy vs. Torah
- Explain why Greeks opposed specifically chukkim
- Add more about Yehudis's character
- Include other Chanukah heroines
- Develop cheese-eating custom

**Shorten If Needed:**
- Skip or simplify the joke
- Condense Greek context
- Reduce number of modern examples
- Go straight from story to lesson

---

### Audience Adaptation

**For Younger Women:**
- Add social media examples
- Discuss peer pressure
- Reference college experiences
- Talk about dating challenges

**For Mothers:**
- Emphasize parenting examples
- Discuss school challenges
- Talk about family traditions
- Share parenting tips

**For Mixed Group:**
- Keep examples broad
- Include workplace scenarios
- Discuss community involvement
- Appeal to multiple life stages

**For Senior Women:**
- Reference longer perspective
- Discuss grandparenting
- Talk about changing times
- Honor their own courage

---

## Follow-Up Materials

### Handout Suggestions

**Include:**
- Yehudis story summary
- "Modern Yehudit" checklist
- Discussion questions
- Additional resources
- Contact information

**Design:**
- Attractive formatting
- Menorah graphics
- Quote boxes
- Space for notes

---

### Discussion Questions (If Time Allows)

1. When have you been a "modern Yehudit"?
2. What Jewish practice is hardest for you to maintain?
3. Where do you face pressure to assimilate?
4. How do you explain Judaism to non-Jewish friends?
5. What would you be willing to sacrifice for?

---

### Action Items

**Challenge Participants:**
- Light menorah in visible window
- Share Chanukah with non-Jewish friend
- Teach children one hero story
- Stand up for Jewish values once this week
- Be courageous in one small way

---

## Why This Speech Works

### Structure

**Classic Three-Part:**
1. **Opening:** Warm welcome, humor, unity message
2. **Body:** Historical context, hero story, lesson
3. **Closing:** Modern applications, inspirational ending

**Emotional Arc:**
- Start light (joke)
- Build seriousness (Greek threat)
- Peak drama (Yehudis story)
- Personal application (modern examples)
- Inspiring ending (college story)

---

### Content

**Accessible:**
- Not too academic
- Personal and relatable
- Clear takeaway message
- Actionable examples

**Inclusive:**
- "No labels" message
- Multiple life stage examples
- Everyone can be a Yehudit
- Small acts count

**Inspiring:**
- Heroic story
- Relatable applications
- Empowering message
- Clear call to action

---

### Delivery

**Conversational:**
- "Y'know, they tell a story"
- "A friend once shared with me"
- Personal pronouns
- Natural flow

**Engaging:**
- Question format
- Pauses for impact
- Repetition ("SHE is a modern-day Yehudit")
- Story within story

**Memorable:**
- Opening joke
- Dramatic climax (beheading)
- Repeated phrase
- Final revelation

---

## Variations

### Shorter Version (5 minutes)

- Skip joke or simplify
- Minimal Greek context
- Brief Yehudis story
- Three modern examples
- Quick closing

### Longer Version (15 minutes)

- Add Matityahu's daughter story
- Discuss halachic sources
- More modern examples
- Audience participation
- Extended Q&A

### Alternative Endings

**Option 1: Challenge**
"So tonight, as you light your menorah, ask yourself: How will I be a Yehudit? What will I stand up for? Who will I inspire? The world is waiting for your light."

**Option 2: Blessing**
"May we all merit to be modern-day Yehudits, bringing light to darkness, courage to fear, and the special beauty of Judaism to a world that desperately needs it."

**Option 3: Call to Action**
"Before you leave tonight, commit to one act of Jewish courage this week. Write it down. Share it with a friend. And then do it. That's how we honor Yehudis - not just by telling her story, but by living it."

---

**Bottom Line:**
This speech balances warmth with substance, history with relevance, and inspiration with practicality. It works for diverse audiences while delivering a powerful message: every Jewish woman can be a heroine. All it takes is one act of courage.
