# [Misc > For Writer > _5 Chanukah > General] Dignitary Proclamation Letters - Two Examples

## Sample Letters Requesting Proclamations from Officials

**Format:** Two actual letters sent (1996 and 2004)
**Organization:** Chabad Jewish Community Center of the Space & Treasure Coast
**Author:** Rabbi [REDACTED-NAME]

---

## Letter #1: To Congressman (1996)

### Opening: Congratulations

> "Honorable Congressman Weldon,
>
> I would like to take this opportunity to congratulate you on your election for second term. May the A-lmighty grant you much success in your worthy endeavors."

**Strategy:**
- Start with congratulations (relationship building)
- Religious blessing (appropriate tone)
- Establishes goodwill

---

### The Invitation

> "It is an honor to invite you once again to our Grand Menorah Lighting Ceremony at the Melbourne Square Mall following a Live Inter-Continental Satellite link up of simultaneous Chanukah Celebrations around the globe to be viewed on a large screen set up in the mall, on Sunday Dec. 8, 1996 at 5:00 PM."

**Key Elements:**
- "Once again" (continuing relationship)
- "Grand" Menorah Lighting
- Location: Melbourne Square Mall
- Special feature: **Live Inter-Continental Satellite link-up**
- Global celebrations shown on large screen
- Specific date and time

**Why This Works:**
- Technology hook (1996 - satellite was impressive!)
- Global connection
- Not just local event
- Visual spectacle

---

### National Context

> "Nationally, Chabad is sponsoring over 275 Chanukah Celebrations from coast to coast, highlighted by President Clinton's participation from the Oval Office in the kindling of the National Freedom Menorah in Lafayette Park, adjacent to the White House."

**Power Statement:**
- 275 celebrations nationwide
- **President Clinton participating**
- From Oval Office
- National Freedom Menorah
- Lafayette Park (iconic location)

**Message:** This is significant enough for the President

---

### The Religious Freedom Frame

> "As the Chanukah holiday is a celebration of religious freedom and expression, it would be appropriate for the elected representatives of our great country to participate in its celebration. It would be an honor if you would join us and give your greetings at this joyous event."

**Key Themes:**
- Religious freedom (American value)
- Freedom of expression (First Amendment)
- Appropriate for elected officials
- "Our great country" (patriotic)
- Simple ask: "give your greetings"

---

### Proclamation Request

> "I would like to request a proclamation from your office once again attesting to the significance of the celebration and universal message of the Chanukah lights. I have attached a proposed text for the Proclamation. If you have any questions please feel free to call me at [REDACTED-PHONE]."

**Elements:**
- "Once again" (done before)
- "Attesting to significance"
- "Universal message"
- Text attached (makes it easy!)
- Direct phone contact

---

### Personal Touch

> "P.S. Regards from Dr. Jeffrey Greenspoon."

**Strategy:**
- Personal connection
- Mutual acquaintance
- Relationship building
- Humanizes the letter

---

## Letter #2: To Mayor (2004)

### Opening: Congratulations on New Position

> "December 6, 2004
>
> The Honorable Harry Goode - Mayor
> Melbourne City Hall
> 900 Strawbridge Ave.
> Melbourne, FL 32901
>
> Dear Mayor Goode,
>
> Firstly let me take this opportunity, on behalf of the entire Jewish community of the Space Coast, to congratulate you on your new position as Mayor of the City of Melbourne."

**Strategy:**
- Recent election (timely)
- On behalf of entire Jewish community (not just Chabad)
- Establishes he represents constituents

---

### The Invitation

> "It is an honor to invite you to our Grand Menorah Lighting Ceremony at the Melbourne Square Mall on Wednesday, Dec. 8, 2004 at 5:45 PM."

**Specific Details:**
- Same venue (established event)
- Exact day, date, time
- Simple, clear

---

### National Context (Updated)

> "Nationally, Chabad is sponsoring over 565 Chanukah Celebrations from coast to coast, highlighted by President Bush's participation from the Oval Office in the kindling of the National Freedom Menorah in Lafayette Park, adjacent to the White House."

**Growth Shown:**
- 275 events (1996) → **565 events (2004)**
- Now President Bush (updated administration)
- Same iconic location
- Shows organizational growth and legitimacy

---

### Precedent Established

> "Annually, we have had the honor of the participation of the Mayor of the City of Melbourne at our Chanukah event. A short greeting and reading of a proclamation by the City of Melbourne was always an honor for us. I have taken the liberty to attach a proposed proclamation using the same text as..."

**Key Points:**
- **Annual tradition** (not new request)
- Previous mayors participated
- Sets expectation
- "Short greeting" (not burdensome)
- Same proclamation text (consistency)

---

## Analysis: What Makes These Effective

### Letter #1 (Congressman) Strengths

**1. Relationship Building**
- Congratulations on re-election
- "Once again" (continuing participation)
- Personal P.S.
- Religious blessing

**2. Impressive Scale**
- Satellite link-up (cutting edge in 1996)
- Global celebrations
- 275 national events
- President participating

**3. Political Safety**
- Religious freedom frame
- Appropriate for officials
- Universal message
- Patriotic language

---

### Letter #2 (Mayor) Strengths

**1. Timely**
- New mayor
- Congratulations on new position
- On behalf of community

**2. Precedent**
- Annual tradition
- Previous mayors participated
- Expected continuation
- "Short greeting" (low commitment)

**3. Growth**
- 275 → 565 events nationally
- Shows momentum
- Organizational legitimacy

**4. Makes It Easy**
- Same text as before
- Proposed proclamation attached
- Clear expectations

---

## Key Differences Between Letters

### Congressman Letter
- More elaborate event description
- Technology focus (satellite)
- Longer, more detailed
- Request is primary

### Mayor Letter
- Emphasizes tradition/precedent
- Shorter, more direct
- Assumes continuation
- Precedent is primary argument

---

## Template for Your Use

### Basic Structure

```
[Date]

[Title] [Full Name]
[Address]

Dear [Title] [Last Name],

[CONGRATULATIONS if applicable - election, re-election, new position]

It is an honor to invite you [once again/for the first time] to our [event name] at [location] on [date] at [time].

[Optional: Special features - satellite, entertainment, etc.]

Nationally, Chabad is sponsoring over [number] Chanukah celebrations from coast to coast, highlighted by [President/notable figure]'s participation [location detail].

As Chanukah is a celebration of religious freedom and expression, it would be appropriate for elected representatives of our great country to participate. It would be an honor if you would join us and give your greetings.

[IF CONTINUING]: Annually, we have had the honor of [previous official]'s participation.

I respectfully request a proclamation from [office] attesting to the significance of the celebration and universal message of Chanukah. I have attached a proposed text. Please contact me at [phone] with questions.

[IF PERSONAL CONNECTION]: P.S. Regards from [mutual acquaintance].

Sincerely yours,
Rabbi [Name]
[Title]
[Organization]
[Contact Info]
```

---

## Customization Checklist

### Update These Elements

**For Your Event:**
- [ ] Number of national Chabad events (check current year)
- [ ] Current President's name
- [ ] Your location and venue
- [ ] Your date and time
- [ ] Special features (satellite, entertainment, etc.)
- [ ] Your organization name
- [ ] Your contact information

**For Your Recipient:**
- [ ] Correct title and name
- [ ] Current address
- [ ] Congratulations (if applicable)
- [ ] Previous participation (if applicable)
- [ ] Mutual acquaintances (if applicable)

---

## When to Send Each Type

### Use Congressman Letter Style When:
- First-time invitation to official
- Want to emphasize event scale/importance
- Have special features to highlight
- Need to establish significance
- Requesting new participation

### Use Mayor Letter Style When:
- Continuing relationship
- Previous participation established
- Emphasizing tradition/precedent
- Local official (not federal)
- Want to keep it brief

---

## National Event Numbers (Update Annually)

**Historical Context:**
- 1996: 275 Chabad Chanukah celebrations
- 2004: 565 Chabad Chanukah celebrations
- [Current Year]: [Check Chabad.org or merkos.org]

**Where to Find:**
- Chabad.org news releases
- Merkos L'Inyonei Chinuch communications
- ChabadOne.org resources
- Contact Merkos 302 for official number

---

## Additional Tips

### Make It Easy for "Yes"

**Include:**
1. Proposed proclamation text
2. Event flyer/details
3. Previous year photos (if continuing)
4. Media coverage samples
5. Parking/logistics

### Follow-Up Strategy

**Timeline:**
- Send 6-8 weeks before
- Follow up call 1 week after
- Confirm 2 weeks before
- Final reminder 3 days before

### After Event

**Send:**
- Thank you letter
- Photos with official
- Media coverage clips
- Invitation to next year

---

## Proclamation Text

*(See File 070 for complete proclamation template)*

**Key Elements:**
- WHEREAS paragraphs (historical context)
- Religious freedom theme
- Universal message
- Specific event details
- NOW THEREFORE proclamation
- Signature lines

---

**Bottom Line:**
These letters work because they frame Chanukah as celebration of religious freedom (American value), provide impressive national context (President participating, hundreds of events), and make the ask easy (proposed text attached, "short greeting"). The Congressman letter emphasizes scale and technology; the Mayor letter emphasizes precedent and tradition. Both use congratulations to build goodwill and include specific event details. Update the national numbers annually, customize for your official's situation, and always attach proposed proclamation text to make saying "yes" effortless.


---
**End of Document 70**
---

# [Misc > For Writer > _5 Chanukah > General] Dignitary Speech Samples

## Actual Speeches Delivered at Public Menorah Lightings

**Format:** Two short speeches from different officials
**Location:** Gainesville, Florida
**Speakers:** City Commission representative and County Commission representative

---

## Speech #1: City Commission Greeting

### Full Text

> "Good afternoon and a happy Chanukah to all. It is a pleasure and an honor to be here and to deliver Chanukah greetings on behalf of the city commission and the entire city of Gainesville.
>
> In a few minutes we will all light a candle of unity followed by the kindling of this giant nine-foot menorah.
>
> The Menorah, a traditional eight branch candelabra symbolizes to Jew and non-Jew alike the universal message of freedom from oppression and freedom of religion.
>
> It is thus an opportune time to give thanks to G-d for allowing us to live in the United States, a country that epitomizes the message of Chanukah.
>
> I would like to thank the Jewish Community of Gainesville for giving me the opportunity to participate in this joyous ceremony.
>
> Happy Chanukah to all and G-d bless America."

---

### Speech Analysis

**Opening (30 seconds):**
- Greeting and happy wishes
- Establishes role (on behalf of city commission and entire city)
- Expresses honor

**Bridge to Action (15 seconds):**
- Preview what's about to happen
- "Candle of unity" (inclusive language)
- Describes menorah (nine-foot - impressive!)

**Core Message (45 seconds):**
- Universal symbolism explained
- "To Jew and non-Jew alike" (inclusive)
- Freedom from oppression
- Freedom of religion
- Thanks to G-d for America
- America epitomizes Chanukah's message

**Closing (15 seconds):**
- Thanks to Jewish community
- "Joyous ceremony" (positive tone)
- Happy Chanukah
- G-d bless America (patriotic)

**Total Length:** ~2 minutes

---

## Speech #2: County Commission Greeting

### Full Text

> "Ladies and gentlemen, girls and boys, I'm proud to be standing here on behalf of the Alachua County Commission, participating in this momentous occasion, the first public menorah lighting ceremony in Gainesville.
>
> Now that the Menorah is lit, we must all look at the flames and listen to the message it tells."

---

### Speech Analysis

**Opening (20 seconds):**
- Inclusive greeting (ladies/gentlemen, girls/boys)
- Expresses pride
- Establishes role (County Commission)
- Historic moment emphasized: **"first public menorah lighting"**

**Core Message (10 seconds):**
- Action oriented ("now that menorah is lit")
- Meditative instruction
- "Look at the flames"
- "Listen to the message"
- Brief but profound

**Total Length:** ~30 seconds

---

## Why These Speeches Work

### Speech #1 Strengths

**1. Universal Language**
- "Jew and non-Jew alike"
- Freedom themes
- American values
- Inclusive throughout

**2. Gratitude Emphasized**
- Thanks to G-d
- Thanks to Jewish community
- Thanks for America
- Humble tone

**3. Patriotic Close**
- "G-d bless America"
- Ties to national values
- Safe, unifying

**4. Clear Structure**
- Greeting
- Preview
- Message
- Thanks
- Blessing

---

### Speech #2 Strengths

**1. Brevity**
- Under 1 minute
- Gets out of the way
- Lets ceremony speak

**2. Historic Framing**
- "First public menorah lighting"
- Creates significance
- Memorable moment

**3. Contemplative Close**
- "Look at the flames"
- "Listen to the message"
- Invites reflection
- Poetic

**4. Inclusive Opening**
- Names all demographics
- Children included
- Community-wide

---

## Template Speeches for Dignitaries

### Version 1: Standard (2-3 minutes)

```
Good [morning/afternoon/evening] and a happy Chanukah to all.

It is a pleasure and an honor to be here and to deliver Chanukah greetings on behalf of [your position/organization].

[OPTIONAL: Describe what's about to happen]
In a few moments we will light this [description of menorah].

[CORE MESSAGE - Choose one theme:]

OPTION A - Freedom Theme:
The Menorah symbolizes to people of all faiths the universal message of freedom from oppression and freedom of religion. It reminds us that we are blessed to live in [country/city], where these freedoms are protected and celebrated.

OPTION B - Light Over Darkness:
The Chanukah lights remind us that even a small light can dispel great darkness. In times of challenge, we must each be a light to others, bringing hope and warmth to our community.

OPTION C - Perseverance:
Chanukah teaches us that with faith and determination, seemingly impossible challenges can be overcome. The few prevailed over the many, and light triumphed over darkness.

[CLOSING:]
I would like to thank [organization/community] for giving me the opportunity to participate in this joyous ceremony.

Happy Chanukah to all, and may these lights inspire us to bring more light into our world.
```

---

### Version 2: Brief (30-60 seconds)

```
[Greeting that includes all ages],

I'm honored to be here on behalf of [organization] participating in this [momentous/joyous/historic] occasion.

[Choose ONE:]
- The lights of Chanukah remind us that freedom is worth fighting for.
- These flames teach us that even small lights can dispel great darkness.
- Chanukah celebrates the enduring strength of faith and community.

May these lights bring warmth and hope to all.

Happy Chanukah!
```

---

### Version 3: First-Time Event (2 minutes)

```
Good [time of day] and happy Chanukah!

It is truly special to be here for [city/location]'s very first public menorah lighting ceremony. This is a historic moment for our community.

Chanukah celebrates religious freedom - the right of all people to practice their faith without oppression. As [your position], I am proud that [city/county] embraces and protects this fundamental freedom for all our residents.

The menorah we light today will stand as a symbol of our community's commitment to diversity, inclusion, and mutual respect.

Thank you to [Chabad/Jewish organization] for bringing this meaningful tradition to our [city/county]. And thank you all for being here to celebrate together.

Happy Chanukah, and may these lights inspire us all!
```

---

## What to Provide to Dignitaries

### Speech Prep Package

**Send 1 Week Before Event:**

1. **Sample Speech** (customize one of above)
2. **Pronunciation Guide:**
   - Chanukah: HAH-noo-kah or KHAN-uh-kah
   - Menorah: men-OR-ah
   - Chabad: khah-BAHD
3. **Event Program** (so they know when to speak)
4. **Key Themes to Emphasize:**
   - Religious freedom
   - Light over darkness
   - Community unity
   - Universal message
5. **What NOT to Say:**
   - Don't call it "Jewish Christmas"
   - Don't pronounce it "CHAWN-oo-kah"
   - Don't make it exclusively religious
6. **Length Guidance:** "Brief remarks, 1-2 minutes ideal"

---

## Coaching Points for Rabbi

### Before the Event

**If Dignitary Asks for Help:**
- Offer sample speeches
- Emphasize brevity (1-2 min max)
- Suggest universal themes
- Provide pronunciation guide
- Reassure them ("very informal, just greetings")

**If They Want to Wing It:**
- Suggest 2-3 key points only:
  1. Thanks for invitation
  2. One universal message
  3. Happy Chanukah

---

### During the Event

**Introduction:**
> "We are honored to be joined by [Title] [Name], representing [organization]. [Title] [Name], please share your greetings with us."

**If Speech is Too Long:**
- Smile and nod
- Don't show impatience
- Audience will forgive
- Thank them warmly after

**If Speech Goes Wrong:**
- Keep smiling
- Move on quickly
- Don't draw attention to it
- Thank them anyway

---

## Common Dignitary Speech Patterns

### What They Usually Say

**Opening:**
- Thanks for invitation (90%)
- Honor to be here (85%)
- Happy Chanukah (95%)

**Body:**
- Freedom/liberty theme (70%)
- Light over darkness (60%)
- Community unity (50%)
- Religious pluralism (40%)
- Personal story (20%)

**Closing:**
- Happy Chanukah again (80%)
- God bless (60%)
- Thanks to organizers (70%)

---

## Handling Different Types

### The Natural Speaker
- Will do great without help
- Just provide pronunciation guide
- Give time limit
- Enjoy!

### The Nervous Speaker
- Send sample speech
- Offer to review their remarks
- Reassure multiple times
- "Just speak from heart"
- They'll be fine

### The Over-Preparer
- Will write detailed speech
- May be too long
- Gently suggest time limit
- Offer to review and edit
- "Shorter is more powerful"

### The Politician
- Will make it about them
- That's okay!
- Keep smiling
- Thank them for coming
- Worth it for the presence

### The No-Show
- Have backup plan
- Rabbi gives greetings instead
- Don't mention they cancelled
- Move on smoothly

---

## Follow-Up

### After Their Speech

**Immediate:**
- Thank them warmly
- Specific compliment if possible
- ("Your words about freedom were perfect")
- Take photo together

**Next Day:**
- Send thank you email
- Attach photos from event
- Quote their best line
- Invite to future events

---

## Special Situations

### If Multiple Dignitaries

**Structure:**
- Introduce all at once or separately
- Each speaks 1-2 minutes
- Rabbi moderates
- Thank all together at end

**Order:**
- Lowest rank to highest
- Or: Local → County → State → Federal
- Or: In order of arrival

---

### If They Brought Proclamation

**Dignitary Script:**
> "I'm honored to read this proclamation from [office] recognizing [dates] as Chanukah in [city/county]..."

**After Reading:**
- Present to rabbi
- Photo with proclamation
- Display prominently
- Thank them specifically

---

### If Media Present

**Brief Them:**
- Media here (heads up)
- Speak clearly
- Good photo opportunity
- They'll look good!

---

## Sample Thank You Notes

### After Event

**Email:**
```
Dear [Title] [Name],

Thank you so much for joining us at last night's menorah lighting and for your inspiring words about [specific theme they mentioned]. Your presence meant so much to our community.

[If media covered]: Your remarks were featured in [publication/station].

We hope to have the honor of your participation again next year.

With gratitude,
Rabbi [Name]

[Attach photos]
```

---

**Bottom Line:**
These sample speeches show that effective dignitary remarks are brief (1-2 minutes), emphasize universal themes (freedom, light over darkness), include gratitude, and close patriotically. The first speech provides substance and structure; the second shows that brevity can be powerful. Provide speech templates to nervous officials, pronunciation guides to all, and always emphasize that shorter is better. The goal is dignitary presence and blessing, not lengthy remarks. Their attendance matters more than their words, but good words make it even better.


---
**End of Document 71**
---

# [Misc > For Writer > _5 Chanukah > General] Thank You Letter to Dignitary

## Sample Follow-Up Letter After Event

**Date:** December 26, 2001
**Organization:** Chabad of Glendale and the Foothill Communities
**Author:** Rabbi [REDACTED-NAME]
**Recipient:** Councilmember Frank Quintero

---

## The Letter

### Header

```
December 26, 2001

Councilmember Frank Quintero
613 East Broadway Suite 200
Glendale, CA 91206
```

---

### Opening: Immediate Thanks

> "Dear Councilmember Quintero,
>
> I would like to thank you for joining us at the Grand Menorah lighting at the Glendale Galleria. Your participation was very meaningful to the community and I was grateful for the opportunity to have met you in person."

**Elements:**
- Specific event mentioned
- "Very meaningful to the community" (impact statement)
- Personal touch: "met you in person"

---

### Character Appreciation

> "It is most gratifying and encouraging for us to know that there are people like you who are so willing to give of themselves to help others."

**Why This Works:**
- Compliments character, not just action
- "Give of themselves" (recognizes sacrifice)
- "Help others" (altruistic framing)
- Personal affirmation

---

### Broader Significance

> "Assuredly, it speaks gracious words of inspiration and encouragement for the future of the City of Glendale and our great country the United States of America."

**Strategic Elements:**
- Ties to city's future
- Patriotic reference
- Elevated language
- Inspiration and encouragement

---

### Future Relationship

> "Our mutual efforts for the City of Glendale complement each other and I look forward to working with you on future community projects."

**Key Points:**
- "Mutual efforts" (partnership)
- "Complement each other" (synergy)
- **Looking forward** (future-oriented)
- "Community projects" (broader than Chanukah)
- Door open for future collaboration

---

### Closing

> "With best wishes for your good health, happiness and prosperity.
>
> Sincerely,
>
> Rabbi Simcha Backman
> Director, Chabad of Glendale and the Foothill Communities"

**Traditional Blessings:**
- Health, happiness, prosperity
- "Sincerely" (warm but professional)
- Full title included

---

## Why This Letter Works

### Structure

**1. Specific Thanks**
- Names event (Glendale Galleria)
- Acknowledges attendance
- Personal connection

**2. Character Praise**
- Goes beyond "thanks for coming"
- Recognizes personal sacrifice
- Affirms values

**3. Broader Impact**
- City benefit
- National significance
- Elevated language

**4. Future Focus**
- Ongoing relationship
- Partnership framing
- Open door

**5. Warm Wishes**
- Traditional blessings
- Genuine care
- Professional close

---

### Tone Analysis

**Formal But Warm:**
- "Councilmember" (formal title)
- "Your good health" (traditional)
- "Met you in person" (personal)

**Elevated Language:**
- "Most gratifying and encouraging"
- "Speaks gracious words"
- "Assuredly"

**Future-Oriented:**
- "Look forward to working"
- "Future community projects"
- "Mutual efforts"

---

## Template for Your Use

### Basic Structure

```
[Date within 1-3 days of event]

[Title] [Full Name]
[Address]

Dear [Title] [Last Name],

Thank you for joining us at the [event name] at [location]. Your participation was very meaningful to the community and I was grateful for the opportunity to [meet you/see you again].

[OPTIONAL - Specific compliment about their remarks/actions]
Your words about [theme] were particularly inspiring and resonated with many attendees.

It is gratifying to know that there are community leaders like you who are willing to give of themselves to help others. Your presence speaks to the strength and unity of [city/community].

Our efforts for [city/community] complement each other and I look forward to working with you on future community initiatives.

With best wishes for your health, happiness and prosperity.

Sincerely,

Rabbi [Name]
[Title]
[Organization]
[Contact Info]
```

---

## Customization Options

### Add These If Applicable

**Media Coverage:**
> "Your remarks were featured in [publication/station], bringing positive attention to our community's commitment to religious freedom and diversity."

**Specific Quote:**
> "Your words, '[quote their best line],' perfectly captured the spirit of the occasion."

**Proclamation:**
> "The proclamation from [office] now holds a place of honor in our center and serves as a reminder of our city's commitment to religious freedom."

**Photos:**
> "I've enclosed photos from the event. You're welcome to use them for your newsletter/website."

**Personal Connection:**
> "It was a pleasure to meet your [family member] and I hope we have the opportunity to connect again soon."

---

## When to Send

### Timing Strategy

**Ideal:** 1-3 days after event
- Fresh in their mind
- Shows respect and efficiency
- While excitement is high

**Acceptable:** Within 1 week
- Still timely
- Professional
- Expected

**Late:** 2+ weeks
- Still send!
- Better late than never
- Acknowledge delay if very late

---

## Delivery Method

### Email vs. Mail

**Email (Fastest):**
- Send within 24 hours
- Attach photos
- Easy to forward
- Quick response

**Mail (More Formal):**
- Send within 3 days
- On letterhead
- Signed personally
- More traditional

**Both (Best):**
- Email immediately with photos
- Follow with mailed letter
- Shows extra effort
- Multiple touchpoints

---

## What to Include With Letter

### Attachments/Enclosures

**Always:**
- [ ] Photos of dignitary at event
- [ ] Your business card

**Often:**
- [ ] Event photo collage
- [ ] Media coverage clips
- [ ] Event program/flyer
- [ ] Newsletter featuring event

**Sometimes:**
- [ ] Proclamation copy (if they issued it)
- [ ] Thank you from attendees
- [ ] Next event invitation
- [ ] Annual report/impact statement

---

## Follow-Up Strategy

### Building the Relationship

**Immediate (1-3 days):**
- This thank you letter

**Short-Term (1 month):**
- Email with media coverage
- Share related community news
- Invite to next event

**Medium-Term (3-6 months):**
- Holiday greetings
- Update on programs
- Invitation to other events

**Long-Term (Annual):**
- Next year's Chanukah invitation
- Annual report
- Major event invitations

---

## Common Mistakes to Avoid

**Don't:**
- ✗ Wait too long (send within a week)
- ✗ Generic template without personalization
- ✗ Forget their name/title
- ✗ Overlook their specific contribution
- ✗ Miss opportunity to suggest future collaboration
- ✗ Send without proofreading
- ✗ Forget to include photos
- ✗ Make it all about you/your organization

**Do:**
- ✓ Send promptly
- ✓ Personalize with specific details
- ✓ Use correct title
- ✓ Mention their impact
- ✓ Open door for future
- ✓ Proofread carefully
- ✓ Include photos
- ✓ Focus on them and community

---

## Variations for Different Situations

### First-Time Participant

Add:
> "We hope this is the beginning of a wonderful partnership and look forward to your participation in future events."

---

### Long-Time Supporter

Add:
> "Your continued support over the years has been invaluable to our community. Thank you for once again honoring us with your presence."

---

### No-Show (They Cancelled)

```
Dear [Title] [Name],

We understand that unexpected circumstances prevented you from joining us at our menorah lighting. We missed you!

[Brief event description]

We hope to have the honor of your participation at a future event. Please know you are always welcome.

With best wishes,
Rabbi [Name]
```

---

### They Went Above and Beyond

Add:
> "Your willingness to [specific action - stay late, bring your family, read proclamation, etc.] demonstrated extraordinary support and we are deeply grateful."

---

## Sample Photo Captions

### When Emailing Photos

**Individual Shot:**
> "Councilmember Quintero at the Grand Menorah Lighting, Glendale Galleria, December 2001"

**Group Shot:**
> "Community leaders gather for Chanukah celebration: [L-R names]"

**Action Shot:**
> "Councilmember Quintero helps light the menorah at Glendale's public ceremony"

---

## Social Media Coordination

### Ask Permission First

**In Thank You Letter or Follow-Up Email:**
> "We'd love to share photos from the event on our social media. Please let us know if you'd prefer we not tag you or if you'd like approval before posting."

**After Approval:**
- Tag them appropriately
- Use respectful captions
- Share to their office page if public
- Highlight their contribution

---

## Record Keeping

### For Your Files

**Save:**
- Copy of letter sent
- Their response (if any)
- Photos from event
- Media coverage
- Notes on their preferences
- Contact info confirmed
- Future event ideas

**Use For:**
- Next year's invitation
- Annual report
- Donor cultivation
- Grant applications
- Website testimonials
- Building relationship database

---

## Long-Term Relationship Building

### Beyond Thank You

**Quarterly Touchpoints:**
1. **Thank you** (immediately after event)
2. **Holiday greeting** (appropriate holiday)
3. **Program update** (show impact)
4. **Next event invitation** (continue relationship)

**Annual Cycle:**
- Chanukah invitation (8 weeks before)
- Thank you (within 3 days)
- Holiday card (appropriate time)
- Program update (mid-year)
- Next year's Chanukah (repeat)

---

**Bottom Line:**
This thank you letter succeeds by being prompt (within days), specific (mentions event and location), complimentary (affirms character, not just attendance), forward-looking (future collaboration), and warm (traditional blessings). It elevates the dignitary's participation from attendance to partnership, from one event to ongoing relationship. Send within 1-3 days, include photos, be specific about their contribution, and always open the door for future collaboration. This isn't just courtesy - it's relationship building that pays dividends for years to come.


---
**End of Document 72**
---

# [Misc > For Writer > _5 Chanukah > General] Public Menorah Lighting Guidelines - Halachic

## Official Guidelines from Vaad Rabbonei Lubavitch

**Issuing Body:** Central Committee of Chabad-Lubavitch Rabbis in the United States and Canada (ועד הרבנים הכללי)

**Date:** Yud Ches Kislev, Chodesh HaGeulah, 5772

**Author:** Rabbi Levi Yitzchok Raskin of London, England

**Purpose:** Address halachic questions regarding public menorah lightings

---

## Introduction from Vaad

### Cover Letter

> "Dear Shliach שיחי',
>
> We all know how the פעולות of Chanukah were especially dear to the Rebbe זי"ע. As Shluchim reach out and expand these פעולות, we have been asked numerous שאלות in Halacha. To address some of those issues we asked Rabbi Levi Yitzchok Raskin of London England, to write some general guidelines for public menorah lightings and related Halachic issues, and we are pleased to make this available to you.
>
> With our best wishes for a להוסיף אורה ושמחה בגו"ר,
>
> Vaad Rabbonei Lubavitch"

---

## The 14 Guidelines (Hebrew and English)

### 1. Location

**Hebrew:**
> א. מצוה גדולה להדליק נרות חנוכה ברחובות קריה, "במקום הציבורי והמרכזי ביותר".

**English:**
> "It is a great Mitzvah to light Chanukah lights in the thoroughfares of the city 'in the most public and central location'."

**Source:** Sicha of 6th day of Chanukah 5747; and elsewhere

---

### 2. Seven Noachide Laws

**Hebrew:**
> ב. יש לנצל את המעמד לעורר גם על דבר קיום ז' מצות בני נח.

**English:**
> "The occasion of the public Menorah lighting should be utilized to also highlight the Sheva Mitzvos Bnai Noach."

---

### 3. Does Not Fulfill Personal Obligation

**Hebrew:**
> ג. טוב להכריז שאין אדם יוצא ידי חובתו בהדלקה זו, ואשר כל אחד מצווה להדליק נר חנוכה בביתו.

**English:**
> "It is important to inform those present that the public Menorah lighting does not fulfill one's personal obligation to light Chanukah lights and that it is incumbent upon each individual to light Chanukah lights at home."

**Source:** Sefer Hasichos 5747 vol. 1 p. 172; Hisvaduyos 5747 vol. 2 p. 98

**Halachic Basis:** Rema (Shulchan Aruch 671:7) - One does not fulfill obligation with synagogue candles

---

### 4. Nevertheless, We Make a Brocho

**Hebrew:**
> ד. ואף על פי כן, מברכים על הדלקה זו, וכדין ההדלקה שבבית הכנסת.

**English:**
> "Nevertheless, we recite a Brocho at the public lighting, similar to the Halacha regarding the lighting of Chanukah lights in a Shul etc."

**Source:** Extensive discussion in Nesivim BeS'dei HaShlichus, pp. 242+

**Yaavet'z Quote (cited in sources):**
> "For this mitzvah of Chanukah lights is different, certainly its Brocho is essential, because its entire purpose is for Pirsumei Nissa (publicizing the miracle), and if one lights without a Brocho, one accomplishes nothing, for the observer will think he is lighting for his own needs... therefore there is no place to light without a Brocho."

---

### 5. Women Do Not Make the Brocho

**Hebrew:**
> ה. מדין צניעות, אין לכבד אשה לברך על ההדלקה.

**English:**
> "For reason of Tznius we do not honor a woman with making the Brocho."

**Source:** Megillah 23a; Shulchan Aruch (and Shulchan Aruch HaRav) Orach Chaim 282:3 (5)

---

### 6. Multiple People Can Be Honored

**Hebrew:**
> ו. יכולים לכבד כמה אנשים בהדלקת הנרות. שכל אחד ידליק נר אחד והדומה. אכן בזה האופן, הרי את ההכרזות - את מי מכבדים באיזה נר - יש לעשות לפני הברכות, שלא יהוו ההכרזות וכו' הפסק בין הברכה וקיום המצוה.

**English:**
> "A number of individuals may be honored to each kindle a Chanukah light. However, when doing so all the announcements of the names etc, should be made prior to the Brocho so as not to make a Hefsek (interruption) between the Brocho and kindling of all the lights."

**Practical Application:**
- Can honor multiple people
- Each lights one candle
- **IMPORTANT:** Announce all names BEFORE blessings
- Prevents interruption between brocho and mitzvah

---

### 7. Non-Jews and the Shamash

**Hebrew:**
> ז. אין לתת לנכרי להדליק נרות המצוה. ורבים נוהגים לכבדו בהדלקת השמש.

**English:**
> "A non-Jew should not be honored to light a Chanukah light. Instead, many will honor a non-Jew with kindling the Shamash – which is acceptable."

**Halachic Basis:** "Hadlaka Oseh Mitzvah" - the lighting itself performs the mitzvah (Orach Chaim 671:1)

**Practical Solution:**
- Non-Jews cannot light the main lights
- CAN honor them with lighting shamash
- Common practice

---

### 8. Height Limit

**Hebrew:**
> ח. גובה המנורה לא יעלה על עשרים אמה, היינו שתחתית הלהבות תהא תוך עשרים אמה מן הקרקע.

**English:**
> "The height of the Menorah should not exceed twenty cubits from the ground, i.e. the lowest part of the lights should be within twenty cubits of the ground."

**Source:** Shulchan Aruch 671:6; Pri Megadim Mishbetzos Zahav 5

**Measurement:** 20 cubits ≈ 30-40 feet (depending on which cubit measurement used)

**Key Point:** LOWEST part of flames must be within 20 cubits

---

### 9. Real Flames, Not Electric

**Hebrew:**
> ט. במקום שאפשר להדליק להבה ממש, אין להדליק בנרות חשמליות, כי על נרות של חשמל אי אפשר לברך.

**English:**
> "Whenever it is possible, one should use real flames for the public Chanukah lights, rather than using electric lights - as a Brocho cannot be recited on electric lights."

**Sources:**
- Shu"t Yitzchak Yoreh Deah 120
- She'arim Hametzuyanim BeHalacha 139:4
- Encyclopedia Talmudit vol. 18, entry "Chashmal"
- Igros Kodesh vol. 10 p. 345

---

### 10. Gas/Butane Lights

**Hebrew:**
> י. אף נר של גאז (butane) אין לברך על הדלקתו.

**English:**
> "Likewise, a Brocho should not be recited on lights which are fueled by gas or butane."

**Rationale (from sources):**
- Rav Moshe Feinstein zt"l ruled one doesn't fulfill obligation with gas
- With gas lights, small flame burns above gas canister
- Flame is surrounded by mesh covered in powder that glows when heated
- Observer doesn't see actual flame, only glowing powder
- Therefore problematic for brocho

---

### 11. Kerosene Lights

**Hebrew:**
> יא. רבים נוהגים להדליק נרות הללו בנפט, ויש להם על מה שיסמוכו.

**English:**
> "Many kindle the public menorah using kerosene lights, and there's sufficient Halachic basis for that."

**Source:** Piskei Teshuvos (beginning of 673) discusses this

**Considerations:**
- Some permit in times of need
- Concern about smell causing people to extinguish - not applicable outdoors
- Concern about thick wick being like "avukah" (torch) - varies by setup

**Conclusion:** "Yesh lahem al ma she'yismoch" - there's what to rely on

---

### 12. Minyan Preferred But Not Required

**Hebrew:**
> יב. יש להשתדל שההדלקה תהא בנוכחות עשרה מישראל. ואם אין עשרה, יכול להדליק בברכה.

**English:**
> "Effort should be made to kindle the public Menorah in the presence of at least ten people. However, when that is not achieved, a Brocho may nevertheless be recited."

**Source:** Magen Avraham 671:10 and other commentaries there

**Practical Application:**
- TRY for minyan
- But don't cancel if fewer
- Can make brocho either way

---

### 13. Timing: Plag HaMincha and Duration

**Hebrew:**
> יג. זמן ההדלקה הכי מוקדמת היא מפלג המנחה. אך צריך לתת די שמן שידליק עד חצי שעה תוך הלילה.

**English:**
> "The earliest time that the Menorah may be lit is Plag Hamincha, but there should be sufficient fuel for the lights to last at least 30 minutes past nightfall."

**Source:** Orach Chaim beginning of 672

**Calculation:**
- **Plag HaMincha** = 1¼ hours (sha'os zmaniyos) before sunset
- **Must burn until:** 30 minutes after nightfall (tzeis hakochavim)

**Why This Matters:**
"That is why R. Shmuel Butman needs to fly in a helicopter on Friday" - to light early enough before Shabbos while ensuring it burns 30 minutes into night

---

### 14. Gender Separation

**Hebrew:**
> יד. כבכל אירוע ציבורי, יש להשתדל שתהא הפרדה בין גברים לנשים.

**English:**
> "As with all public events, effort should be made to achieve gender separation."

**Source:** Shulchan Aruch HaRav 315:3

**Rebbe's Language (cited):**
From Seder HaHora'os for Birchas HaChamah: "צריך להיות כפשוט אנשים בפני עצמם ונשים בפני עצמן" - "It must be as is obvious, men by themselves and women by themselves"

**Note in sources:** There it's simpler as each person makes their own brocho, unlike here. "V'yalu'i"

---

### 15. Daily Lighting (Bonus)

**Added note:**
> "With the menorah it should be lit/turned on every day, and not all at once"

**Meaning:** Add one light each night progressively, don't light all eight at once

---

## Additional Halachic Discussion: Shehecheyanu

### Forum Question

**Scenario:**
Person lighting public menorah on Monday (not first night) has not yet lit at home this Chanukah. Should he say Shehecheyanu out loud?

**Answer:**
> "Being that the lighting he is doing 'b'tzibur' (in public) is totally unrelated to his personal obligation to light, what difference would it make whether or not he lit a menorah yet? Even after he lights the Public menorah he will still be obligated to light a menorah at home with a bracha, and if it is the first time this year (at home) he should also say a Shehecheyanu."

**Conclusion:**
- Public lighting ≠ personal obligation
- If it's past first night, NO Shehecheyanu at public lighting
- Will say it at home when lights for first time
- "Neither out loud or quietly" at public lighting after first night

---

## Practical Summary for Shluchim

### Must Do

1. ✓ Most public location possible
2. ✓ Announce: doesn't fulfill home obligation
3. ✓ Make brocho (like shul lighting)
4. ✓ Real flames if possible (not electric)
5. ✓ Lowest flames within 20 cubits
6. ✓ After Plag HaMincha
7. ✓ Fuel for 30 min after nightfall

### Should Do

1. ○ Highlight 7 Noachide Laws
2. ○ Try for minyan (10 men)
3. ○ Gender separation
4. ○ Use kerosene if can't use candles/oil

### Don't Do

1. ✗ Don't let woman make brocho publicly
2. ✗ Don't let non-Jew light main lights
3. ✗ Don't announce names after brocho
4. ✗ Don't use electric lights with brocho
5. ✗ Don't use gas/butane with brocho

### May Do

1. △ Honor multiple people (announce before brocho)
2. △ Honor non-Jew with shamash
3. △ Light without minyan (still make brocho)
4. △ Use kerosene (with brocho)

---

## Special Situations

### Multiple Honorees

**How to structure:**
1. Announce ALL names first
2. "We will honor [names] to light..."
3. THEN make brochos
4. THEN each person lights their candle
5. No talking/announcing between brocho and last candle

---

### Non-Jewish Dignitaries

**Problem:** Want to honor but can't light main lights

**Solution:**
- Honor with lighting shamash
- "Rabim nohagim" - many do this
- Acceptable and common
- Dignitary participates meaningfully

---

### Fuel Types Priority

**Best to Worst:**
1. **Olive oil** (ideal)
2. **Other oils** (kosher)
3. **Wax candles** (acceptable)
4. **Kerosene** (has what to rely on)
5. **Gas/Butane** (don't make brocho)
6. **Electric** (don't make brocho)

---

### Friday Afternoon

**Challenge:** Must light before Shabbos but must burn 30 min into night

**Rav Butman's Solution:** Helicopter lighting early

**Alternatives:**
- Light as late as possible before Shabbos
- Use LOTS of fuel
- Calculate exact times carefully
- Some use Thursday night public lighting instead

---

## Common Questions Addressed

### Q: Can we make brocho if fewer than 10 people?
**A:** Yes. Try for minyan but brocho is valid either way.

### Q: Can woman light the menorah?
**A:** She can light, but should not make the brocho publicly (tznius).

### Q: Can mayor/non-Jewish dignitary light?
**A:** Not the main lights, but can honor with shamash.

### Q: Electric menorah okay?
**A:** If real flames possible, no. Can't make brocho on electric.

### Q: What about gas lights?
**A:** Brocho should not be recited. Use kerosene instead.

### Q: How high can menorah be?
**A:** Lowest part of flames must be within 20 cubits (~30-40 feet).

### Q: What time to light?
**A:** Earliest: Plag HaMincha. Must burn 30 min past nightfall.

### Q: Multiple people lighting - when announce names?
**A:** BEFORE brochos, not between brocho and lighting.

---

## Sources and References

**Key Sources Cited:**
1. Sichos of the Rebbe (5747 and elsewhere)
2. Shulchan Aruch and commentaries
3. Shulchan Aruch HaRav
4. Rema
5. Magen Avraham
6. Pri Megadim
7. Yaavet'z
8. Rav Moshe Feinstein zt"l
9. Piskei Teshuvos
10. Encyclopedia Talmudit
11. Igros Kodesh
12. Nesivim BeS'dei HaShlichus

---

## For Further Study

**Detailed discussions available in:**
- Nesivim BeS'dei HaShlichus vol. 1 pp. 242+, 256+
- Sefer HaMivtzaim KeHilchasam vol. 2 pp. 100
- Hisvaduyos journal 5747
- Piskei Teshuvos Siman 671-673

---

**Bottom Line:**
These authoritative guidelines from Vaad Rabbonei Lubavitch address the most common halachic questions about public menorah lightings. Key takeaways: Use real flames when possible, make brocho (like shul), announce it doesn't fulfill home obligation, honor non-Jews with shamash only, announce all honorees before brocho, light after Plag with fuel for 30 min past nightfall, and try for minyan but not required. When in doubt about fuel type, kerosene has what to rely on, but gas/electric should not have brocho. These aren't just suggestions - they're halachic requirements and best practices from the central Chabad rabbinic authority.


---
**End of Document 73**
---

# [Misc > For Writer > _5 Chanukah > General] Practical Halachos and Q&A for Chanukah Events

## Forum Discussion: Real-World Halachic Questions

**Format:** Community questions and answers about Chanukah event halachos

**Topics:** Pre-lighting restrictions, home vs. event lighting, kashrus policies, menorah placement, Moshiach themes

---

## Question #1: Pre-Lighting Restrictions

### The Issue

> "There are halachos that govern the time and place of lighting the Menorah, and I think we need to be careful with ourselves and our parties, public lightings etc."

**Statement:**
> "From the time of lighting until we light we are forbidden to eat and learn"

---

### The Question

> "Q: Does that mean you can't eat a Latke? or is it a meal? al kol ponum a sit down meal is for sure osur"

**Translation:** At minimum, a sit-down meal is definitely forbidden

---

### Practical Application

**What's Forbidden:**
- Sit-down meals (definitely)
- Formal eating
- Learning Torah

**Gray Area:**
- Snacking on latkes
- Standing/mingling food
- Light refreshments

**Recommendation:**
Either schedule food AFTER lighting, or keep it to light snacks before

---

## Question #2: Bringing Menorahs to Parties

### The Concern

> "When you are at a party, I heard some encourage people to bring their Menorahs to light at the event. (a very Israeli thing to do) isn't everyone mechuyav to light at home?"

---

### The Problem

> "And if they light with you, you are discouraging them from doing it when they get home, additionally they are MAKING A BROCHO LEVATOLA"

**Issues:**
1. Everyone obligated to light at HOME
2. Lighting at party doesn't fulfill obligation
3. If they make brocho at party, it's a **brocho levatola** (wasted blessing)
4. Discourages home lighting

---

### Israeli Custom Note

**Context:** Israeli practice differs
- In Israel, one menorah per household often
- Might light together as family at event
- Different from Chabad/Diaspora practice

**Chabad Practice:**
- Each person lights at home
- Public lighting is SEPARATE
- Public doesn't fulfill personal obligation

---

### Recommendation

**Don't encourage bringing menorahs to party**

**Instead:**
1. Public lighting for pirsumei nisa
2. Encourage everyone to ALSO light at home
3. Announce clearly: "This doesn't fulfill your home obligation"

---

## Question #3: Timing for Public/Shul Lightings

### The Rule

> "Public lightings and shul lightings need to be after plag hamincha"

**Source:** See File 074, guideline #13

---

### Famous Example

> "(that is why R Shmuel Butman needs to fly in a helicopter on Friday)"

**The Challenge:**
- Friday: Must light before Shabbos
- Must also burn 30 min after nightfall
- Solution: Light very early (Plag) with lots of fuel
- Helicopter allows traveling between locations fast enough

---

## Question #4: Making Brocho Together

### The Question

> "Can everyone in the crowd make the bracha together? or it must be one person?"

---

### The Answer

**Based on Vaad Guidelines (File 074):**
- ONE person makes brocho OUT LOUD
- Others listen and answer "Amen"
- Similar to shul lighting
- If multiple honorees lighting, announce ALL names BEFORE brocho

**Not a communal brocho** where everyone says it together

---

## Kashrus Policy Question

### The Situation

> "We have a big Chanukah event every year for between 300 - 500 people. We have included more food stalls which we run either on our own or through Beth Din approved vendors."

---

### The Question

> "The issue came up this year of whether it is ok to have both milchig and fleishig for sale - obviously not near each other etc but still at the same event."

---

### Beth Din Response

> "The Beth Din said that it's not at all a problem, it happens at other communal events, just make it very clear, and if we want to be extra careful we should ask people to be conscious of it on the fliers, announcements etc."

---

### Asker's Concern

> "Does my theoretically entertaining the idea make me the subject line of the next Nshei Newsletter (unless Rabbi Posner saves me) or does an event that size allow for that?"

**Translation:** Will I get in trouble for this? Is it okay for large events?

---

### Practical Guidelines

**It's Permitted When:**
1. Event size justifies variety (300-500 people - yes!)
2. Clear separation
3. Clear signage
4. Announcements made
5. Fliers note it
6. Beth Din approved

**Make It VERY Clear:**
- Sign each station (Dairy/Meat)
- Announce at beginning
- Put on flier
- Different colored tablecloths
- Physical distance between stations

---

## Menorah Near Christmas Tree

### The Questions

**Question 1:**
> "We're trying to put up a menorah & event in a new town. The town only allows displays (religious or otherwise) in one area. There is a gigantic xmas tree there. What are your thoughts about putting a menorah at that location? We could put it off to the side, say 20 or 30 ft away, but it would still be the only display other than tree at that location. would it be perceived that we're 'acknowledging' or 'competing with' chogo shelohem?"

---

**Question 2:**
> "Is it totally mufrach to attend a conservative temple's annual menorah lighting? even just to make an appearance?"

---

**Question 3:**
> "Anyone have any advice on how to incorporate the ikkar shlichus of kabolas pnei moshiach tzidkeinu into the mivtzoim of chanukah?"

---

### Analysis

**Menorah Near Tree Issue:**

**Concerns:**
- Appearing to acknowledge their holiday
- Looking like we're "competing"
- Association with avodah zarah symbols

**Considerations:**
- If it's the ONLY permitted location, may be necessary
- 20-30 feet separation helps
- Menorah has own significance
- Not about them, about us
- Consult local Rav

**Possible Approach:**
- If unavoidable location, proceed
- Make it clearly separate
- Focus on Jewish message
- Don't reference tree
- Emphasize religious freedom for ALL

---

**Conservative Temple Attendance:**

**"Mufrach"** = inappropriate/not fitting

**Considerations:**
- Depends on purpose
- Building relationships? Maybe
- Endorsing their approach? No
- Just appearance without participation? Gray area
- Consult Mashpia

---

## Incorporating Moshiach Theme

### The Answer: Multiple Approaches

> "There are many ways how to incorporate Moshiach into Mivtza Chanukah"

---

### In Print Materials

**Slogan:**
> "Lighting the way to redemption"

**Works Because:**
- Light theme fits Chanukah
- Forward-looking
- Hopeful message
- Not preachy

---

### Gematria Connection #1

**Moshiach = Roshei Taivos:**
> משיח : מדליקין שמונה ימי חנוכה
> "Madlikin Shmone Yemei Chanukah"
> (We light eight days of Chanukah)

**Letter Breakdown:**
- מ = Madlikin (we light)
- ש = Shmone (eight)
- י = Yemei (days of)
- ח = Chanukah

---

### Gematria Connection #2

> משיח : גמטרי' נס גדול הי' שם
> "Moshiach = Gematria of Nes Gadol Haya Sham"
> (A great miracle happened there)

**Numerical Value:**
Both equal 358

---

### The Number Eight

> "'Eight' is indicative of Moshiach and Geulah the time of infinity and as such Neros Chanukah einom betailim Leolom"

**Kabbalah Concept:**
- 7 = natural world (7 days of creation)
- 8 = beyond nature (supernatural)
- 8 = Moshiach era
- Therefore Chanukah lights (8 days) = eternal, not nullified

---

### Source to Study

> "In the sicha of kislev nun bais the Rebbe explains extensively the concept of oil and chasidus and Geula"

**Reference:** Sicha of 22 Kislev (exact year not specified in document)

**Topics:** Oil, Chassidus, and Geulah connection

---

## Practical Takeaways

### For Event Planning

**Before Lighting:**
- [ ] Don't serve sit-down meals
- [ ] Light refreshments okay if necessary
- [ ] Announce: "Please refrain from eating until after lighting"

**Regarding Home Menorahs:**
- [ ] Don't encourage bringing to event
- [ ] Clearly announce: public lighting ≠ home obligation
- [ ] Remind everyone to light at home
- [ ] Provide times for home lighting

**Timing:**
- [ ] Public/shul: After Plag HaMincha
- [ ] Must burn 30 min past nightfall
- [ ] Friday: Special planning needed

**Brochos:**
- [ ] One person makes brocho out loud
- [ ] Others listen and answer Amen
- [ ] Not communal recitation

---

### For Food at Events

**Kashrus:**
- [ ] Meat and dairy permitted at large events
- [ ] MUST have clear separation
- [ ] MUST have clear signage
- [ ] Announce at beginning
- [ ] Note on flyers
- [ ] Get Beth Din approval

---

### For Moshiach Integration

**Print Materials:**
- [ ] "Lighting the way to redemption"
- [ ] Explain Moshiach = רא"ת Madlikin Shmone Yemei Chanukah
- [ ] Note: Moshiach = gematria Nes Gadol Haya Sham
- [ ] 8 = beyond nature = Moshiach era

**Teaching:**
- [ ] Eight days = supernatural
- [ ] Oil miracle = beyond nature
- [ ] Chanukah lights eternal (like Moshiach era)
- [ ] Study Kislev 22 sicha on oil/chassidus/geulah

---

### Sensitive Situations

**Menorah Near Tree:**
- Consult local Rav
- If only option, may proceed
- Maintain separation
- Don't reference tree
- Focus on our message

**Other Movements' Events:**
- Case-by-case basis
- Consider purpose
- Building relationships vs. endorsing
- Consult Mashpia

---

## Discussion Questions These Raise

### For Your Community

1. **Pre-lighting food:** How do we structure timing to avoid eating before lighting?
2. **Home lighting:** How do we encourage home lighting while having public event?
3. **Multiple venues:** If doing several locations, how to schedule all after Plag?
4. **Kashrus policy:** What's our standard for large events?
5. **Tree proximity:** What would we do in similar situation?
6. **Moshiach theme:** Which approach resonates with our community?

---

## Additional Halachic Resources

**For More Detailed Guidelines:**
- See File 074: Official Vaad Rabbonei Lubavitch Guidelines
- Consult Nesivim BeS'dei HaShlichus
- Contact Vaad HaRabbonim for specific shailos
- Check regional Chabad Rabbonim

---

**Bottom Line:**
These real-world questions highlight practical challenges Shluchim face: balancing halacha with hospitality (food before lighting), encouraging home observance while having public events, maintaining kashrus standards at large gatherings, navigating municipal restrictions (tree proximity), and incorporating Moshiach themes appropriately. The answers show nuanced thinking: don't encourage bringing menorahs to parties (brocho levatola), meat/dairy at large events is fine with clear separation, timing must be after Plag, and Moshiach can be integrated through slogans, gematria, and the number eight's symbolism. When in doubt - especially on tree proximity and other movement's events - consult your Rav or Mashpia. Document these discussions as they help other Shluchim facing similar situations.


---
**End of Document 74**

# [Misc > For Writer > _5 Chanukah > General] Supreme Court Case: Public Menorah Display Constitutional

## U.S. Supreme Court Decision Establishing Legal Precedent

**Case:** County of Allegheny v. American Civil Liberties Union, Greater Pittsburgh Chapter

**Citation:** 492 U.S. 573 (1989)

**Decided:** July 3, 1989

**Significance:** Landmark ruling permitting public menorah displays

---

## Case Summary

### The Displays in Question

**Location:** Downtown Pittsburgh public property

**Display #1: Creche**
- Placed on Grand Staircase of Allegheny County Courthouse
- Donated by Holy Name Society (Roman Catholic group)
- Banner proclaimed "Gloria in Excelsis Deo" ("Glory to God in the Highest")
- Most prominent, beautiful, public part of courthouse

**Display #2: Chanukah Menorah**
- 18-foot Chanukah menorah
- Placed outside City-County Building
- Next to city's 45-foot decorated Christmas tree
- Sign at tree's foot: mayor's "salute to liberty"
- Menorah owned by Chabad
- Stored, erected, and removed annually by city

---

### The Challenge

**Plaintiffs:** ACLU Greater Pittsburgh Chapter + seven local residents

**Claim:** Both displays violated Establishment Clause of First Amendment

**District Court:** Denied relief (relied on Lynch v. Donnelly)

**Court of Appeals:** Reversed - both displays unconstitutional endorsement of religion

**Supreme Court:** SPLIT DECISION
- **Creche:** Unconstitutional (affirmed)
- **Menorah:** Constitutional (reversed)

---

## The Supreme Court's Ruling

### On the Creche: UNCONSTITUTIONAL

**Majority Opinion (Justice Blackmun):**

> "When viewed in its overall context, the creche display violates the Establishment Clause. The creche angel's words endorse a patently Christian message: Glory to God for the birth of Jesus Christ."

**Key Distinctions from Lynch v. Donnelly:**
- Nothing in setting detracts from religious message
- No secular symbols surrounding it
- Placed in most prominent government location
- Government appearing to praise God for Jesus's birth

**Why This Matters:**
- Government may acknowledge Christmas as cultural phenomenon
- BUT cannot observe it as Christian holy day
- Cannot suggest people should praise God for birth of Jesus

---

### On the Menorah: CONSTITUTIONAL

**Majority Opinion (Justice Blackmun):**

> "The menorah display does not have the prohibited effect of endorsing religion, given its 'particular physical setting.'"

**Why It's Permitted:**

**1. Combined Display Context**
- Christmas tree (secular symbol)
- Menorah (religious symbol)
- "Salute to Liberty" sign
- Together = recognition of cultural diversity, not endorsement

**2. Christmas Tree as Predominant Element**
- 45 feet vs. 18 feet
- Central position
- Clearly the main feature
- Menorah is secondary

**3. Message Conveyed**
- Both holidays part of same winter season
- Both have attained secular status in our society
- Recognition that Christmas not only way to celebrate season
- Celebrates pluralism and freedom

**4. No Secular Alternative**
- Unlike creche (could use Santa, reindeer, etc.)
- Menorah is THE symbol of Chanukah
- Absence of alternative negates inference of endorsement

**5. Mayor's Sign**
- "Salute to liberty"
- Confirms recognition of cultural diversity
- Not sponsorship of religious beliefs
- Emphasizes freedom theme

---

## Justice O'Connor's Concurring Opinion

### Her Framework (The "Endorsement Test")

**Question:** Would a reasonable observer view the display as government endorsement or disapproval of religion?

**Her Analysis:**
- Christmas tree = secular symbol (whatever its origins)
- Menorah = religious symbol (Chanukah primarily religious holiday)
- **Together** = message of pluralism and freedom
- Context prevents reasonable interpretation as endorsement

**Key Quote:**
> "By including the menorah with the tree, and with the sign saluting liberty, the city conveyed a message of pluralism and freedom of belief during the holiday season."

---

## Justice Kennedy's Dissent (Would Permit Both)

### His Position

**Both displays should be constitutional.**

**His Reasoning:**

**1. Government Accommodation of Religion**
- Policies of accommodation are accepted part of heritage
- Establishment Clause permits government latitude
- Recognizing central role of religion in society

**2. Not Proselytization**
- No coercion to support or participate
- No direct benefits establishing state religion
- No effort to convert anyone
- Purely passive symbols

**3. Historical Practice**
- Many unchallenged religious acknowledgments throughout history
- Legislative chaplains (Marsh v. Chambers)
- "In God We Trust" on currency
- Thanksgiving proclamations

**4. The Alternative Is Worse**
- Recognizing only secular = "callous indifference"
- Would require government to exclude religious
- Borders on hostility to religion

**Joined by:** Chief Justice Rehnquist, Justice White, Justice Scalia

---

## Key Legal Principles Established

### The Lemon Test

**From Lemon v. Kurtzman (1971):**

Government practice touching religion must:
1. Have secular purpose
2. Not advance or inhibit religion (primary effect)
3. Not create excessive entanglement with religion

**This case refined #2:** "Advance" means endorsement, favoritism, preference, or promotion

---

### The Endorsement Test

**From Justice O'Connor's Framework:**

> Government violates Establishment Clause when it makes "adherence to a religion relevant in any way to a person's standing in the political community."

**Application:**
- Would reasonable observer see endorsement?
- Consider overall context
- Look at physical setting
- Evaluate message conveyed
- Account for secular elements

---

### Context Matters Enormously

**Same Symbol, Different Results:**

**Creche Alone in Courthouse:**
- Unconstitutional endorsement
- Government taking position
- Religious message primary

**Menorah with Tree and Liberty Sign:**
- Constitutional acknowledgment
- Cultural diversity message
- Secular context predominates

---

## Practical Implications for Shluchim

### What This Ruling Permits

**Public Menorah Displays ARE ALLOWED When:**

✅ Displayed with secular holiday symbols
- ✅ Christmas tree nearby
- ✅ "Season's greetings" type signage
- ✅ Lights, decorations, etc.

✅ Conveys message of pluralism/diversity
- Not "Judaism is true"
- But "We celebrate religious freedom"
- Multiple traditions recognized

✅ No coercion or proselytization
- Passive display
- No religious services at location
- No pressure to participate

✅ Liberty/freedom theme emphasized
- Signs about freedom
- References to religious liberty
- American values language

---

### What To Avoid

**Risk Factors That Could Make Display Unconstitutional:**

❌ Menorah alone with no secular context
❌ Religious services held at display
❌ Government officials leading prayers
❌ Display in most sacred government space
❌ Religious messaging without secular balance
❌ Excluding other faiths from participation

---

## Strategic Guidance

### For Working with Government

**When Requesting Public Menorah Display:**

**1. Frame as Cultural Diversity**
> "Recognizing that both Christmas and Chanukah are part of our community's winter celebration"

**2. Emphasize Religious Freedom**
> "Chanukah celebrates religious freedom - a core American value"

**3. Offer Inclusive Approach**
> "Our display celebrates liberty and pluralism during the holiday season"

**4. Reference This Case**
> "The Supreme Court in County of Allegheny v. ACLU (1989) specifically upheld public menorah displays when presented with appropriate context"

**5. Include Secular Elements**
> "We'll place the menorah alongside the community Christmas tree with signage about freedom and diversity"

---

### Addressing Concerns

**If Official Worries About Church-State Separation:**

**Point 1:** Supreme Court already decided this
- Menorah displays are constitutional
- When properly contextualized
- Not theoretical - actual precedent

**Point 2:** This recognizes diversity, not establishes religion
- Acknowledges community's various traditions
- Celebrates American pluralism
- Consistent with government neutrality

**Point 3:** Excluding religion also problematic
- "Callous indifference" toward religious citizens
- Government need not be hostile to religion
- Accommodation is American tradition

**Point 4:** It's about freedom
- Chanukah itself celebrates religious freedom
- Display reinforces American values
- Not asking government to endorse Judaism

---

## Historical and Religious Context from Opinion

### Chanukah Background (As Described by Court)

**The Historical Event:**
- 164 BCE (165 BC)
- Maccabees recaptured Temple of Jerusalem
- From Seleucid Empire (Greek-influenced)
- Political rebellion with religious dimensions
- Rededicated Temple on 25th of Kislev

**The Miracle:**
- Temple menorah needed to burn continuously
- Only enough oil for one day
- Oil miraculously lasted eight days
- Time needed to obtain more oil

**The Ritual:**
- Mitzvah (religious commandment)
- Place lamp with eight lights outside home or in window
- Celebrate and publicly proclaim miracle
- Recite blessings before lighting
- Each night of eight-day holiday

---

### Cultural Dimensions the Court Recognized

**Not Purely Religious:**
1. **National/Political Dimension**
   - Story of national heroism
   - Military victory
   - Political independence
   - Emphasized especially in Israel

2. **Cultural/Ethnic Dimension**
   - Some nonreligious Jews celebrate
   - Expression of ethnic identity
   - Cultural or national event
   - Like some Americans celebrate Christmas secularly

3. **Winter Holiday Dimension**
   - Associated with winter solstice in ancient times
   - Proximity to Christmas
   - Part of "holiday season" in America
   - Giving of Chanukah gelt enhanced by Christmas timing

4. **American Context**
   - Greater social prominence than religious significance would suggest
   - Lower in hierarchy of Jewish holidays religiously
   - But widely observed in America
   - Heightened cultural/secular status

**Court's Understanding:**
> "Chanukah, like Christmas, is a cultural event as well as a religious holiday."

---

## Technical Details About Menorah

### From the Court's Description

**Temple Menorah:**
- Seven branches
- Central candlestick + six branches
- Tree-and-branch design
- Burned continuously
- Sanctified object

**Chanukah Menorah:**
- Eight branches (one per day)
- Plus ninth for shamash (helper candle)
- Tree-and-branch design evokes Temple
- Not a sanctified object
- Need not be treated with special care
- No specific rule on shape or substance in Jewish law

**Traditional Placement:**
- Just outside entrance to home
- Or in front window
- Where practicality/safety requires: inside
- Public proclamation of miracle

**Court's Note:**
> "Lighting the menorah is the primary tradition associated with Chanukah."

---

## The Pittsburgh Display Details

### Exact Specifications

**The Menorah:**
- 18 feet tall
- Abstract tree-and-branch design
- Owned by Chabad
- Stored, erected, removed by city annually
- Placed December 22
- Removed January 13

**The Christmas Tree:**
- 45 feet tall
- Middle arch of Grant Street entrance
- Decorated with lights and ornaments
- Erected November 17
- Clearly predominant element

**The Sign:**
- Bearing mayor's name
- Entitled "Salute to Liberty"
- Text: "During this holiday season, the city of Pittsburgh salutes liberty. Let these festive lights remind us that we are the keepers of the flame of liberty and our legacy of freedom."
- At foot of tree

**The Setting:**
- Grant Street entrance to City-County Building
- Three rounded arches supported by columns
- Menorah next to tree, against column
- Public, prominent location
- Jointly owned city/county building

---

## Quotes to Use in Advocacy

### From the Supreme Court Opinion

**On Constitutionality:**
> "The menorah display does not have the prohibited effect of endorsing religion, given its particular physical setting."

**On Pluralism:**
> "The combined display...simply recognizes that both Christmas and Chanukah are part of the same winter-holiday season, which has attained a secular status in our society."

**On Religious Freedom:**
> "The Chanukah menorah has become a universal symbol of religious liberty." (from proclamation language cited)

**On Context:**
> "The placement of the menorah beside [the Christmas tree] is readily understood as simply a recognition that Christmas is not the only traditional way of celebrating the season."

**On Liberty Theme:**
> "The presence of the mayor's sign confirms that...the government's association with a religious symbol does not represent sponsorship of religious beliefs but simply a recognition of cultural diversity."

---

### From Justice O'Connor's Concurrence

**On Message Conveyed:**
> "The city conveyed a message of pluralism and freedom of belief during the holiday season."

**On Reasonable Observer:**
> "Could not be interpreted by a reasonable observer as an endorsement of Judaism or Christianity or disapproval of alternative beliefs."

---

### From Justice Kennedy's Opinion

**On Accommodation:**
> "Government policies of accommodation, acknowledgement, and support for religion are an accepted part of our political and cultural heritage."

**On Participation:**
> "If government is to participate in its citizens' celebration of a holiday that contains both a secular and a religious component, enforced recognition of only the secular aspect would signify the callous indifference toward religious faith."

**On Passive Symbols:**
> "The creche and menorah are purely passive symbols of religious holidays."

---

## Legal Strategy Checklist

### Before Approaching Government

**Research:**
- [ ] Review this case thoroughly
- [ ] Check if locality has had menorah displays before
- [ ] Learn what holiday displays currently exist
- [ ] Identify secular elements (tree, lights, etc.)
- [ ] Research any local ordinances

**Preparation:**
- [ ] Prepare one-page case summary
- [ ] Draft proposal with liberty/diversity framing
- [ ] Include visual mockup of proposed display
- [ ] List secular context elements
- [ ] Anticipate concerns and prepare responses

---

### In the Proposal

**Must Include:**
- [ ] Reference to Allegheny County case by name
- [ ] Explanation of secular context (tree, signs, etc.)
- [ ] Liberty/pluralism/diversity theme
- [ ] No government endorsement of religion
- [ ] Celebration of American values
- [ ] Insurance/liability coverage information
- [ ] Setup and takedown plan
- [ ] No cost to government (if applicable)

**Helpful to Include:**
- [ ] List of other cities that do this
- [ ] Photos from previous years (if any)
- [ ] Letters of support from diverse community
- [ ] Offer to include other faith symbols if desired
- [ ] Explanation of Chanukah's freedom theme

---

### If Challenged

**Legal Defenses:**
1. **Directly on point:** Supreme Court upheld this exact scenario
2. **Secular context:** Display includes tree, lights, liberty signs
3. **No endorsement:** Message is pluralism, not "Judaism is true"
4. **Historical:** Long tradition of religious accommodation
5. **Passive:** No coercion, proselytization, or government prayer
6. **Freedom:** Recognizes liberty and diversity - core American values

**Practical Responses:**
7. **Inclusive:** Open to adding other symbols
8. **Community:** Reflects actual religious diversity
9. **Constitutional:** Not even a close call legally
10. **Precedent:** Decades of similar displays nationwide

---

## Bottom Line

### The Holding

**Public menorah displays on government property ARE CONSTITUTIONAL when:**
1. Displayed alongside secular holiday symbols (especially Christmas tree)
2. Secular symbols are predominant
3. Signage emphasizes liberty, freedom, diversity
4. Overall message is pluralism, not religious endorsement
5. No coercion or religious services

**This is settled Supreme Court precedent since 1989.**

---

### Why This Matters for Chabad

**Permission to Light:**
- Not asking for special favor
- Established constitutional right
- Supported by highest court
- Mainstream American practice

**Framework to Use:**
- Freedom and liberty theme
- Cultural diversity celebration
- Recognition of pluralism
- American values emphasis

**Legal Backing:**
- Supreme Court precedent
- Not theoretical
- Directly on point
- Favorable ruling

---

### Historical Significance

**This Case Established:**
- Public menorah displays are permissible
- Context and setting are critical
- Secular framing protects religious display
- Government can acknowledge religious holidays
- Pluralism is legitimate government message

**Impact:**
- Enabled thousands of public menorah lightings
- Provided legal framework for outreach
- Validated Chabad's public menorah campaign
- Affirmed religious freedom principles
- Balanced Establishment Clause concerns

---

## Additional Notes

### The Vote Split

**On the Creche:**
- 5-4 against (unconstitutional)
- Majority: Blackmun, Brennan, Marshall, Stevens, O'Connor

**On the Menorah:**
- Different coalition
- Some justices voted to uphold both
- Some to strike down both
- Menorah survived with majority support

**No Single Majority Opinion:**
- Multiple concurrences
- Different reasoning
- But clear result: menorah constitutional

---

### Related Cases Cited

**Lynch v. Donnelly (1984):**
- Upheld creche in larger holiday display
- Different context (private park, secular symbols)
- Influenced this case's analysis

**Lemon v. Kurtzman (1971):**
- Established three-part test
- Still controlling law
- Applied in this case

**Marsh v. Chambers (1983):**
- Upheld legislative chaplains
- Shows accommodation tradition
- Cited by Kennedy dissent

---

**Bottom Line:**
This landmark 1989 Supreme Court decision explicitly permits public menorah displays when contextualized with secular holiday symbols and liberty/pluralism messaging. The 18-foot Chabad menorah in Pittsburgh, displayed next to a 45-foot Christmas tree and "Salute to Liberty" sign, was held constitutional because the overall message conveyed cultural diversity rather than religious endorsement. For Shluchim, this provides firm legal ground for requesting public menorah displays: frame the request around freedom, pluralism, and cultural celebration; include secular context; emphasize the liberty theme of Chanukah; and cite this precedent directly. The Court's reasoning - that the combined display "simply recognizes that both Christmas and Chanukah are part of the same winter-holiday season" and "conveys a message of pluralism and freedom" - gives both legal and rhetorical framework for successful public menorah campaigns. This is not asking for a favor; it's an established constitutional right affirmed by the nation's highest court.
