# [Misc > For Writer > _5 Chanukah > General] Press Release Template: Borough Approves Public Menorah

## Sample Press Release for Municipal Approval

**Example:** Bernardsville, NJ - Borough Council approval

**Tone:** Professional, celebratory, community-focused

**Format:** Standard press release structure

---

## The Press Release

### Header

```
PRESS RELEASE
```

---

### Headline

```
Light Up Your Life:
CHANUKAH IN BERNARDSVILLE CENTER
```

**Elements:**
- Catchy phrase ("Light Up Your Life")
- Location (Bernardsville Center)
- Holiday name (Chanukah)
- Active, inviting

---

### Dateline and Opening Paragraph

```
[Bernardsville] - Bernardsville's Chanukah celebrations will receive a significant boost this year as a nine-foot Menorah is erected in the center of the town's Olcott Square. A special celebration - with local dignitaries, including Mayor Hugh Fenwick, participating - will be held at the Menorah on Tuesday December 3rd at 6:30 p.m.
```

**Key Elements:**

**The What:**
- Nine-foot menorah
- Erected in Olcott Square (town center)
- "Significant boost" to celebrations

**The When:**
- Tuesday, December 3rd
- 6:30 p.m.
- Specific date and time

**The Who:**
- Local dignitaries participating
- **Mayor Hugh Fenwick** named specifically
- Public invited (implied)

---

### Approval Paragraph

```
Bernardsville's Borough Council approved the request, put forth by longtime local resident Sid Sussman and Chabad of Greater Somerset County, at its meeting on Monday evening, December 7th.
```

**Key Elements:**

**The Approval:**
- Borough Council approved
- Official government action
- Establishes legitimacy

**The Requestors:**
- **Longtime local resident** (not just outsider rabbi)
- Plus Chabad organization
- Partnership model

**The When:**
- Monday evening, December 7th
- Recent approval
- Fresh news

---

### Rabbi Quote

```
"Chanukah's a time for celebrating the freedom to openly celebrate our values; this Menorah proclaims that message to the world", said Rabbi Mendel Herson, Director of the Basking Ridge based Chabad, "we appreciate the town's eagerness to bring a comprehensive Holiday spirit to the town. They displayed a marvelous sense of leadership and understanding."
```

**Quote Analysis:**

**First Part - The Message:**
- "Freedom to openly celebrate our values"
- **Universal theme** (not just Jewish)
- "Proclaims that message to the world"
- Bigger than one community

**Second Part - Gratitude:**
- "Appreciate the town's eagerness"
- "Comprehensive Holiday spirit"
- "Marvelous sense of leadership and understanding"
- **Praises the officials** (they love this)

**Tone:**
- Grateful, not entitled
- Emphasizes universal values
- Makes officials look good
- Inclusive language

---

### Event Details

```
Light refreshments and chocolate Chanukah 'gelt' will be available on Tuesday evening. The entire community is invited for this momentous event. For more information please call Rabbi Yossi Lazaroff at 908-604-8844
```

**Elements:**

**Refreshments:**
- Light refreshments (food!)
- Chocolate Chanukah gelt (specific, traditional)
- Free (implied)

**The Invitation:**
- "Entire community invited"
- "Momentous event"
- Open to all

**Contact:**
- Rabbi Yossi Lazaroff
- Phone: 908-604-8844
- Clear point of contact

---

### Media Notice

```
Media Notice: the event is open to all reporters, journalists and photographers; your coverage is invited. Rabbi Mendel Herson will be on hand to answer questions.
```

**Purpose:**
- Explicitly invites media
- Makes coverage easy
- Offers spokesperson
- Welcomes questions

**Why Include:**
- Reporters may not assume they're invited
- Makes it clear: this is newsworthy
- Available spokesperson identified
- Professional media relations

---

## Why This Press Release Works

### Structure Analysis

**Inverted Pyramid:**
1. Most important: what, when, where, who
2. Background: approval, partnership
3. Quote: adds human element, praises officials
4. Details: food, contact, media

**If Editor Cuts:**
- First paragraph stands alone
- Has all essential information
- Rest adds color and detail

---

### Strategic Elements

**1. Local Partnership**
> "Longtime local resident Sid Sussman and Chabad..."

**Why This Matters:**
- Not just "outside rabbi"
- Community member requested it
- Chabad partnered with local
- More legitimate, less "them vs. us"

**Lesson:**
- Find local partner when possible
- Jewish community member
- Prominent resident
- Makes it community initiative

---

**2. Official Endorsement**
> "Borough Council approved..."

**Why This Matters:**
- Government blessing
- Legitimate, not controversial
- Official action, not fringe activity
- Safe for others to support

**Lesson:**
- Lead with approval
- Shows government support
- Makes participation comfortable
- Establishes credibility

---

**3. Mayor by Name**
> "Including Mayor Hugh Fenwick, participating"

**Why This Matters:**
- Name recognition
- Adds importance
- Personal connection
- Mayor's office will likely promote

**Lesson:**
- Name officials specifically
- Gives them credit
- They'll share/promote
- Personal stake in success

---

**4. Universal Framing**
> "Freedom to openly celebrate our values"

**Why This Matters:**
- Not "Jewish values" but "our values"
- Freedom theme (American)
- Inclusive language
- Transcends single faith

**Lesson:**
- Universal language
- Freedom, celebration, community
- Not sectarian
- Everyone can relate

---

**5. Praising Officials**
> "Marvelous sense of leadership and understanding"

**Why This Matters:**
- Officials love being praised
- Reinforces their decision
- Harder to reverse
- Encourages future support

**Lesson:**
- Thank profusely
- Make them heroes
- Public recognition
- Builds relationship

---

## Template for Your Use

### Customizable Version

```
PRESS RELEASE

[Catchy Headline]:
CHANUKAH IN [YOUR TOWN]

[Your Town] - [Your town]'s Chanukah celebrations will receive a significant boost this year as a [size]-foot Menorah is erected [location description]. A special celebration - with local dignitaries, including [Mayor/Official Name], participating - will be held at the Menorah on [day, date] at [time].

[Your governing body] approved the request, put forth by [local partner name, if any] and Chabad of [Your Area], at its meeting on [date of approval].

"Chanukah's a time for celebrating the freedom to openly celebrate our values; this Menorah proclaims that message to the world", said Rabbi [Your Name], Director of [Your Chabad], "we appreciate [the town/city]'s eagerness to bring a comprehensive Holiday spirit to the community. They displayed a marvelous sense of leadership and understanding."

Light refreshments and chocolate Chanukah 'gelt' will be available [day] evening. The entire community is invited for this momentous event. For more information please call Rabbi [Name] at [phone].

Media Notice: the event is open to all reporters, journalists and photographers; your coverage is invited. Rabbi [Your Name] will be on hand to answer questions.
```

---

## Distribution Strategy

### Who Gets This Release

**Local Media:**
- Newspaper (main one)
- Weekly community papers
- Local radio stations
- TV stations (if applicable)
- Online news sites

**Community:**
- Email to congregation
- Post on social media
- Send to Jewish organizations
- Share with synagogues
- Community email lists

**Officials:**
- Mayor's office
- Council members who voted yes
- Town administrator
- Their communications staff
- Let them share too

---

### When to Send

**Timing:**
- Immediately after approval
- 1-2 weeks before event
- Not too early (people forget)
- Not too late (can't plan)
- Enough time for media to schedule

**Example:**
- Approval: December 7
- Event: December 3 (wait, that's backwards in the example!)
- Send: Shortly after approval

**Note:** The example has date inconsistency (approval Dec 7, event Dec 3), but principle is clear

---

### How to Send

**Format:**
- PDF attachment
- Word doc attachment
- Text in email body
- Subject: "PRESS RELEASE: Chanukah Celebration in [Town]"

**Email to Media:**
- Brief cover note
- Attach press release
- Offer interviews
- Provide photos if available
- Include your cell phone

---

## Variations for Different Situations

### First-Time Approval

**Add:**
> "This is the first time [town name] will host a public menorah display, joining hundreds of cities nationwide in celebrating religious diversity during the holiday season."

**Why:**
- Emphasizes historic nature
- Shows nationwide context
- Makes it newsworthy

---

### Annual Event

**Add:**
> "This marks the [X]th year that [town name] has hosted the public menorah lighting, which has become a beloved community tradition."

**Why:**
- Shows staying power
- Tradition angle
- Community acceptance

---

### After Initial Resistance

**Soften or Omit:**
- Don't mention previous denials
- Don't reference opposition
- Focus on current approval
- Positive only

**Why:**
- No need to remind of controversy
- Officials prefer positive framing
- Past is past
- Look forward

---

### Multiple Sponsors

**Add All Partners:**
> "Approved request put forth by [Organization 1], [Organization 2], and Chabad of [Area]..."

**Why:**
- Share credit
- Broader coalition
- More community buy-in
- Others will promote too

---

## Follow-Up Press Release

### After the Event

**New Release:**
> "[Town] Celebrates First Public Menorah Lighting"
>
> "Over [X] community members gathered in [location] Tuesday evening as Mayor [Name] helped light [town]'s first public menorah. The event featured [details], bringing together people of all faiths to celebrate religious freedom and community diversity..."

**Include:**
- Attendance numbers
- Official quotes
- Community reaction
- Photos
- "Annual tradition" language

**Why:**
- Second round of publicity
- Shows success
- Builds momentum for next year
- Makes refusal harder in future

---

## Key Phrases to Adapt

### Headlines

- "Light Up Your Life"
- "Chanukah in [Town] Center"
- "[Town] Welcomes Chanukah"
- "Festival of Lights Comes to [Town]"
- "Community Celebrates Freedom with Menorah Lighting"

---

### Opening Sentences

- "Chanukah celebrations will receive a significant boost..."
- "[Town] will join hundreds of cities nationwide..."
- "For the first time, [town] will host..."
- "The Festival of Lights comes to [location]..."
- "Community leaders will gather to light..."

---

### Rabbi Quotes

**Freedom Theme:**
- "Chanukah's a time for celebrating the freedom to openly celebrate our values"
- "This menorah proclaims the message of religious freedom"
- "Celebrating liberty and light"

**Gratitude:**
- "We appreciate the town's eagerness"
- "They displayed a marvelous sense of leadership"
- "Grateful for the community's support"
- "Thank the [council/commission] for their vision"

**Community:**
- "Brings comprehensive holiday spirit"
- "Celebrates our community's diversity"
- "Welcomes people of all faiths"
- "Unites our community"

---

### Event Details

- "Light refreshments and chocolate Chanukah 'gelt' will be available"
- "The entire community is invited for this momentous event"
- "Free and open to the public"
- "Family-friendly celebration"
- "Features music, refreshments, and holiday joy"

---

## Media Relations Tips

### For the Reporter Who Calls

**Be Ready With:**
- Exact date/time/location
- Background on Chanukah (brief)
- Why this matters to community
- Other cities doing this
- Mayor's participation angle
- Human interest stories
- Photo opportunities

**Offer:**
- Interview time
- Access to event
- Background materials
- Connect with community members
- Photos from other years/cities

---

### Photo Opportunities

**Suggest to Media:**
- Mayor lighting menorah
- Children watching
- Community gathering
- Close-up of menorah
- Wide shot of location
- Food/celebration

**Provide:**
- Schedule (exact lighting time)
- Best vantage points
- Access to officials
- Background on participants

---

## Checklist for Your Press Release

**Before Sending:**
- [ ] All names spelled correctly
- [ ] All dates/times accurate
- [ ] Phone number works
- [ ] Location clearly described
- [ ] Mayor/officials named (with permission)
- [ ] Quote is good and quotable
- [ ] Contact person identified
- [ ] Media invitation included
- [ ] Proofread carefully
- [ ] Formatted professionally

**After Sending:**
- [ ] Follow up with phone calls
- [ ] Offer interviews
- [ ] Provide additional materials
- [ ] Thank reporters who cover it
- [ ] Post on social media
- [ ] Share with officials
- [ ] Use for future years

---

**Bottom Line:**
This Bernardsville press release exemplifies effective municipal menorah announcement: lead with government approval (Borough Council voted yes) and official participation (Mayor Hugh Fenwick by name), emphasize local partnership (longtime resident Sid Sussman plus Chabad—not just outside rabbi), use universal framing ("freedom to openly celebrate our values"), and lavish praise on officials ("marvelous sense of leadership and understanding"). Structure follows inverted pyramid (key facts first, details later), explicitly invites media coverage, and keeps tone celebratory rather than controversial. Key strategies: name officials specifically (they'll promote it), partner with local resident (community legitimacy), frame as "comprehensive Holiday spirit" (not sectarian), provide all logistics (date, time, location, contact), and make coverage easy for journalists. The phrase "freedom to openly celebrate our values" is masterful—simultaneously Jewish and universal, religious and American. Adapt this template by filling in your town, officials, dates, and partners, but keep the structure and tone: government blessing, official participation, universal values, grateful not entitled, and invitation to all.

# [Misc > For Writer > _5 Chanukah > General] Press Release: First-Ever Community Menorah Lighting

## Comprehensive Press Release Template

**Example:** Charlottesville, VA - First-ever Downtown menorah lighting

**Date:** Friday, November 14, 2002

**Occasion:** Part of city's "Downtown for the Holidays" program

**Tone:** Educational, inclusive, celebratory

---

## The Press Release

### Header Block

```
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

Contact: Channa Mayer, Program Director
Friday, November 14, 2002
Phone: 434.293.5994
Email: chabadofuva@earthlink.net
```

**Format Elements:**
- "FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE" (standard)
- Contact person (not rabbi - Program Director)
- Date of release
- Phone number
- Email address
- All info for follow-up

**Strategic Choice:**
- Contact is "Program Director" Channa Mayer
- Not rabbi (less religious, more organizational)
- Woman's name (may seem less intimidating)
- Professional title

---

### Headline

```
Chabad of Charlottesville Holds First Ever
Community Chanukah Celebration & Giant Menorah Lighting
As Part of "Downtown for the Holidays"
```

**Headline Analysis:**

**Line 1:** Organization and historic nature
- "Chabad of Charlottesville" (local organization)
- "First Ever" (newsworthy!)
- "Community" (not just Jewish)

**Line 2:** The events
- "Chanukah Celebration" (broader)
- "Giant Menorah Lighting" (visual, specific)

**Line 3:** The context
- "Part of 'Downtown for the Holidays'" (city program!)
- Shows integration, not separate
- Official city participation

---

### Sub-Headline

```
Mayor Maurice Cox does the honors of lighting the candles to commemorate the holiday's fourth night on Monday, December 2nd, 5:00 p.m. at Central Place on the Downtown Mall.
```

**Key Elements:**

**Mayor Participation:**
- Mayor Maurice Cox BY NAME
- "Does the honors" (dignified language)
- Active role, not just attending

**Specifics:**
- Fourth night (specific day of Chanukah)
- Monday, December 2nd
- 5:00 p.m. (exact time)
- Central Place on the Downtown Mall (precise location)

**Why This Works:**
- Mayor's name in sub-headline (huge)
- All essential info up front
- Can excerpt just this
- Complete story in two sentences

---

### Opening Paragraph: The Hook

```
Something brand new is being added this year to the already lively, fun-filled mix of winter holiday events in Charlottesville that make up "Downtown for the Holidays." For the first time "Downtown for the Holidays" will include a Chanukah Celebration & Giant Menorah Lighting on Monday, December 2nd, 5:00 p.m. at Central Place on the Downtown Mall, with Charlottesville Mayor Maurice Cox doing the honors of lighting the menorah (Chanukah candelabra).
```

**Strategy:**

**"Brand New":**
- Fresh, exciting
- First-time news
- Historic moment

**"Already lively, fun-filled mix":**
- Positive framing of existing events
- Not competing, but adding
- Part of something bigger
- Celebrating what exists

**"Downtown for the Holidays":**
- Mentioned THREE times in one paragraph
- City's official program name
- Shows integration
- Not separate Jewish event

**Parenthetical Definition:**
- "(Chanukah candelabra)"
- Assumes audience may not know
- Educational without condescending
- Accessible to all readers

---

### Chanukah Explanation

```
Chanukah is the eight-day Jewish "Festival of Lights," this year beginning on the evening of November 29th. Each evening at sunset an additional candle is lit to commemorate the rededication of the Temple in Jerusalem some 2000 years ago. The holiday also celebrates the miracle of one day's worth of pure ritual oil burning for eight days until a new supply could be obtained.
```

**What This Paragraph Does:**

**Basic Facts:**
- Eight-day holiday
- "Festival of Lights" (poetic name)
- When it starts this year
- Nightly candle lighting
- Historical background (Temple, Jerusalem, 2000 years)
- The oil miracle

**Tone:**
- Educational
- Assumes no knowledge
- Brief but complete
- Respectful to tradition
- Accessible language

**Why Include:**
- General newspaper audience
- Many don't know basics
- Provides context
- Makes it interesting
- Shows substance behind celebration

---

### The Message Paragraph

```
"The message of Chanukah," explains Rabbi Shlomo Mayer, Executive Director of Chabad of Charlottesville and spiritual advisor for the Chabad Jewish Heritage Student Association at the University of Virginia, "is one of hope in the face of extreme adversity. It's a message with broad appeal to everyone who believes in religious freedom and that faith and determination can triumph against even the most overwhelming odds."
```

**Quote Analysis:**

**Rabbi's Credentials:**
- Executive Director (administrative, not just religious)
- Chabad of Charlottesville (local)
- Spiritual advisor for CJHSA (student connection)
- At University of Virginia (major local institution)

**The Message - Universal Themes:**
- "Hope in the face of extreme adversity"
- Religious freedom
- Faith and determination
- Triumph against overwhelming odds

**Strategic Language:**
- NOT "Jewish message"
- "Broad appeal to everyone"
- "Everyone who believes in religious freedom"
- Universal American values
- Transcends single faith

**Why This Works:**
- Shows substance
- Not just ritual
- Meaningful message
- Appeals to all
- Religious freedom (American theme)

---

### Activities Paragraph

```
People of all ages will enjoy singing traditional songs like "Rock of Ages" and "The Dreidel Song," and eating the free, delectable holiday treats, including tasty potato latkes (pancakes) with applesauce and sour cream, jelly doughnuts, plus chocolate gelt (coins) and prizes for the children.
```

**Elements:**

**"People of all ages":**
- Family-friendly
- Inclusive
- Not just for Jews

**Songs:**
- "Rock of Ages" (familiar to Christians too!)
- "The Dreidel Song" (specifically Jewish but fun)
- Participatory, not performative

**Food:**
- **"Free, delectable"** (important!)
- Latkes with explanation "(pancakes)"
- Applesauce and sour cream (specific, traditional)
- Jelly doughnuts (sufganiyot, but accessible name)
- Chocolate gelt with explanation "(coins)"
- Prizes for children

**Why Food Matters:**
- Draws people
- Shows hospitality
- Cultural experience
- Family-friendly
- FREE emphasized

---

### "Downtown for the Holidays" Context

```
"Downtown for the Holidays" is the effort of representatives from dozens of downtown businesses, non-profit organizations and the City of Charlottesville.
```

**Purpose:**
- Shows menorah is part of city program
- Not separate Jewish event
- Integration with broader community
- City participation established
- Business and non-profit coalition

**Strategic Value:**
- Legitimacy
- Not controversial addition
- Part of existing framework
- City blessing implicit

---

### Chabad Description

```
Chabad of Charlottesville is a non-profit organization dedicated to Jewish worship and study, and to fostering an appreciation of Jewish cultural heritage. 'Chabad' is an acronym of the three Hebrew words for wisdom (chachma), understanding (binah) and knowledge (da'at).
```

**Bottom Line:**
This Charlottesville press release exemplifies comprehensive "first ever" event announcement with brilliant strategic choices: integrates into city's "Downtown for the Holidays" program (mentioned three times in opening alone), features Mayor Maurice Cox in sub-headline doing honors, provides educational Chanukah explanation for general audience, emphasizes universal message ("hope in face of adversity," "religious freedom," "faith and determination"), lists multiple events (downtown lighting, UVA menorah distribution, campus lighting with Hillel, Catholic nursing home visit), shows coalition approach (city program, Hillel partnership, Beth Israel Hebrew School), and uses "Program Director" as contact rather than rabbi (less religious framing). The interfaith nursing home visit is strategic gold—Jews bringing Chanukah to Catholic facility shows community service and cross-faith relationships. Contact is Channa Mayer (Program Director, woman's name) rather than rabbi, making it seem organizational not clerical. Educational tone assumes no knowledge, defines terms in parentheses ("Chanukah candelabra," "pancakes," "coins"), and frames everything as addition to existing celebration, not separate Jewish event. Released 2.5 weeks before event—perfect timing for media planning. Adapt for your "first ever" by emphasizing historic nature, listing all related programming to show robust effort, partnering with other organizations, and integrating into existing city holiday framework when possible.

## Template Adaptations

### For Mall Partnership

```
FROM: [Your Chabad] and [Mall Name]

[MALL NAME] AND CHABAD JOIN IN A GRAND CHANUKAH CELEBRATION ON [DATE] AT [TIME]. COMMUNITY LEADERS TO LIGHT THE GIANT "MENORAH OF FREEDOM".

Chanukah - The Festival of Lights - brings fond memories and serves to renew our sense of identity. The Chanukah lights provide warmth, joy, strength and inspiration. Such is the purpose of a community-wide celebration at [Mall Name].

[Mall Name] joins [Your Chabad] in inviting the entire community to celebrate the Festival of Lights at a public Menorah kindling ceremony on [date] at [time] at [specific mall location].

Community leaders will attend and assist in kindling the giant "Menorah of Freedom".

Following the kindling, the program will feature live music, entertainment, refreshments and activities for all ages.

"In ancient times our ancestors rededicated the Temple with the Menorah," said Rabbi [Name]. "Today, we rededicate ourselves to making this world a better and brighter place."

Chanukah propagates the universal message that good will prevail over evil, freedom over oppression, and light over darkness.

This event joins thousands of Chabad centers worldwide staging similar celebrations, from Australia to Hong Kong, Ground Zero to the White House lawn. Hundreds of thousands will experience the joy of Chanukah with Chabad.

Join us in this exciting celebration. Bring your family and make this your special Chanukah experience.

For more information: [Phone]
```

## Checklist for Mall Event Release

**Partnership Elements:**
- [ ] Mall name prominently featured
- [ ] "Join in" collaborative language
- [ ] Benefits both partners
- [ ] Joint invitation to community

**Location Details:**

**Family Focus:**

**Scale and Legitimacy:**

**Universal Message:**

**Practical Information:**

- [ ] Free admission (if applicable)
- [ ] Parking information (if relevant)
- [ ] Contact for more info

---

**Bottom Line:**
This Glendale Galleria press release exemplifies successful mall partnership with powerful strategic elements: the branded "Giant 'Menorah of Freedom'" phrase (patriotic, universal), prominent mall partnership ("Glendale Galleria AND Chabad join"), mall-appropriate entertainment (clowns, balloons, live music), and crucial global context placing local event within worldwide campaign. The geographic sweep is strategic gold—"from Australia to Africa, Columbia to Hong Kong, New York City's ground zero to the White House lawn"—establishing legitimacy and mainstream acceptance. Ground Zero reference (2002, one year post-9/11) is emotionally powerful for freedom-over-oppression theme. White House lawn mention implies presidential blessing, making local officials comfortable participating. Three-part universal message (good over evil, freedom over oppression, light over darkness) transcends religion while rabbi's quote bridges ancient Temple rededication to modern "making this world better and brighter." For mall approach: emphasize foot traffic benefits, provide turnkey professional event, carry own insurance, time for maximum shoppers (4:30 PM Sunday), specify exact location using store landmarks ("Banana Court, front of Banana Republic"), and keep tone festive not overly religious. The global campaign framing—"thousands of Chabad centers," "hundreds of thousands participating"—transforms local menorah into participation in international movement, providing legitimacy that makes approvals easier and attendance higher.

---

**Bottom Line:**
This real-world checklist from an experienced Shaliach provides comprehensive categories (food setup, food items, art table, marketing, signage, program items) with specific brand recommendations learned through trial and error ("ONLY regular glazed doughnuts from Byerlys - smaller, cheaper, delicious"). The invaluable "FOR NEXT YEAR 2018" section documents improvements needed: spotlights on menorah, turn off competing tree lights, 4 tables instead of 3, higher ladder, designated crowd photographers in addition to professional, and explore storefront vs. hallway location. Key operational insights: order gelt, stickers, and dreidels in advance from Shluchim Office (they sell out), designate specific people to photograph from crowd for better coverage and angles, and basket for lids plus other organizational details matter. The list shows evolution—what works (latkes, doughnuts, art table, core equipment) and what needs refinement (lighting, space, documentation). Adapt by creating digital version with quantities and costs, maintain master supply box year-round, and immediately document improvements after each event while fresh. The specificity ("Banana Court," "Byerlys," "yard stick for Chabad sign") shows this is real battle-tested wisdom, not theoretical planning.

# [Misc > For Writer > _5 Chanukah > General] Complete Operations Guide for Public Menorahs

## Comprehensive Resource: Technical, Strategic, and Halachic

**Coverage:** Lighting equipment, opposition strategies, halachic guidelines, practical tips

**Format:** Forum discussions, resource links, real-world examples

---

## Section 1: What to Use to Light a Public Menorah

### Overview

**For Outdoor:** Tiki torches
**For Indoor:** Candle conversion kit
**Critical:** Make sure wicks are pulled out enough

---

### Best Lighting Tool

**Recommended:**
> "Best to use a Blow torch or butane torch taped to a stick or pole"

**Why:**
- Reliable ignition
- Works in wind
- Easy to control
- Can reach high

**Avoid:**
> "Very difficult to use a tiki torch to light the other candles"

**Problems with Using Tiki to Light:**
- Tiki cover gets in the way
- Tilting makes fuel spill
- Takes 60 seconds per candle
- Oil spills everywhere
- Inefficient

---

### Option 1: Tiki Torch

**Advantages:**
- Pretty powerful
- Works well in wind
- Good flame
- Traditional look

**Fuel Options:**

**1. Tiki Brand Torch Fuel**
- Available at Home Depot/Lowe's
- Standard product
- Easy to find

**2. Paraffin**
- Alternative fuel
- Bring insert to Home Depot
- Find best fit for your torch
- Works well

**Wick Configuration:**
- Only has 1 wick (big, but just 1)
- Good for menorah
- Not good for Havdalah (need multiple wicks)

**Setup:**
- Unless you have different type
- Standard tiki has single wick
- Check your specific model

---

### Option 2: Candle Conversion Kit

**Components:**
- Paraffin fuel
- Glass chimney
- Professional look

**Best For:**
- Indoor menorahs
- Klarr menorah
- When tiki conversion not available

**Alternative Method:**
> "I did tape and big candles"

**When No Kit Available:**
- Use tape
- Secure big candles
- Workable solution

---

### Option 3: Gas Lantern

**Important Specification:**
> "Make sure that it is ONE Mantel (wick) not two"

**Recommended Model:**
- Coleman One-Mantle Compact Propane Lantern
- Available on Amazon
- Propane-powered

**Fuel Duration:**
- One propane can: about 4 hours on high
- Sufficient for event
- Easy refueling

**Product Link (from 2009):**
http://www.amazon.com/Coleman-One-Mantle-Compact-Propane-Lantern/dp/B0009PUR54/ref=sr_1_35?s=sporting-goods&ie=UTF8&qid=1286520336&sr=1-35

---

### Giant Menorah Conversion Kit

**Commercial Solution:**
- Available from ShlichusMarket.com
- Purpose-built for menorahs
- Professional-grade

**Link:**
https://www.shlichusmarket.com/holiday-supplies/chanukah/candle-lighting-kit.html

**Advantages:**
- Designed for purpose
- Reliable
- Professional appearance
- Consistent results

---

### PSA: Don't Forget Lighters!

> "PSA. Never forget a lighter for your Menorah lighting event. These days Noone has lighters on them 😬🤦🏻‍♂️"

**Modern Reality:**
- People don't carry lighters anymore
- Less smoking
- Can't count on crowd
- Bring multiple lighters
- Have backup matches
- Check batteries in electric lighters

---

## Section 2: Dignitaries and Invitations

### Resources

**Dignitary Materials Folder:**
https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1N8VrGXGDzd-ce-CyRZFbYdMD_1lJHVpX?usp=share_link

---

### Sample Invitation: Liverpool Example

**Context:**
- Fifth year of public menorah
- 20-foot menorah
- Outside St. George's Hall
- Lord Mayor participating

---

**Full Invitation Text:**

```
Dear Mr. & Mrs. [Name]

This Chanukah, for the fifth time, we will be having a Public Menorah lighting ceremony in Liverpool City Centre. The 20-foot menorah will be erected outside St. George's Hall and lighting will take place every evening at 6:00.

As a friend and long-time supporter of Lubavitch Foundation Liverpool, please accept this personal invitation to attend the special communal lighting ceremony, which will take place at 6:00 on Tuesday evening, December 3, the 5th candle of Chanukah, in the presence of the Lord Mayor of Liverpool. This will be an event for the entire community, young and old, not to be missed.

Wishing you a very joyous Chanukah,

Rabbi Avremi Kievman
Lubavitch Liverpool
```

---

**Invitation Analysis:**

**Personal Touch:**
- "Dear Mr. & Mrs." (personalized)
- "Friend and long-time supporter" (relationship acknowledged)
- "Personal invitation" (not mass mailing)
- Rabbi's signature

**Key Information:**
- When: Tuesday evening, December 3, 6:00
- Where: Outside St. George's Hall, Liverpool City Centre
- What: 5th candle lighting
- Who: Lord Mayor of Liverpool present
- Duration: Lighting every evening at 6:00

**Appeal:**
- Established tradition ("fifth time")
- Prestigious location (St. George's Hall)
- High-profile participation (Lord Mayor)
- Community event ("entire community, young and old")
- "Not to be missed" (FOMO appeal)

## Section 4: Ideas to Jazz Up Small Town Menorah Lighting

### The Challenge

**Initial Post:**
> "We have been doing a public menorah in our small and cold town. Have done a juggler, magician at a free party we host right after. But its getting boring though and people are taking for granted (smaller numbers etc). Any ideas to make it exciting for adults and kids who stopped coming to want to come again?"

**Common Problem:**
- Initial excitement wears off
- Attendance declining
- Same format boring
- Taking it for granted
- Need fresh ideas

---

### Ideas from Forum

#### Idea 1: Fire Dancers

**Suggestion:** Fire dancers

**Warning:**
> "Fire Dancers warning. We had a mix up and the female dancer that showed up was not dressed for the right event."

**Lesson:**
- Specify appropriate attire
- Family event standards
- Check in advance
- Get photos/videos of past performances
- Tznius concerns

---

#### Idea 2: Multiple Enhancements

**Shaliach's Success Story:**
> "Experiencing the same problem and a very dwindled crowd... we added the following. Over the years (each year adding something else, and BH the last few years has been successful)"

**Strategy:** Incremental additions, not all at once

---

**Enhancement #1: Day of Week Matters**
> "The day of the week matters, we found Sunday to be best."

**Why Sunday:**
- No work/school next day
- Families available
- Can stay later
- Better attendance
- More relaxed

---

**Enhancement #2: Dreidel Mascot**
> "Dreidle mascot (we had ours made locally, Shluchim services now has a blow up one)"

**Options:**
- Custom-made locally (original approach)
- Blow-up version from Shluchim Services (newer option)

**Appeal:**
- Kids love mascots
- Photo opportunities
- Recognizable symbol
- Fun atmosphere
- Social media friendly

---

**Enhancement #3: Special Gift**
> "Special gift (one year we did the light up menorah necklace, and one year the light up dreidle glasses (both from Shluchim services))"

**Examples:**
- Light-up menorah necklaces
- Light-up dreidel glasses
- From Shluchim Services

**Why This Works:**
- People come for free gift
- Kids want them
- Wearable = walking advertisement
- Unique each year
- Something to take home

---

**Enhancement #4: Doughnut Decorating Station**
> "Doughnut decorating station (doughnuts bought from my bakery, the station had icing (large bucket bought at sams club), sprinkles, chocolate chips etc)"

**Setup:**
- Plain doughnuts from local bakery
- Large bucket of icing (Sam's Club)
- Sprinkles
- Chocolate chips
- Other toppings

**Why Popular:**
- Interactive activity
- Kids engaged while waiting
- Creative outlet
- Everyone loves doughnuts
- Keeps people longer
- Instagram-worthy

---

**Enhancement #5: Real Chanukah Gelt**
> "Real chanukah gelt - got crisp one dollar bills from bank (make sure to ask bank in advance)"

**Details:**
- Actual money, not chocolate
- Crisp $1 bills
- Order from bank in advance
- Bank needs notice for crisp bills

**Why Effective:**
- Real value
- Memorable
- Kids excited about money
- Different from chocolate
- Talk about it later
- "They gave out real money!"

---

#### Idea 3: Kibudim (Honors)

**Strategy:**
> "Just one eitza on top of all these, give kibudim, they will bring their family and friends, children could sing a song so all their families will come..."

**Honor Ideas:**
- Light a candle
- Recite blessing
- Lead song
- Children sing song
- Read explanation
- Welcome guests

**Psychology:**
- Honoree brings whole family
- Family brings friends
- Invested in success
- Share on social media
- More attendees
- Personal connection

---

#### Idea 4: Comprehensive Strategy

**From Shaliach Facing Same Challenge:**
> "Big challenge. Here are some things we tried"

---

**Strategy #1: Rename the Event**
> "If you haven't done so yet, change the event name to 'Chanukah celebration' from 'menorah lighting'"

**Why:**
- "Menorah lighting" sounds brief
- "Chanukah celebration" sounds like party
- More than just lighting
- Full experience
- Broader appeal

---

**Strategy #2: Ice Menorah**
> "Ice menorah when possible is a big hit."

**Wow Factor:**
- Unique
- Instagram-worthy
- Memorable
- Different every time
- Weather-dependent but special

---

**Strategy #3: Perspective on Variations**
> "Keep in mind that years vary and have ups and downs. Weather and vacation times make a difference."

**Don't Panic:**
- Some years just better
- Weather affects turnout
- Holiday schedules vary
- Chanukah dates change
- Week before Christmas different than week after
- Not always your fault

---

**Strategy #4: Search for Entertainers**
> "Search and search for entertainers. We just found a fire eater and performers whom we didn't know about by asking and asking and asking."

**Persistence:**
- Keep looking
- Ask everyone
- Hidden talents in community
- New performers arrive
- Try different searches
- Call entertainment agencies

---

**Strategy #5: Hot Chocolate**
> "Hot chocolate is a big hit."

**Why:**
- Cold weather
- Warms people up
- Keeps people longer
- Kids love it
- Inexpensive
- Easy to prepare
- Seasonal appeal

---

**Strategy #6: Aggressive Follow-Up**
> "As with every event: calls, calls, text, calls, emails, calls, negotiations ('I think I would rather hang out in Starbucks' 'I have to pack for my trip in two weeks'), and rsvp list (for yourself to know)."

**Reality:**
- People need multiple reminders
- Text, call, email, repeat
- Negotiate with excuses
- Track RSVPs
- Personal outreach
- Don't assume people remember

---

## Section 5: Fire Truck Menorah

### Innovative Idea for Future

**The Concept:**
> "In our area, the firemen go around to neighborhoods before December 25 giving out candy canes."

**Chanukah Version:**
> "We put a Menorah on a Fire Truck and went around to neighborhoods giving out Chanukah Gelt and Dreidels."

---

### How It Worked

**Partnership:**
- Fire Chief in Chabad House
- Asked if could do something for Chanukah
- Fire department cooperation

**Route Planning:**
- Set up specific route
- Told people we were coming
- Asked them to get neighbors
- Six neighborhoods in two hours

**The Experience:**
- Lights flashing
- Chanukah music on loudspeakers
- Giving out gelt and dreidels
- Over 100 people in some neighborhoods
- Impressive sight

---

### The Impact

**Kiddush Hashem:**
> "It was a Kiddush Hashem"

**Community Response:**
- People loved it
- Previously only saw this for Christmas
- Equal treatment
- Recognition

**Fire Department:**
> "The firemen...said that for next year we need to plan on doing it for more than one night"

- Firemen enjoyed it
- Want to expand
- Became annual tradition
- Their enthusiasm

**Outreach:**
> "Got us to meet a bunch of people who we never who have Met"

- New contacts
- Neighborhoods reached
- People came out
- Word spread

---

### Replicating This

**If Your Area Has Similar:**
> "If you have a similar system with firemen going around before December 25, ask them if they would be willing to do something for Chanukah as well."

**Key:**
- Existing Christmas tradition
- Request equal treatment
- Chanukah parallel
- Fire department willing
- Community expects it

**Credit:** Sholom Raichik

---

## Section 6: Important Sicha About Public Lighting

### Not Yotzei with Public Menorah

**Critical Information:**
> "I saw this in a sicha today, where the Rebbe says that an announcement should be made by the public lighting, that one is not yotze!"

**Halachic Requirement:**
- Announce at public lighting
- People NOT yotzei with public menorah
- Must light at home
- Public is in addition, not replacement
- Important to clarify

**Why Announce:**
- People might think they fulfilled obligation
- Need to light at home still
- Public is pirsumei nisa (publicizing miracle)
- Personal obligation separate
- Educational moment

---

## Section 7: City Wants to Copy Event

### Time-Sensitive Issue

**The Situation:**
> "We are planning the first public menorah lighting in our city. We confirmed the place we will be doing it and got the Mayor's confirmation that he will be joining. Then someone from the Mayor's office contacted me and told me that the Mayor is only available on a different day and that the city likes the idea (of a public menorah lighting) so much that they are planning to do it (with our menorah in the place that we arranged) every day that we are not doing it."

**The Problem:**
- City wants to take over event
- Use your menorah
- Different days
- Mayor at their event, not yours
- Their own publicity
- Replacing your event

---

### Advice from Forum

**Response #1: Combine Efforts**
> "You might want to point out that you will bring your community and it is more effective to combine efforts for one big night"

**Plus:**
> "We in chabad are good marketers and can bring ppl that wouldn't come otherwise plus you'll make it more fun with party kids entertainment etc which they won't do"

**Argument:**
- Better to combine
- One big event better than multiple small
- You bring community
- You bring marketing
- You bring entertainment
- More successful together

---

**Response #2: Community Connection**
> "U can tell then The reason you want this to be one coordination is because in a small town it is important that people get to know other people in the Jewish community so the more the merrier"

> "It would be silly to have 2 parties for a smallish Jewish community"

**Framing:**
- Small Jewish community
- Unity important
- Meeting each other matters
- Splitting attendance silly
- Stronger together

---

**Response #3: Alternative for Mayor**
> "If the mayor cant be there on that day have him send other city representative on his behalf -it works just fine"

**Solution:**
- Deputy mayor
- City council member
- Other official
- Mayor sends greetings
- Not worth splitting event

---

**Response #4: Your Value-Add**
> "Bottom line : with you involved it will be on a much grander scale and they will look strange doing they're own thing (besides that your party will be better etc)"

> "Maybe bring another community member with u to share their perspective like yours"

**Strategy:**
- Emphasize your expertise
- City doing it alone looks strange
- Your event will be better
- Bring community member to meeting
- Show community support

---

**Response #5: You're Lighting Every Night Anyway**
> "But you are lighting it every night, aren't you? Maybe change the date of your 'big event' to accommodate mayor."

> "Also explain to them that its not 'your' event but its The Community event. you are thrilled that they want there to be a lighting event each night and you will be happy to facilitate."

**Reframe:**
- You're doing nightly lighting anyway
- One is "big event"
- Others are daily lighting
- Community event, not Chabad event
- Offer to facilitate all nights
- Takes over their plan

---

## Section 8: Opposition from Reform

### The Scenario

**Initial Problem:**
> "I had a public menorah lighting arranged in the only mall in town. The flyers are printed, the word is out! I just received a call from the manager at the mall canceling it, because the Reform Rabbi met him and told him that it offends his congregation."

**Context:**
- Only moved there 6 weeks ago
- Reform rabbi "hates Chabad"
- Dedicated Rosh Hashana sermon to opposing Chabad
- Active opposition
- Last-minute cancellation

---

### The Question

**Three Parts:**
a) Any way to get around this?
b) Anyone with menorah in Simon Property Group mall? (for list to show mall)
c) How to deal with him long-term?

**Shaliach:** Zalmy Heber, Tacoma, Washington

---

### Responses

#### Response #1: Media Threat

**From Simcha Backman:**
> "He basically told them that he already informed the media about it and that they were planning on coming and that if you tell them that you are canceling and why it will bring them tremendous negative publicity specially during the holiday season."

**Strategy:**
- Already told media
- Media planning coverage
- Cancellation = negative PR
- Especially during holidays
- "Rabbi says menorah offensive" headline
- Mall looks bad

**Effectiveness:**
- Mall fears bad press
- Holiday season sensitivity
- Don't want controversy
- Rabbi looking intolerant
- Mall caught in middle

---

#### Response #2: Caution for New Shluchim

**From Reb Dov Mandel:**
> "Bichlal, I don't think that it is a good idea to enetr a small town with a big splash like that. oros detohu bekeilim detikun. Just my heretical opinion. Specially in the beginning, you need to avoid putting yourself in a situation where you are vulnerable and don't have balebatim to back you in the community."

**Philosophy:**
- Don't start with big splash
- "Oros detohu bekeilim detikun" (lights of chaos in vessels of order)
- Build slowly
- Get community backing first
- Avoid vulnerable positions
- Especially when new

---

#### Response #3: Opposite View

**From Chaim Zvi Konikov:**
> "Zalmy, I prefer to differ with Reb Dov, You have the biggest BB (Kaviyochol) - the Rebbe - backing you. When I first stepped into town, our biggest success was our 'splash' in the mall - same scenario as you with the rabbis etc 'publicizing' our presence from the pulpets."

**Counter-Philosophy:**
- Rebbe backing you
- Big splash worked for him
- Same scenario (rabbi opposition)
- Rabbi opposition publicized Chabad
- Success story

**His Experience:**
> "I received a 5-6 line answer from the Rebbe right after the duch was submitted."

- Direct guidance from Rebbe
- Positive response
- Rebbe encouraged

---

**Practical Advice:**
> "I would suggest you play totally dumb. Be real nice but tell the mngr that you already invited the world to come (tell her something like - the Chief Rabbi of Kiev.. is coming - already bought his tickets) and there's no way you can stop it from here."

**Tactics:**
- Play innocent
- Too far along to stop
- Important people coming
- Tickets bought
- No way to cancel now
- Make it their problem, not yours

**Simon Corporation Info:**
> "For the facts about the Simon Corporation, just from reading this forum there must be many Shluchim using them this year. We for one, are using them - Melbourne Square Mall. (so is Yosef Konikov in Orlando - I think it's called The Florida Mall - both under Simon."

- Build list of Simon malls with menorahs
- Show it's common practice
- Precedent at corporate level
- Other locations doing it

---

#### Response #4: Context Matters

**From Reb Dov Mandel (Follow-up):**
> "Keep in mind that perhaps your community is larger than Zalmy Heber's. Just the fact that you mention that there are various other synagogues shows that you do. You have to be very careful when addressing new shluchim as they will literally follow your advice from this forum otherwise they wouldn't be asking here."

**Important Point:**
- Different situations
- Your community ≠ his community
- Advice not always universal
- Consider context
- New Shluchim follow advice literally
- Be responsible

**Rebbe's Guidance Varies:**
> "Just because the Rebbe told you to do it in your place doesn't mean that it applies everywhere. From what I understand Rabbi Shlomo Cunin was told by the Rebbe to fir zich lechatchiula ariber. Other shluchim however were told to do it bemedida vehagbala."

- R' Cunin: "Fir zich lechatchiula ariber" (charge ahead full force)
- Others: "Bemedida vehagbala" (with measure and limitation)
- Different guidance for different situations
- Can't copy someone else's approach
- Need to know your situation

**Warning:**
> "I have heard guys moving in to small communities talking about acting like Rabbi Cunin in their place. This is a distortion of reality that gets them in to big trouble."

---

#### Response #5: Don't Fight Without Support

**From Laizer Gurkov:**
> "I agree with Rabbi Mandel. In my town there is a lot of opposition to menorah on public property especially from the Reform and Conservative clergy. Rabbi Yudel Krinsky told me that I should befayrush NOT put up a menorah on public property until I have a lot of community support."

**Guidance from RYK:**
- Don't create machlokes
- Despite Rebbe's chavivus for public menorah
- Not kedai without support
- Build support first
- Then do menorah

---

#### Response #6: Success Story - Fight Put Them on Map

**From Zalman Bukiet (Boca Raton):**
> "When we came to boca raton the first fight we had with all the rabbis in the city was about the menorah and it put us on the map. we won the fight and got great publicity."

**Different Result:**
- Fight happened
- Won the fight
- Great publicity
- Put Chabad on map
- Established presence

**But Note:** Boca Raton ≠ Tacoma (different size, different dynamics)

---

#### Response #7: Opposition Can Turn Around

**From Yossie and Chanie Nemes (New Orleans):**
> "The first Shabbos I came to town (I was also Rabbi in a tiny Young Israel) the President of the Reform Congregation across the street was in Shul before me. He used to be called as a Tzenter. When I walked in, he came over and said 'My Rabbi in N.Y. thinks you are the worst thing to happen to New Orleans in the last twenty years!.' He then stormed out of the trailer. Today he comes a few times a year to Chabad and even donates a few hundred dollars."

**Lesson:**
- Fierce initial opposition
- "Worst thing in twenty years"
- But over time...
- Now attends Chabad
- Now donates
- Relationships can change

**Encouragement:**
> "ZALMY hang in there and always remain positive!"

---

#### Response #8: Nuanced View on Public Property

**From Laizer Gurkov (Clarification):**
> "Of course you are right that there is a difference between public property and private property. What RYK told me was that the Rebbe was not encouraging shluchim to create machlokes and that despite the chavivus the Rebbe felt for the inyan of menorah davka in public property, it was not kedai to begin a machlokes without support."

**Distinction:**
- Public property (government) = constitutional right, stronger case
- Private property (mall) = owner's choice, weaker case
- But even with right, avoid machlokes if no support
- Rebbe valued menorah but valued shalom too
- Pick battles strategically

**Additional Advice:**
> "BTW, aside from the menorah issue, the new shliach might benefit from a personal meeting with the Reform clergyman."

- Meet personally
- Build relationship
- Not just fight
- Long-term presence
- May reduce opposition

---

### Synthesis: When to Fight, When to Wait

**Fight (or Push Hard) When:**
- You have community support
- Public property (stronger rights)
- Larger community
- Established presence
- Bad to back down now
- Rebbe's specific guidance to "charge ahead"

**Wait (or Build First) When:**
- New to community (6 weeks!)
- No community backing
- Private property (weaker case)
- Small community
- More to lose than gain
- Vulnerable position

**Strategy for Mall Situation:**
- Media threat (already public)
- Simon Corporation precedent
- "Too far along to stop"
- But also...
- Meet Reform rabbi personally
- Build relationships
- Think long-term

## Section 10: Halacha of Public Menorah

### 15 Halachic Guidelines

**Source:** Compiled halachic guidelines for public menorah lightings

---

**1. Location**
> "It is a great Mitzvah to light Chanukah lights in the thoroughfares of the city 'in the most public and central location'."

---

**2. Sheva Mitzvos Bnai Noach**
> "The occasion of the public Menorah lighting should be utilized to also highlight the Sheva Mitzvos Bnai Noach."

**Educational opportunity for universal values**

---

**3. Announcement About Personal Obligation**
> "It is important to inform those present that the public Menorah lighting does not fulfill one's personal obligation to light Chanukah lights and that it is incumbent upon each individual to light Chanukah lights at home."

**Critical announcement - must make clear**

---

**4. Bracha Despite Not Being Yotzei**
> "Nevertheless, we recite a Brocho at the public lighting, similar to the Halacha regarding the lighting of Chanukah lights in a Shul etc."

**Bracha is appropriate even though not fulfilling personal obligation**

---

**5. Tznius - Women Don't Make Bracha**
> "For reason of Tznius we do not honor a woman with making the Brocho."

**Women can light, but man makes bracha**

---

**6. Multiple Honorees**
> "A number of individuals may be honored to each kindle a Chanukah light. However, when doing so all the announcements of the names etc, should be made prior to the Brocho so as not to make a Hefsek between the Brocho and kindling of all the lights."

**Process:**
1. Announce all names first
2. Make bracha
3. Then light all candles
4. No interruption between bracha and lighting

---

**7. Non-Jews and the Shamash**
> "A non-Jew should not be honored to light a Chanukah light. Instead, many will honor a non-Jew with kindling the Shamash – which is acceptable."

**Compromise:**
- Non-Jew shouldn't light actual candles
- But can light shamash
- Honors them appropriately
- Halachically sound

---

**8. Height Restriction**
> "The height of the Menorah should not exceed twenty cubits from the ground, i.e. the lowest part of the lights should be within twenty cubits of the ground."

**20 cubits = approximately 30 feet**

**Measure from:**
- Lowest part of flames
- To ground
- Not top of menorah

---

**9. Real Flames Preferred**
> "Whenever it is possible, one should use real flames for the public Chanukah lights, rather than using electric lights - as a Brocho cannot be recited on electric lights."

**Priority:**
1. Real flames (can make bracha)
2. Electric lights (no bracha)

---

**10. No Bracha on Gas or Butane**
> "Likewise, a Brocho should not be recited on lights which are fueled by gas or butane."

**Fuel types:**
- Kerosene: Yes, bracha
- Gas: No bracha
- Butane: No bracha
- Oil: Yes, bracha

---

**11. Kerosene Lights**
> "Many kindle the public menorah using kerosene lights, and there's sufficient Halachic basis for that."

**Kerosene:**
- Widely used
- Halachically sound
- Bracha permitted
- Practical for outdoors

---

**12. Minyan Preferred**
> "Effort should be made to kindle the public Menorah in the presence of at least ten people. However, when that is not achieved, a Brocho may nevertheless be recited."

**Ideal:** 10 people (minyan)
**Minimum:** Can do with less, still make bracha

---

**13. Timing**
> "The earliest time that the Menorah may be lit is Plag Hamincha, but there should be sufficient fuel for the lights to last at least 30 minutes past nightfall."

**Earliest:** Plag HaMincha
**Fuel requirement:** Lasts 30 minutes past nightfall (tzeis)

---

**14. Gender Separation**
> "As with all public events, effort should be made to achieve gender separation."

**Mechitza:**
- Try to implement
- Seating arrangements
- Separate areas
- As feasible

---

**15. Daily Lighting**
> "With the menorah it should be let/ turn on every day, and not all at once"

**Important:**
- Light each day's candles on that day
- Not all at once
- Follow actual Chanukah progression
- Educational value

---

---

**Bottom Line:**
This comprehensive operations guide covers everything from technical lighting solutions (blow torch on stick beats tiki torch for lighting, kerosene for fuel, Coleman one-mantle lantern works, need multiple lighters - no one carries them anymore) to opposition strategies (Reform/Conservative often oppose, media threat works for malls, personal meeting helps long-term, don't fight without community support if new) to critical halacha (announce people NOT yotzei with public menorah, non-Jew can light shamash not actual candles, no bracha on gas/butane but yes on kerosene, max 20 cubits height, women shouldn't make bracha for tznius). For declining attendance: rename to "Chanukah celebration" not "menorah lighting," add doughnut decorating station, real dollar bills as gelt from bank, dreidel mascot, light-up necklaces/glasses, give out kibudim so honorees bring family, hot chocolate, Sunday works best, pre-order supplies from Shluchim Services during Kinus. Fire truck menorah innovation: partner with fire department doing Christmas candy cane rounds, put menorah on truck with music and flashing lights, visit 6 neighborhoods in 2 hours giving gelt/dreidels, huge kiddush Hashem. When city wants to copy your event: emphasize you bring community/marketing/entertainment, better one big event than split small Jewish community, offer to facilitate daily lightings with mayor at your main event. The Reform opposition debate: some say charge ahead with Rebbe's backing (worked in Boca), others say build support first before creating machlokes (especially new Shluchim in small towns), RYK guidance varies by situation, even fierce opponents may come around over time.

# [Misc > For Writer > _5 Chanukah > General] Walmart Foundation Matching Grants

## Easy $1,000 Grants for Chanukah Events

**Program:** Walmart Foundation Community Grant Program

**Maximum Grant:** $1,000 per non-profit

**Difficulty:** Very straightforward

**Success Rate:** High (based on forum reports)

---

## Success Stories

### Report #1

> "I recently filled out a form for a matching grant at my local Wal-Mart, and today they called me to pick up a check for $1,000 (the maximum that they give per non-profit)."

**Process:**
- Filled out form
- Received call
- Picked up check for $1,000
- Simple and successful

---

### Report #2

> "B"H I recently applied and was approved for a $1,000 grant. I simply went into a Walmart store asked for a community grant application (filled it out by hand inside the store) and a few weeks later they called to let me know a check was waiting for me."

**His Application:**
- Applied as educational organization
- Described program involving teens in community service
- Hand-filled form in store
- Few weeks later: approved

**His Assessment:**
> "I don't have any additional insight to share. It was fairly simple and straightforward. I hope it is as simple for all shluchim!"

---

## How the Program Works

### Official Program Description

**From Walmart Website:**
(http://walmartstores.com/GlobalWMStoresWeb/navigate.do?catg=759)

---

### Community Grant Program Overview

> "The Community Grant Program is the largest program funded by the Wal-Mart Foundation and includes both matching and direct grants."

**Two Types of Grants:**
1. **Matching Grants** (fundraiser-based)
2. **Direct Grants** (no fundraiser needed)

---

### Matching Grant Program

**How It Works:**

**Option A: On-Premises Fundraiser**
- Local nonprofit holds fundraiser outside Walmart or Sam's Club
- Walmart/Sam's Club can match portion of funds raised
- **Up to $1,000 match**

**Option B: Off-Premises with Associate Involvement**
- Event held off Walmart/Sam's Club premises
- BUT: Walmart or Sam's Club associate actively involved
- Also eligible for funding
- Still up to $1,000

---

### Direct Grants

**After Meeting Criteria:**
- Once store/club meets certain criteria in Matching Grant Program each year
- Second source of funding unlocked: Direct Grants
- **Do not require fundraiser**
- Funds awarded directly to deserving organization
- No event needed

**This is likely what forum posters received**

---

## Eligible Organizations

### Who Qualifies

**501(c)(3) Non-Profit Organizations:**
- Standard non-profits
- With IRS tax-exempt status

**OR Organizations Exempt from Needing 501(c)(3):**
- **Public schools**
- **Faith-based institutions** (churches, synagogues, etc.)
  - Must be conducting project that benefits community at large
  - Not just internal congregation activities
- **Government agencies**

---

### Faith-Based Institution Requirement

**Key Phrase:**
> "Faith-based institutions such as churches (must be conducting a project that benefits the community at large)"

**What This Means:**
- Chabad qualifies as faith-based institution
- Project must benefit broader community
- Not just for members/attendees
- Public menorah lighting = community benefit
- Chanukah celebration = open to all
- Educational programs = community service

---

## How to Apply

### Simple Process

**Step 1: Go to Local Walmart**
- Visit your nearest Walmart store
- Or Sam's Club if you prefer

**Step 2: Ask for Form**
> "Asked for a community grant application"

- Ask at customer service
- Or ask for Community Involvement Coordinator
- They'll provide the form

**Step 3: Fill Out Application**
> "Filled it out by hand inside the store"

- Can fill out right there
- Simple form
- Hand-written fine
- Don't need fancy proposal

**Step 4: Submit**
- Give to store staff
- They process internally

**Step 5: Wait**
> "A few weeks later they called"

- Takes a few weeks
- They'll call if approved
- Pick up check at store

---

## Application Strategy

### What to Emphasize

**From Successful Application:**
> "I applied as an educational organization and wrote about a program we have that involves teens in community service."

---

**Frame as:**
1. **Educational organization**
   - Teaching Jewish heritage
   - Cultural education
   - Holiday traditions
   - Historical significance

2. **Community service component**
   - Teens involved
   - Volunteering
   - Giving back
   - Building community

3. **Benefits community at large**
   - Open to all
   - Not just members
   - Brings community together
   - Inclusive event

---

### For Chanukah Event

**Possible Description:**

```
Chabad is an educational non-profit conducting our annual Community Chanukah Celebration, a free public event celebrating religious freedom and cultural diversity. The event includes:

- Public menorah lighting ceremony
- Educational programming about Chanukah history
- Teen volunteers serving food and running activities
- Free refreshments and children's entertainment
- Open to entire community, all ages and backgrounds

This event promotes religious tolerance, celebrates America's founding principles of religious freedom, and brings our diverse community together during the holiday season. Last year we served over [X] community members.

Funds will support food, entertainment, and materials for this community-wide celebration.
```

---

## Tips for Success

### 1. Apply as Educational Organization

**Why:**
- Faith-based allowed, but educational broader
- Less potential questions
- Emphasizes programming aspect
- Community benefit clear

---

### 2. Highlight Community Service

**Examples:**
- Teen volunteers
- Serving food to community
- Free event for all
- Bringing people together
- Educational outreach

---

### 3. Emphasize "Community at Large"

**Language:**
- "Open to entire community"
- "Free public event"
- "All ages and backgrounds welcome"
- "Community-wide celebration"
- "Benefits broader community"

---

### 4. Be Specific About Use of Funds

**Good:**
- Food for community event
- Children's entertainment
- Art supplies for activities
- Event materials

**Avoid:**
- Vague "operating expenses"
- Internal congregation needs
- Religious education for members only
- Anything not clearly community-benefit

---

### 5. Keep It Simple

**Don't Overthink:**
- Simple application
- Can fill out by hand
- Few weeks turnaround
- High approval rate
- Just ask for the form

---

## When to Apply

### Timing Considerations

**For Chanukah Event:**
- Apply at least 4-6 weeks before event
- "Few weeks" processing time mentioned
- Allow buffer for any questions
- Better early than last-minute

**Annual Consideration:**
- Can apply once per year per organization
- Use strategically
- Chanukah is good timing (holiday season)
- Or use for other major program

---

## Both Walmart AND Sam's Club

### Separate Opportunities

**Walmart Store:**
- Apply at local Walmart
- Up to $1,000

**Sam's Club:**
- Separate application
- Also up to $1,000
- Same foundation
- Different location

**Could Potentially:**
- Apply at both?
- Check if allowed
- Might be separate allocations
- Each has own coordinator

---

## Contact Person

### Community Involvement Coordinator

**At Each Store:**
> "To learn more about receiving a grant from your local Wal-Mart or Sam's Club, please see the Community Involvement Coordinator at the location closest to you."

**Who They Are:**
- Store employee with this role
- Handles grant applications
- Knows the process
- Can answer questions
- Makes initial decision

**How to Find:**
- Ask at customer service
- "I'd like to speak with the Community Involvement Coordinator about a grant application"
- They'll direct you or get the person

---

## Additional Information

### Official Walmart Foundation Pages

**Community Giving:**
- http://walmartstores.com/CommunityGiving/8916.aspx
- http://walmartstores.com/CommunityGiving/238.aspx

**Note:** These links from 2000s, URLs may have changed
**Current:** Search "Walmart Foundation Community Grants" for updated site

---

### What Walmart Gets

**Benefits for Walmart:**
- Positive community relations
- Local goodwill
- Demonstrates corporate responsibility
- Relatively small investment
- Supports local nonprofits
- Good PR

**Why They're Generous:**
- Tax deductible
- Corporate giving program
- Community engagement strategy
- Makes locations good neighbors
- Small amounts, big impact

---

## For Multiple Locations

### If You Have Multiple Shluchim Nearby

**Different Stores:**
- Each Walmart is separate
- Each has own coordinator
- Each has own allocation
- Multiple Chabads could apply to different stores

**Don't:**
- Apply to same store multiple times
- Duplicate applications
- Appear to game system

**Do:**
- Each Shliach use their local store
- Apply for your specific program
- Independent applications
- Legitimate if truly separate organizations

---

## Record Keeping

### Documentation

**Save:**
- Copy of application
- Approval notice
- Check/deposit record
- Correspondence

**Why:**
- Tax records
- Future applications
- Show donors/board
- Reference for next year

**Thank You:**
- Thank you note to coordinator
- Recognition in event materials
- "Supported by Walmart Foundation"
- Photo opportunity with check?

---

## Matching Grant vs. Direct Grant

### Understanding the Difference

**Matching Grant:**
- You hold fundraiser
- Raise money
- Walmart matches up to $1,000
- Doubles your fundraising

**Direct Grant:**
- No fundraiser needed
- Walmart just gives
- Up to $1,000
- Based on store's status in program

---

### Which One for You?

**Direct Grant Seems Easier:**
- Forum posts sound like direct grants
- No fundraiser needed
- Just application
- Straight $1,000

**Ask Coordinator:**
- "Does your store have direct grant funding available?"
- If yes: apply for that
- If no: consider matching grant with event

**Matching Grant with Event:**
- Could hold menorah lighting
- Pass pushka
- "Fundraiser" for Chabad programs
- Walmart matches up to $1,000
- Get both: donations + match

---

## Common Questions

### Q: Can any 501(c)(3) apply?

**A:** Yes, plus faith-based and schools
- Need community benefit
- Not internal-only programs

---

### Q: How long does approval take?

**A:** "Few weeks" mentioned
- Not immediate
- Not months
- Budget 4-6 weeks to be safe

---

### Q: Can I apply online?

**A:** Process seems in-person
- Go to store
- Ask for form
- Fill out there
- Hand to coordinator

---

### Q: What if denied?

**A:** Try again next year
- Ask for feedback
- Adjust application
- Different store if nearby
- But approval rate seems high

---

### Q: Can I use for anything?

**A:** Must benefit community at large
- Community events
- Public programs
- Educational activities
- Service projects
- Not: Operating expenses, salaries, etc.

---

## Success Factors

### Why These Applications Succeeded

**1. Simple, Clear Application**
- Not complicated
- Direct description
- Specific program

**2. Community Benefit Obvious**
- Open to all
- Public event
- Community service
- Educational

**3. Legitimate Non-Profit**
- 501(c)(3) or faith-based
- Real organization
- Established presence

**4. Appropriate Use of Funds**
- Event expenses
- Materials
- Food
- Programming
- Not vague or inappropriate

---

- [ ] Answer any questions if called
- [ ] If approved: pick up check
- [ ] Deposit and document

**After Event:**
- [ ] Send photos to coordinator
- [ ] Thank you note
- [ ] Consider for next year

---

## Budget Planning

### $1,000 Grant Covers

**For Chanukah Event:**
- Food: $300-400
  - Latkes
  - Doughnuts
  - Drinks
- Entertainment: $200-300
  - Musician/performer
  - Or supplies for activities
- Materials: $150-200
  - Art supplies
  - Giveaways
  - Signage
- Gelt/Treats: $100-150
  - Chocolate gelt
  - Dreidels
  - Take-home items

**$1,000 goes far for community event**

---

## Additional Grant Programs

### Walmart Has More

**Local Grants:** What we discussed

**State Grants:** Larger amounts
- More competitive
- Different application
- Higher thresholds

**National Grants:** Major initiatives
- Significant funding
- Very competitive
- Specific focuses

**Start with Local:**
- Easiest
- Most accessible
- Build relationship
- Success enables future asks

---

## Sam's Club Specifics

### Same Foundation, Separate Process

**Sam's Club:**
- Same parent company (Walmart)
- Same foundation
- Same grant amounts
- Separate store management
- Separate coordinator
- Separate application

**If You're Sam's Member:**
- Good relationship entry point
- "I shop here regularly"
- Known face
- Easier conversation

---

## Relationship Building

### Beyond the Grant

**Long-Term Value:**
- Relationship with coordinator
- Future grants possible
- Partnership opportunities
- Corporate donations
- In-kind support

**Maintain Relationship:**
- Thank you notes
- Event invitations
- Progress updates
- Annual applications
- Recognition

---

**Bottom Line:**
Walmart Foundation Community Grants provide straightforward $1,000 funding for non-profits with simple in-store application process—just walk into local Walmart, ask Community Involvement Coordinator for grant application, fill out by hand (can do right there), submit, and wait few weeks for approval call. Multiple Shluchim report success: "fairly simple and straightforward." Eligible organizations include 501(c)(3) nonprofits plus faith-based institutions (like Chabad) conducting projects benefiting "community at large"—key is framing as open public event, not internal congregation programming. Winning strategy from forum: apply as "educational organization" describing "program involving teens in community service"—emphasize community benefit, open to all, educational component. For Chanukah event, frame as celebrating religious freedom and cultural diversity, free public celebration, teen volunteers, benefits entire community. Two grant types: matching grants (up to $1,000 match for fundraisers) and direct grants (straight $1,000, no fundraiser needed—this is what forum posters received). Apply 4-6 weeks before event, be specific about fund use (food, entertainment, materials), keep description simple and clear. Both Walmart AND Sam's Club offer separate grants—each location has own allocation. Save documentation, send thank-you note and photos after event, build relationship with coordinator for future years. $1,000 covers substantial portion of community Chanukah event costs. Start with local grants (easiest), then explore state/national programs once established.

**End of Document 87**

# [Misc > For Writer > _5 Chanukah > General] Sponsorship Program: 8 Candles = 8 Sponsors at $1,000 Each

## Elegant Fundraising Through Candle Sponsorship

**Concept:** Honor 8 individuals/couples with lighting candles, $1,000 sponsorship each

**Total Raised:** $8,000+ (plus additional sponsors when program oversubscribed)

**Experience:** "Remarkably successful" - could be used by Shluchim in many ways

---

## The Forum Post

### Initial Share

> "We just concluded our Chanukah event (Yehudah Glantz Concert & Menorah Lighting) and thought to share an idea that was remarkably successful and could be used by shluchim in many ways to add both class and financial success to your program."

**Event:** Yehudah Glantz Concert & Menorah Lighting

**Idea Origin:**
> "(similar to what has been posted on this forum a few years ago)"

**Results:**
> "B"H the results were so good that we had to add independent candlesticks to the menorah."

**Translation:** More than 8 sponsors! Had to add extra candles.

---

## The Concept

### Basic Structure

**Selection:**
> "We selected 8 individuals from the community to be honored with the lighting of 'our symbolic Menorah' and asked them for a sponsorship of $1000 each."

**Process:**
1. Identify potential sponsors
2. Send personalized letters
3. Request $1,000 sponsorship
4. Honor with candle lighting at ceremony
5. Public recognition with grammen

---

### The Ask

**Outreach:**
> "We sent letters to many potential sponsors"

**Multiple approaches:**
- Written invitation letters
- Personal follow-up
- Clear value proposition
- Specific honor

---

## The Ceremony

### The Experience

**Setting the Scene:**

**Young Girl Reader:**
- Read grammen (rhyming verses)
- Theme: light and giving
- Each stanza concluded with sponsor's name
- Called them to stage

**Music:**
- As honorees walked up: "There's a Light" (from Miracle Days video)
- For first half
- Then switched to "Candles" (from HASC 4 Disc 2 Track 8)
- Professional atmosphere

**Elegant Touch:**
- Girl elegantly dressed
- Small table with white tablecloth on stage
- Handed candle to each sponsor
- Refined presentation

---

### The Impact

> "The couples who came up felt like a million bucks, especially with the music, spotlight and ambience, walked like they were going down the aisle to their wedding."

**Emotional Experience:**
- Music playing
- Spotlight on them
- Walking to stage
- Everyone watching
- Handed candle elegantly
- Like wedding processional
- Felt honored and special

---

### FOMO Effect

> "This was the first time I think balebatim (those who didn't respond to the letter) really felt left out that they didn't participate."

**Powerful:**
- Those who said no regretted it
- Saw how special it was
- Felt left out
- Easier ask next year
- Social proof effect

---

## The Materials

### Documents Available

**Uploaded to ShluchimExchange.com:**
1. Letters of request for potential sponsors
2. Grammen (rhyming verses)
3. Program handout (includes lyrics to songs)
4. 2 audio tracks

**Also Available:**
- Photos from newspaper
- Online gallery

---

## The Grammen

### Format and Structure

**Pattern:**
- 4-6 lines per stanza
- Theme related to light, giving, miracles
- Connection to Chanukah story
- Concludes with sponsor's names
- Call to come up and light candle

---
