# [Misc > For Writer > _5 Chanukah > General] Community Seder Tips and Best Practices

## Note: Passover Content (Not Chanukah)

**Resource Type:** Practical advice compilation from Shluchim

**Source:** Shluchim Exchange community discussion

**Purpose:** Share successful strategies for public/community Sedarim

**Format:** Six major topics with multiple perspectives and practical tips

**Audience:** Shluchim planning community Passover Sedarim

---

## 1) To Charge or Not to Charge

### Strategy A: "Suggested Donation"

**Approach:**
> "We offer a 'suggested donation.' Almost everyone chooses the paying option! People want to feel comfortable eating as much as they want and drinking as much as they want - and they do!"

**Benefits:**
- Optional but encouraged
- Removes guilt about consumption
- Most choose to pay
- Dignified approach

---

### Strategy B: Deposit System

**Experience Shared:**
> "When we didn't charge we had a load of RSVPs and half didn't show up. We are on a college campus."

**Solution:**
> "The next year we charged with the option to click 'I can't afford it now'. (we only charge about $25, it's really just a deposit to make sure we get cancellations or don't waste food)."

**Result:**
> "Anyway, that first year we began 'charging' we got more people than before."

**Benefits:**
- Reduces no-shows
- Prevents food waste
- "Can't afford" option preserves dignity
- $25 = deposit not full cost
- Actually increases attendance

---

### The Rebbe's Guidance: Yechidus to Chief Rabbis

**Source:**
> "In the yechidus to the chief rabbis Shapira and Eliyahu of Israel."

**Caution:**
> "Not so simple what lessons one can derive for our public Seders in the states."

**Access:**
> "Read the transcript of the talk Hisvadyos 5746 vol 2 page 851 available on otzar770"

> "Or listen here at about 1:42: https://www.chabad.org/therebbe/article_cdo/aid/554285/jewish/26-Adar-II-5746-Yechidus-Rabonim-Haroshim.htm"

---

### The Rebbe's Six Points

**1) Not Associated with Specific Group:**
- Don't make Sedarim associated with any specific group or party
- Broad community appeal

**2) Avoid Embarrassment:**
- Don't make communal Seder where some will be embarrassed to come
- This would imply they don't have their own Seder
- Rather: Rabbi doing his Seder in public space inviting everyone

**3) Hosted by Local Rabbis:**
- Should be hosted by Rabbis of each city and town and neighborhood
- Local leadership essential

**4) Rabbis Should Be Reimbursed:**
- Rabbis should be reimbursed for expenses
- Don't expect them to cover costs

**5) Rebbe Will Be Mistatef:**
- Rebbe will be mistatef (participate/contribute)
- Get some others to
- Philanthropists in America will be happy to sponsor if organized by chief rabbinate

**6) Comfortable Flexibility:**
- People should feel comfortable staying as much or as little as they like
- No pressure to remain entire time

---

## 2) When to Start

### The Dilemma

> "There is always a question when to start after nacht [nightfall] or before."

**Important:**
> "If starting early the Rabbanim gave guidelines how to do it (like what should go first)."

---

### Strategy A: Start Early

**Rationale:**
> "For most ppl w/ young children, to hope that they'll even do that after 8:20 is overly wishful thinking."

**Additional Benefits:**
- Starting early also allows you to put on tefillin with the men before Shabbos
- Helps curb Chilul Shabbos v'yom tov
- Makes for a calm, attentive audience at the Seder
- A shorter Shulchan Oreich (meal section)
- Which in turn helps more people stay for the whole seder

---

### Strategy B: Start by Nacht (After Nightfall)

**Approach:**
> "The minhag is to start by nacht and to show how its supposed to be."

**Compromise Solution:**
> "You could announce at the beginning that we are going to do the kiddush at the earliest time appropriate, but will precede it with songs divrei torah etc. We will move quickly after the kiddush and not spend too much time in discussion and song, as we have already covered it."

**Benefits:**
- Halachically ideal
- Educational (showing proper way)
- Songs/divrei Torah fill time before kiddush
- Move quickly after since already covered material
- Demonstrates flexibility within halacha

---

## 3) Rush Through the Seder or Not

### The Reality

**Diversity of Opinion:**
> "אין דעותיהן שוות [Their views are not equal/people have different opinions] and you may hear complains from both opposites."

**Key Factor:**
> "It depends on the crowd coming."

---

### Strategy A: Different Nights, Different Paces

**Suggestion:**
> "Can do what night fast another night slow."

---

### Strategy B: Start Slow, End Fast

**Approach:**
> "Start slow, rush by end (in a way that everyone can see that it's rushed) and announce in the beginning that due to families with young children, we can't do it too long. I invite everyone to our 2nd night seder."

**Benefits:**
- Quality beginning (most memorable)
- Visible rushing (not hidden)
- Announce reason (transparency)
- Invitation to second night (deeper option)

---

### Strategy C: Authentic and Alive

**Philosophy:**
> "People who are coming to a Seder that only starts at 8:45 or 9:00 at night, aren't coming for brisket.... They're coming to experience a Seder at my table, which is authentic, alive and real."

**Approach:**
> "They want to receive my warm - full of life - experience, the way I received it from my parents, grandparents and great grandparents. So I don't feel a need to rush."

**Result:**
> "Our experience has been that people don't eat very much by the time we get to Shulchan Oirech."

**Conclusion:**
> "But ultimately, this differs from place to place."

---

### Strategy D: Two Different Sedarim

**Approach:**
> "If doing 2 nights of public sedarim, advertising one Seder more geared for families with young children and the other for adults."

**Benefits:**
> "Much easier time adapting style when the crowd is more similar, plus people know what to expect."

---

## 4) Washing Hands

### The Challenge

**Logistics:** Large group washing hands twice during Seder

---

### Efficient System

**Setup:**
> "We arrange as many washing stations as possible, and appoint a designated 'WASHER' at each station that pours the water on everyone's hands."

**Benefits:**
> "This reduces the time very significantly, especially if the 'washer' is the right person."

**Tznius Consideration:**
> "(Mitzad darkay tznius, you should consider having separate male/female 'washers', or ask a rov if a child could do the washing...)"

---

### Halachic Note

**Important Distinction:**
> "There is a deference between rochtzo and urchatz, rochtzo is not a minhag, it is a din that you make a berocho asher kidshonu bemitzvosov."

**Meaning:**
- Urchatz (first washing): Custom, no blessing
- Rochtzah (second washing): Law, with blessing
- Don't confuse the two

---

## 5) Matzah and Wine Quality

### Matzah Quality Matters

**Experience:**
> "We bought better matzah this year, Montreal for our families and Landau for Seders, both were fresh and people did eat a lot more matzah and honestly many more people fulfilled the mitzvah because the matzah was enjoyable..."

**Lesson:**
- Fresh matzah significantly impacts compliance
- People eat more when quality is better
- Actually fulfilling mitzvah (not just nibbling)
- Worth the investment

**Recommended:**
- Montreal matzah (for families)
- Landau (for Seders)
- Fresh is key

---

### Wine Quality and Variety

**Observation:**
> "On a similar note, I noticed having a variety of good quality wines (nothing too crazy expensive) causes people to actually drink four cups..."

**Lesson:**
- Variety encourages drinking
- Good quality (not necessarily expensive)
- Result: People fulfill four cups mitzvah
- Not just token sips

---

## 6) Maggid - Making It Interesting

### A) Tell the Story

**The Basic Approach:**

> "Tell the story of Yetzias Mitzraim from Yosef to Mattan Torah. Believe it or not, most Jews today don't know the story. And you can make it very exciting if you prepare."

**Why This Works:**
- Most attendees don't know full story
- Naturally engaging narrative
- Can be dramatic
- Preparation key

---

### B) Rabbi Mentz's Ideas (Conference Call)

**Resource:**
> "Rabbi Mentz from California joined a conference call in which he gave some very good ideas. It's a twenty minute recording."

**Access:**
> "https://www.freeconferencecall.com/wall/recorded_audio?audioRecordingUrl=https%3A%2F%2Frs0000.freeconferencecall.com%2Fstorage%2FsgetFCC2%2FDHZ0J%2Fa7Fk&subscriptionId=6729083"

---

### C) Cup Pyramid Building

**Activity:**
> "We put a bunch of plastic cups on each table. When it comes to a part in hagada about yiddin working, each table has to make a cup pyramid. First table wins."

**Benefits:**
- Physical activity
- Team building per table
- Competition element
- Relates to slavery/building theme

---

### D) Jokes Every 18 Minutes

**Planning:**
> "Planning this year (from a chat) print pesach jokes. Put face down on each table. Every 18 minutes another table reads their joke."

**Variation:**
> "Could do the same with inspirational words."

**Why 18 Minutes:**
- Connects to matzah (18 minutes before chametz)
- Regular intervals
- Keeps energy up
- Multiple tables participate

---

### E) Frogs in the Pond Game

**Activity:**
> "Dollar tree sells frogs in the pond game. At makkos, see with table flicks most frogs in the pond."

**Details:**
> "1. Bought this game for every table: https://www.dollartree.com/Jumpin-Frogs-Games/p397187/index.pro"

**Implementation:**
> "We sang the Ma nishtana and every table had 3 players trying to flick as many frogs into the tub before we finished the ma nishtana."

**Educational Connection:**
> "We did a similar game while that same thought 'why focus on maakos' came to mind.. We therefore explain that the focus is Hashems miracles.."

---

### F) JLI "How Jew You Do" Card Game

**Resource:**
> "We used the JLI 'How Jew You Do' card game and spread them out to the 'captains' of every table. Throughout the evening - at random times - we had different people stand up and read from them. Worked out very well."

**Ordering:**
- JLI game Amazon with Prime Shipping: http://amzn.to/2DCjvq4
- Bulk discounts available at: www.myjli.com/game

**Implementation:**
- One card set to each "table captain"
- Random times throughout evening
- Different people read
- Keeps everyone engaged

---

### G) Makos Masks (Headbanz Game)

**Activity:**
> "1. We purchased these Makos masks: https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B01NC0XCHM/ref=oh_aui_detailpage_o01_s00?ie=UTF8&psc=1"

**Game:**
> "When we got to the Makos we called on the children and played the 'headbanz' game. One by one we put a Mask on the children and they had to ask the crowd questions with a yes/no answer until they figured out what Makoh they were wearing."

**Benefits:**
- Children actively involved
- Audience participation
- Educational (learning plagues)
- Interactive and fun

---

### H) Numbered Reading Cards

**System:**
> "#2. I have photocopied maggid and cut it into portions for people to read. I have them pasted onto numbered index cards with Hebrew on one side and English on the other."

**Pre-Seder:**
> "Before the Seder while people are milling about, I have someone walk around offering people if they would like to participate by selecting a reading to recite during the Seder in the language of their choice."

**During Maggid:**
> "During maggid I call out number 1, they read and I might offer a short vort, then I call out number 2."

---

### Benefits of Numbered Card System

**A. Random Movement:**
> "The reading is randomly moving around the room. It keeps it interesting."

**B. No Declining:**
> "No one has to decline to read."
- Voluntary selection beforehand

**C. Practice Time:**
> "They can practice."
- Cards given in advance

**D. Choice of Length:**
> "They can choose a length they are comfortable with, or something on which they have an insight to offer."

**E. Control Important Readings:**
> "You can make sure that shodayim nochonu goes to someone who will read it in Hebrew."

---

### I) Around the Room Reading

**Simple Approach:**
> "Go around and everyone read a paragraph."

**Cultural Variation:**
> "Ask people to read in their cultural language, Spanish, Russian, farsi (everyone else can read on their own quietly)."

**Educational Moment:**
> "You can take a minute to imagine a seder in that respective country, 20 years ago, 100 years ago, etc"

**Benefits:**
- Everyone participates
- Celebrates diversity
- Educational context
- Historical perspective

---

### J) Passover Story Segments

**Approach:**
> "I have taken a Pesach story from Chabad.org and broken it up into 7 or 8 slips of paper and handed it to guests to read aloud."

**Timing:**
> "This works well during the meal."

**Resource:**
> "Here's some ready-made Haggadah Tidbits to give out to people to read out loud: https://www.chabad.org/2512421"

---

### K) Afikoman Bags Activity

**Setup:**
> "We have afikoman bags on the tables, someone in each group hides the afikoman."

**Benefits:**
- Table-based activity
- Traditional element
- Children engaged
- Group dynamic

---

### L) Four Sons Skit

**Activity:**
> "Have a skit prepared for people to read. We use one of the four sons."

**Benefits:**
- Dramatic presentation
- Pre-prepared script
- Involves multiple readers
- Entertaining and educational

---

### M) Songs During Meal

**Simple but Effective:**
> "I have a few songs we sing during shulchan orech."

**Benefits:**
- Maintains atmosphere
- Easy participation
- Joyful mood
- Break between courses

---

### N) Make Your Own Seder Plate

**Activity:**
> "We have a few color inserts of a seder plate, that go into a plastic plate, and we let the people make their own seder plates before the seder."

**Timing:** Before Seder begins

**Benefits:**
- Creative activity
- Educational (learning Seder plate items)
- Keepsake to take home
- Engages early arrivals

---

### O) Dress Up

**Personal Touch:**
> "The last few years, my wife and I dress up - either as Moshe and Yocheved, as Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, as Eliyahu Hanavi..I think it is the same costume each year ⊚"

**Benefits:**
- Visual interest
- Memorable
- Conversation starter
- Sets festive tone

---

### P) Ma Nishtana Visual Cards

**Activity:**
> "Make cards with pictures of the mah nishtana, and have the people hold the correct card while the children sing. (matza / chametz; vegetables / maror; etc.)"

**Benefits:**
- Visual learning
- Audience participation
- Children feel supported
- Interactive

---

### Q) Reusable Pesach Sticker Books

**Gift:**
> "3) Give Reusable Pesach sticker books (ask your Rov about use on Shabbos/Yom Tov) for young kids as prize early in the seder. Keeps them real quiet and happy."

**Timing:** Early in Seder as prize

**Benefit:** Keeps young children occupied

**Important:** Ask Rov about permissibility on Yom Tov

---

## Additional Resources and Suppliers

### Paper Goods and Supplies

**Factory Direct Party:**
> "We purchased for the first time, the majority of our high end and regular paper goods from a wonderful company (owned by Unzere) called http://factorydirectparty.com/ and they are awesome."

---

### Large Aluminum Pans

**Dean Supply Co:**
> "We use an Ohio company called http://deansupplyco.com/ for the *very large* solid aluminum pans and they are very good."

---

### Merkos Bochrim

**Support:**
> "Having the Merkos Bochrim here for Mivtzah Matzah and the Sedorim was amazing and a special thanks to the Merkos Shlichus office and Rabbi Moshe Kotlarsky for being Mishtatef in the costs."

**Benefits:**
- Additional manpower
- Younger energy
- Mivtzah Matzah help
- Cost sharing

---

### Bulk Kosher Food Ordering

**For Communities Without Local Kosher:**

**Weinberg Brothers (Minnesota):**
> "If you don't live in a community with Kosher food and order in bulk (via private trucking), we've used Weinberg brothers in Minnesota for years now and Mr. Meyer Roberts and his team have done wonders for our community."

**System:**
> "We do it coop style with 10-15 families ordering in bulk for their families."

**Contact:**
> "Meyer can be reached @ (952) 217-4355"

---

### Catering Option

**Itcheh Hildesheim (NY):**
> "Had most of the food catered by Itcheh Hildesheim in NY and happy we went that route saving so much work on our end allowing us to focus on everything else."

**Logistics:**
> "You can come in for 11 Nissan and return with food. We're a short flight away & almost everything for 100+ people fit in three 70lb boxes. (Fly first to get the free heavy bags...)"

**Benefits:**
- Saves enormous preparation time
- Professional quality
- Focus on programming not cooking
- Manageable transport (3 boxes for 100+ people)
- Cost-effective with first class baggage allowance

---

## For Shluchim: Implementation Strategies

### Planning Matrix

**Key Decisions:**

| Decision | Options | Factors to Consider |
|----------|---------|---------------------|
| **Charge?** | Free / Suggested donation / Deposit ($25) / Full price | No-shows, food waste, dignity, community economics |
| **Start time?** | Before nacht / At nacht / Mixed (songs then kiddush) | Families with young children, halacha, crowd type |
| **Pace?** | Fast / Slow / Start slow end fast / Different nights | Audience expectation, children, authentic experience |
| **How many nights?** | One / Two (different styles) | Resources, demand, allow for variety |

---

### Maggid Programming Menu

**Pick 3-5 Activities:**

**For Children:**
- Cup pyramid building
- Frogs in pond game
- Makos masks (Headbanz)
- Ma Nishtana visual cards
- Sticker books
- Make your own Seder plate

**For Adults:**
- Tell the full story (Yosef to Mattan Torah)
- Numbered reading cards
- Cultural language readings
- JLI card game
- Haggadah tidbits
- Passover story segments
- Four sons skit

**For Everyone:**
- Jokes every 18 minutes
- Songs during meal
- Afikoman bags per table
- Dress up as characters

**Match to Your Crowd:**
- Families with young children: More games, shorter teachings
- Adult-focused: Deeper story, discussion, fewer activities
- Mixed: Rotate between age groups

---

### Efficiency Hacks

**From Community Wisdom:**

**Washing Hands:**
- Multiple stations
- Designated "washer" per station
- Consider tznius (separate male/female washers)

**Food Quality:**
- Invest in fresh matzah (Montreal, Landau)
- Variety of good wines
- Result: Better mitzvah observance

**Pre-Seder:**
- Make-your-own Seder plate activity
- Distribute numbered reading cards
- Hand out activity materials
- Reduces downtime later

**Time Management:**
- "Every 18 minutes" for regular activities
- Jokes/inspirational words keep energy up
- Built-in pace

**Resource Sharing:**
- Coop bulk ordering (10-15 families)
- Merkos Bochrim cost-sharing
- Community knowledge exchange

---

### Budget Optimization

**Save Money:**
- Deposit system reduces no-shows/waste
- Bulk ordering (Weinberg Brothers)
- Factory direct party supplies (factorydirectparty.com)
- Dean Supply Co for large pans
- Reusable items for second night

**Invest Where It Matters:**
- Fresh, quality matzah
- Variety of good wines
- Activities (games, cards)
- Catering (if saves your sanity)

**Cost Sharing:**
- Merkos Bochrim partnership
- Philanthropist sponsorship (as Rebbe suggested)
- Coop food ordering
- Suggested donation model

---

### Quality of Experience

**What People Remember:**

**Authentic and Alive (Strategy C):**
> "They're coming to experience a Seder at my table, which is authentic, alive and real... the way I received it from my parents, grandparents and great grandparents."

**Don't Sacrifice:**
- Your warmth
- Authenticity
- Family traditions
- Joy and energy

**Do Adapt:**
- Timing (families with children)
- Activities (keep engaged)
- Pace (visible, announced)
- Length (options for different nights)

---

### Learning from the Rebbe's Guidance

**Six Principles Applied:**

**1. Not Party-Affiliated:**
- Advertise broadly
- Welcome all Jews
- Neutral messaging

**2. Avoid Embarrassment:**
- "Rabbi's public Seder inviting everyone"
- Not "for those who don't have"
- "Suggested donation" not "free for needy"
- "Can't afford it now" option (dignified)

**3. Local Rabbi Hosts:**
- You as community leader
- Your authority
- Your rabbinic guidance

**4. Reimburse Costs:**
- Fundraise properly
- Don't expect to cover personally
- Philanthropist sponsorship
- Cost-sharing models

**5. Rebbe Participates:**
- Gives legitimacy
- Encourages others to sponsor
- Creates blessing for event

**6. Comfortable Flexibility:**
- "Stay as much or as little as they like"
- Two different nights (one for families, one for adults)
- Start slow, end fast (announced)
- No pressure

---

## Related Resources

**In This Collection:**
- **File 1118**: Waiter instructions (service operations)
- **File 1119**: Waitress instructions (food service)
- **File 1120**: Service timeline (coordination)

- **File 1110**: "Let My People Know" Seder seminar (educational content)
- **File 1103**: Passover jokes "18 Minute Laughs" (humor resource)
- **File 1106**: Monica study group Seder outline (another Seder approach)

---

**Bottom Line:**

[Continued in next message due to length...]

Community Seder tips and best practices from Shluchim Exchange compilation covering six major topics with multiple perspectives. **(1) To charge or not to charge:** Strategy A "suggested donation" (almost everyone chooses paying option, people want to feel comfortable eating/drinking as much as they want); Strategy B deposit system (when didn't charge had load of RSVPs and half didn't show up especially college campus, next year charged with option "I can't afford it now" only $25 as deposit to ensure cancellations/prevent waste, result: first year began "charging" got more people than before); **Rebbe's guidance yechidus to chief rabbis Shapira and Eliyahu of Israel** (caution "not so simple what lessons one can derive for our public Seders in states," transcript Hisvadyos 5746 vol 2 page 851 otzar770 or listen chabad.org/therebbe/article_cdo/aid/554285 at 1:42) with six points: (1) not associated with any specific group or party, (2) don't make communal Seder where some embarrassed to come implying they don't have own Seder rather rabbi doing his Seder in public space inviting everyone, (3) hosted by rabbis of each city/town/neighborhood, (4) rabbis should be reimbursed, (5) Rebbe will be mistatef and get others/philanthropists in America happy to sponsor if organized by chief rabbinate, (6) people should feel comfortable staying as much or as little as they like. **(2) When to start:** Dilemma "always question when to start after nacht [nightfall] or before" (if starting early Rabbanim gave guidelines how to do it); Strategy A start early (for most with young children "to hope they'll even do that after 8:20 is overly wishful thinking," additional benefits: allows tefillin with men before Shabbos/helps curb Chilul Shabbos v'yom tov/makes calm attentive audience/shorter Shulchan Oreich/helps more people stay for whole seder); Strategy B start by nacht "the minhag is to start by nacht and to show how it's supposed to be" with compromise "announce at beginning that we are going to do kiddush at earliest time appropriate but will precede it with songs divrei torah etc, we will move quickly after kiddush and not spend too much time in discussion and song as we have already covered it." **(3) Rush through seder or not:** Reality "אין דעותיהן שוות [people have different opinions] and you may hear complains from both opposites, it depends on the crowd coming;" Strategy A different nights different paces; Strategy B start slow rush by end "in a way that everyone can see it's rushed and announce in beginning that due to families with young children can't do it too long, I invite everyone to our 2nd night seder;" Strategy C authentic and alive "people who are coming to Seder that only starts at 8:45 or 9:00 at night aren't coming for brisket, they're coming to experience a Seder at my table which is authentic alive and real - they want to receive my warm full of life experience the way I received it from my parents/grandparents/great grandparents so I don't feel need to rush, our experience has been that people don't eat very much by time we get to Shulchan Oirech, but ultimately this differs from place to place;" Strategy D two different Sedarim "if doing 2 nights of public sedarim advertising one Seder more geared for families with young children and other for adults - much easier time adapting style when crowd is more similar plus people know what to expect." **(4) Washing hands:** Efficient system "we arrange as many washing stations as possible and appoint designated 'WASHER' at each station that pours water on everyone's hands - this reduces time very significantly especially if 'washer' is right person" with tznius consideration "mitzad darkay tznius should consider having separate male/female 'washers' or ask rov if child could do washing;" halachic note "there is deference between rochtzo and urchatz, rochtzo is not minhag it is din that you make berocho asher kidshonu bemitzvosov." **(5) Matzah and wine quality:** Matzah "we bought better matzah this year Montreal for our families and Landau for Seders both were fresh and people did eat lot more matzah and honestly many more people fulfilled mitzvah because matzah was enjoyable" (fresh matzah significantly impacts compliance worth investment); wine "I noticed having variety of good quality wines (nothing too crazy expensive) causes people to actually drink four cups." **(6) Maggid making it interesting - 17 ideas:** (A) Tell story of Yetzias Mitzraim from Yosef to Mattan Torah "believe it or not most Jews today don't know the story and you can make it very exciting if you prepare;" (B) Rabbi Mentz California conference call 20 minute recording with ideas (freeconferencecall.com link); (C) Cup pyramid building "put bunch of plastic cups on each table, when comes to part in hagada about yiddin working each table has to make cup pyramid, first table wins;" (D) Jokes every 18 minutes "print pesach jokes put face down on each table, every 18 minutes another table reads their joke (could do same with inspirational words, why 18 minutes: connects to matzah time before chametz/regular intervals/keeps energy up);" (E) Frogs in pond game "dollar tree sells frogs in pond game, at makkos see with table flicks most frogs in pond" (dollartree.com link, sang Ma nishtana while 3 players per table tried to flick frogs before finished, explain focus is Hashem's miracles); (F) JLI "How Jew You Do" card game "spread them out to 'captains' of every table, throughout evening at random times had different people stand up and read from them worked out very well" (Amazon Prime amzn.to/2DCjvq4 or bulk myjli.com/game); (G) Makos masks Headbanz game (Amazon link, when got to Makos called on children put mask on and they had to ask crowd yes/no questions until figured out what Makoh they were wearing); (H) Numbered reading cards "photocopied maggid and cut into portions pasted onto numbered index cards with Hebrew one side English other, before Seder while people milling about someone walks around offering if they would like to participate by selecting reading in language of choice, during maggid call out number 1 they read I might offer short vort then call out number 2" with five benefits (reading randomly moving around room keeps interesting, no one has to decline to read voluntary selection beforehand, they can practice cards given in advance, they can choose length comfortable with or something they have insight to offer, you can make sure shodayim nochonu goes to someone who will read it in Hebrew); (I) Around room reading cultural language variation "ask people to read in their cultural language Spanish/Russian/farsi (everyone else can read on own quietly), you can take minute to imagine seder in that respective country 20 years ago 100 years ago etc;" (J) Passover story segments "taken Pesach story from Chabad.org broken up into 7 or 8 slips of paper handed to guests to read aloud, works well during meal" (ready-made Haggadah Tidbits chabad.org/2512421); (K) Afikoman bags activity "we have afikoman bags on tables someone in each group hides afikoman;" (L) Four sons skit "have skit prepared for people to read, we use one of four sons;" (M) Songs during meal "I have few songs we sing during shulchan orech;" (N) Make your own seder plate "we have few color inserts of seder plate that go into plastic plate and we let people make their own seder plates before seder;" (O) Dress up "last few years my wife and I dress up either as Moshe and Yocheved/as Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya/as Eliyahu Hanavi..I think it is same costume each year ☺;" (P) Ma Nishtana visual cards "make cards with pictures of mah nishtana and have people hold correct card while children sing (matza/chametz; vegetables/maror; etc.);" (Q) Reusable Pesach sticker books "give reusable Pesach sticker books (ask Rov about use on Shabbos/Yom Tov) for young kids as prize early in seder, keeps them real quiet and happy." **Additional resources and suppliers:** Factory Direct Party (factorydirectparty.com owned by Unzere for high end and regular paper goods "awesome"), Dean Supply Co (deansupplyco.com Ohio company for very large solid aluminum pans "very good"), Merkos Bochrim (having them here for Mivtzah Matzah and Sedorim "amazing" special thanks to Merkos Shlichus office and Rabbi Moshe Kotlarsky for being Mishtatef in costs), Weinberg Brothers Minnesota (for communities without local kosher order in bulk via private trucking "done wonders for our community" do it coop style with 10-15 families, Meyer Roberts (952) 217-4355), Itcheh Hildesheim NY (catered most food "happy we went that route saving so much work on our end allowing us to focus on everything else" - come in for 11 Nissan and return with food, short flight and almost everything for 100+ people fit in three 70lb boxes, fly first to get free heavy bags). **For Shluchim implementation:** Planning matrix with key decisions (charge: free/suggested donation/deposit $25/full price considering no-shows/food waste/dignity/community economics; start time: before nacht/at nacht/mixed songs then kiddush considering families with children/halacha/crowd type; pace: fast/slow/start slow end fast/different nights considering audience expectation/children/authentic experience; how many nights: one/two different styles considering resources/demand/variety); Maggid programming menu pick 3-5 activities (for children: cup pyramid/frogs game/Makos masks/Ma Nishtana cards/sticker books/make seder plate; for adults: tell full story Yosef to Mattan Torah/numbered reading cards/cultural language readings/JLI card game/Haggadah tidbits/story segments/four sons skit; for everyone: jokes every 18 minutes/songs during meal/afikoman bags per table/dress up as characters - match to crowd); efficiency hacks (washing hands: multiple stations/designated "washer" per station/consider tznius separate male-female washers; food quality: invest in fresh matzah Montreal/Landau/variety of good wines = better mitzvah observance; pre-Seder: make-your-own seder plate activity/distribute numbered reading cards/hand out activity materials reduces downtime; time management: "every 18 minutes" for regular activities/jokes-inspirational words keep energy up/built-in pace; resource sharing: coop bulk ordering 10-15 families/Merkos Bochrim cost-sharing/community knowledge exchange); learning from Rebbe's guidance six principles applied (not party-affiliated: advertise broadly/welcome all Jews/neutral messaging; avoid embarrassment: "rabbi's public Seder inviting everyone" not "for those who don't have"/"suggested donation" not "free for needy"/"can't afford it now" option dignified; local rabbi hosts: you as community leader/your authority/your rabbinic guidance; reimburse costs: fundraise properly/don't expect to cover personally/philanthropist sponsorship/cost-sharing models; Rebbe participates: gives legitimacy/encourages others to sponsor/creates blessing for event; comfortable flexibility: "stay as much or as little as they like"/two different nights one for families one for adults/start slow end fast announced/no pressure). Related resources: File 1118 (waiter instructions service operations), 1119 (waitress instructions food service), 1120 (service timeline coordination), 1115 ("Unfold" Seder guide ritual structure), 1110 ("Let My People Know" educational content), 1103 (Passover jokes "18 Minute Laughs" humor resource), 1106 (Monica study group Seder outline another approach). Note: This community Seder tips compilation appears in Chanukah directory.

# [Misc > For Writer > _5 Chanukah > General] Detailed Waiter Instructions - Friday April 3

## Note: Passover Content (Not Chanukah)

**Resource Type:** Operational instructions

**Event Date:** Friday, April 3

**Purpose:** Comprehensive waiter guide for community Passover Seder service

**Format:** Timeline with setup and service instructions

**Related:** Files 1119 (waitress instructions), 1120 (service timeline)

---

## Opening Note

**Instruction and Support:**

> "Someone will be there to instruct and show where things are."

**Important Context:**

> "Please note: there are some very unique and interesting traditions which we observe during the Passover dinner, all will be clearly instructed on this outline. Sometimes these random traditions are served to all guests (ex: matza cracker, lettuce, hard boiled egg)."

---

## 6:15 PM - Pre-Event Job

### Room Set-Up

**Tables:**
1. Table cloths
2. Chairs
3. Plates
4. Silverware
5. Napkins
6. Cups
7. Wine cups
8. 1 small plate under wine cup
9. A Passover book on each chair

**Center of Tables:**
1. 1 bottle of water
2. One of each salad

---

### Prepare Seder Plate (Per Table)

**Traditional Passover Plate at Center of Each Table**

**Components:**
1. A hard boiled egg
2. Piece Romaine lettuce
3. Grated white horseradish
4. Roasted chicken bone
5. Slice of potato/onion
6. Apple/wine/nut dip

---

### Extra Tables - Washing Stations

**Purpose:**

> "During the evening we have the tradition for every attendee to wash their hands with a pouring cup, twice."

**Setup:**
- Table set up with 2 basins
- Washing cups
- Paper towel
- Garbages
- Water should be filled up from the bathroom

---

## 6:45 PM - Guests Begin to Arrive

**Task:** First course is served on tables

---

## 7:35 PM - Pre-Ceremony Preparation

**Clear:**
- First course plates
- Salads

**Bring Out:**
- 1 dry wine (per table)
- Grape juice (per table)
- Matza
- Seder plates
- Bowls of saltwater (one per table)
- Bowls of onion/potato (one per table)

---

## 7:55 PM - Formal Program/Ceremony Begins

### First Tradition

**Everyone blesses on cup of wine**

**All guests will be washing their hands**

---

### Hors D'oeuvres/Tradition #1: Potato & Saltwater

**Serve Per Table:**
- 1 small bowl or platter of 1" cube size cooked potato squares
- A bowl of very salty water per table

**After Service:**
- Clear potatoes after guests have taken 1, dipped and eaten
- Refill the washing stations with fresh water

---

### Stories

**Stories from Passover book will be read**

**Duration:** Approx. 20 minutes later...

---

### Second Hand Washing

**All guests will be washing hands again**

**While Washing:**
- Numbers 7-8 should be brought out (referring to next traditions)

---

### Hors D'oeuvres/Tradition #2: Lettuce, Horseradish, Apple

**Serve Each Table:**
- Large bowls filled with pre-washed and dried whole leaves of romaine lettuce
- Grated horseradish
- Apple [dip]

---

### Hors D'oeuvres/Tradition #3: Hard Boiled Egg

**Serve:**
- Every person a hard boiled egg in a small bowl

**Clear:**
- Clear away all the lettuce, horseradish, dip, egg, saltwater at this point (after egg is eaten)

---

## 8:40 PM (Approx.) - Main Course

**MAIN COURSE should be ready to be brought out**

---

## During Main Course - Dessert Preparation

**As guests are enjoying meal:**

**Prepare dessert ready to serve:**
- Cake with a swirl of chocolate sauce

---

## After Main Course - Final Traditions

**Before Clearing:**

Guests will:
1. Eat their last serving of matza cracker
2. Drink 2 more glasses of wine/grape juice

---

## Waiters Can Begin Cleanup

### Clearing Dinner

**Tasks:**
- Clearing the guests' dinner plates
- Consolidating main course back in prep room

**Important:**

> "Please do not discard any of the traditional items on the tables (ex: horseradish, apple dip, matza…) as they are used on 2nd night."

---

### Complete Room Cleaning

**Tasks:**
- Clear all platters/bowls/serving dishes/non-disposables
- Consolidate all drinks
- Place all remaining food back in Ziploc

---

## Hand Washing Blessing

**Blessing Posted for Reference:**

> "Baruch atah Adonai, Eloheinu, melech ha-olam asher kidishanu b'mitz'votav v'tzivanu al n'tilat yadayim."

**Translation:**
> "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us concerning the washing of hands."

---

## THANK YOU!

---

## For Shluchim: Planning Community Seder Service

### Waiter Role Definition

**From This Document:**

**Pre-Event (6:15-6:45):**
- Complete room setup
- Table setting with specific placement
- Seder plate assembly (6 components per table)
- Washing station setup

**Service (7:35-8:40):**
- Clearing and bringing items
- Serving traditional Seder items
- Maintaining washing stations
- Coordinating with Seder progression

**Post-Event:**
- Complete cleanup
- Careful preservation of reusable items
- Food storage

**Compare to Waitress Role (File 1119):**
- Waitress: Food prep, plating, course sequencing
- Waiter: Room setup, traditional items, transitions

---

### Timeline Analysis

**Full Event Duration:**
- 6:15 PM: Setup begins
- 6:45 PM: Guests arrive
- 7:55 PM: Formal ceremony begins
- 8:40 PM: Main course
- Approximate end: 9:00-9:30 PM

**Total Duration:** Approximately 3-3.5 hours

**Staff Hours:**
- Setup: 30 minutes before guests
- Service: 2-2.5 hours
- Cleanup: 30-45 minutes
- Total per waiter: 3.5-4 hours

---

### Seder Traditions Served

**From Waiter Perspective:**

**1. Kadeish (Wine Blessing) - 7:55 PM:**
- Everyone blesses on cup of wine
- Dry wine and grape juice pre-placed

**2. Urchatz (First Washing) - After Kadeish:**
- All guests wash hands
- Washing stations used first time
- Refilled after this use

**3. Karpas (Vegetable Dipping) - Tradition #1:**
- Potato cubes in saltwater
- Cleared after one piece taken

**4. Stories/Maggid - 20 minutes:**
- Stories from Passover book read
- Gives waiters time to prepare next items

**5. Rochtzah (Second Washing) - After Maggid:**
- All guests wash hands again
- With blessing this time
- While washing, bring out lettuce/horseradish/apple

**6. Motzi Matzah/Maror/Korech - Tradition #2:**
- Whole lettuce leaves (for maror)
- Horseradish (bitter herbs)
- Apple dip (charoses)

**7. Hard Boiled Egg - Tradition #3:**
- Not technically part of Seder order
- Traditional addition
- Served individually

**8. Shulchan Orech (Meal) - 8:40 PM:**
- Main course served
- Guests enjoy meal

**9. Tzafun (Afikoman) - After Meal:**
- Last serving of matzah
- Two more glasses of wine

---

### Table Setting Specifications

**Each Place Setting:**
- Plate
- Silverware
- Napkin
- Cup (for water)
- Wine cup
- Small plate under wine cup
- Passover book (Haggadah)

**Each Table Center:**
- Tablecloth
- 1 bottle of water
- One of each salad
- Seder plate (traditional 6 items)

**Later Added:**
- Dry wine
- Grape juice
- Matzah
- Bowls of saltwater
- Bowls of potato/onion

---

### Washing Station Critical Importance

**Why Two Washings:**

**First Washing (Urchatz):**
- Before karpas (vegetable)
- Without blessing
- All guests participate

**Second Washing (Rochtzah):**
- Before matzah
- With blessing (provided in document)
- All guests participate

**Logistics:**
- Each attendee washes with pouring cup
- Twice during event
- Requires basin setup
- Water from bathroom
- Must refill after first washing
- Paper towels and garbage needed

**Planning:**
- For 64-96 guests (estimated from other documents)
- Need multiple stations
- Document says "2 basins" minimum
- More efficient with 4-6 stations
- Dedicated "washer" per station helpful (from File 1116)

---

### Critical Preservation Note

**Important Instruction:**

> "Please do not discard any of the traditional items on the tables (ex: horseradish, apple dip, matza…) as they are used on 2nd night."

**Implications:**

**This Reveals:**
- Two-night Seder operation
- Cost savings through reuse
- Careful item tracking needed
- Ziploc storage system

**Must Preserve:**
- Horseradish (unused portions)
- Apple dip (charoses)
- Matzah (unopened)
- Seder plate items
- Wine/grape juice (unopened)

**Can Discard:**
- Used plates/napkins/cups
- Eaten food
- Saltwater (make fresh)
- Wilted lettuce (use fresh)

---

### Timing Coordination Points

**Notice Gaps:**

**6:45-7:35 (50 minutes):**
- Guests arriving and seated
- Socializing time
- First course on tables
- Pre-ceremony mingling

**7:35-7:55 (20 minutes):**
- Clearing first course
- Setting up for ceremony
- Final preparations
- Guests settling in

**7:55-8:40 (45 minutes):**
- Full Seder ceremony
- Wine blessing
- First washing
- Karpas/potato
- 20 minutes stories/Maggid
- Second washing
- Lettuce/horseradish/apple
- Hard boiled egg
- Transition to meal

**These Timings Allow:**
- Proper pacing
- No rushing rituals
- Smooth transitions
- Staff preparation time

**4. Preservation Awareness:**

stories from Passover book will be read approx 20 min later; all guests washing hands again while washing numbers 7-8 should be brought out, **Hors D'oeuvres/Tradition #2** serve each table large bowls filled with pre-washed and dried whole leaves of romaine lettuce/grated horseradish/apple [dip], **Hors D'oeuvres/Tradition #3** serve every person hard boiled egg in small bowl (clear away all lettuce/horseradish/dip/egg/saltwater at this point after egg eaten). **(8:40pm approx) Main course** should be ready to be brought out; as guests enjoying meal prepare dessert ready to serve (cake with swirl of chocolate sauce); after main course guests will (1) eat their last serving of matza cracker (2) drink 2 more glasses of wine/grape juice. **Waiters can begin cleanup:** Clearing guests' dinner plates/consolidating main course back in prep room, **Important:** "Please do not discard any of traditional items on tables (ex: horseradish, apple dip, matza...) as they are used on 2nd night;" complete room cleaning (clear all platters/bowls/serving dishes/non-disposables, consolidate all drinks, place all remaining food back in Ziploc). Hand washing blessing provided: "Baruch atah Adonai, Eloheinu, melech ha-olam asher kidishanu b'mitz'votav v'tzivanu al n'tilat yadayim." **For Shluchim:** Waiter role definition (pre-event complete room setup/table setting/Seder plate assembly 6 components/washing station setup; service clearing and bringing/traditional Seder items/maintaining washing stations/coordinating with Seder progression; post-event complete cleanup/careful preservation of reusable items/food storage); timeline analysis full event 6:15pm setup to approx 9:00-9:30pm end total duration 3-3.5 hours with staff hours 3.5-4 hours per waiter; Seder traditions served from waiter perspective (Kadeish wine blessing 7:55pm, Urchatz first washing after Kadeish refilled, Karpas potato cubes in saltwater tradition #1, Stories/Maggid 20 minutes, Rochtzah second washing with blessing while washing bring out lettuce/horseradish/apple, Motzi Matzah/Maror/Korech tradition #2 whole lettuce leaves/horseradish/apple dip, hard boiled egg tradition #3 individual, Shulchan Orech meal 8:40pm, Tzafun afikoman last matzah/two more wine glasses); washing station critical importance (two washings: Urchatz before karpas without blessing, Rochtzah before matzah with blessing; logistics each attendee washes with pouring cup twice requiring basin setup/water from bathroom/must refill after first washing/paper towels and garbage; planning for 64-96 guests need multiple stations/document says "2 basins" minimum/more efficient with 4-6 stations); critical preservation note "Please do not discard any of traditional items on tables (ex: horseradish, apple dip, matza...) as they are used on 2nd night" revealing two-night Seder operation/cost savings through reuse/careful item tracking/Ziploc storage system (must preserve horseradish/apple dip/matzah unopened/Seder plate items/wine-grape juice unopened; can discard used plates/napkins/cups/eaten food/saltwater make fresh/wilted lettuce use fresh). # [Misc > For Writer > _5 Chanukah > General] Waitress Instructions - Community Seder Service

## Note: Passover Content (Not Chanukah)

**Resource Type:** Operational instructions

**Purpose:** Service timeline and duties for waitress at community Passover Seder

**Format:** Checklist with timing and food preparation

**Related:** Files 1118 (waiter instructions), 1120 (service timeline)

---

## General Instructions

**Throughout the Meal:**
- Remove empty bottles
- Replenish with new bottles
- Applies to: water, wine, grape juice

---

## Hand Washing Stations

**Guests Wash Hands Twice During Meal**

**After First Washing:**
1. Replenish the water in dispensers
2. Empty tubs in the backyard
3. Clear used paper towels
4. Replace with new paper towels

---

## Schedule

### Upon Arrival

**Preparation Tasks:**
- Put horseradish in small bowls
- Put apple mixture in small bowls
- Prepare salt water (little bowls with water and salt)
- Put lettuce in long bowls

---

### Food Heating

**8:30 PM:**
- Put all food in the oven

**9:30 PM:**
- Light sternos
- Put food on sternos
- **Note:** If food is hot, only light one fire

---

### First Course Preparation

**Task: Plate First Course**

**Each Plate Should Have:**
1. Spring mix
2. 1 slice fish topped with sliced carrot
3. Drizzle basil dressing over salad
4. Half a boiled egg

**After Plating:**
- Cover
- Place in fridge

---

### Service Sequence

#### Lettuce, Horseradish, Apple Service

**When:** As soon as people sit down from washing their hands

**Bring Out:**
1. **LETTUCE** - Not the salad, only the whole lettuce leaves
2. **APPLE MIXTURE** - Add spoon before serving
3. **HORSERADISH** - Add spoon before serving

**Also During This Time:**
- Cut up pineapple

---

#### First Course Service

**When:** On cue

**Serve:** The first course (prepared earlier)

**Then:**
- Prepare soup bowls on the tray

---

#### Soup Service

**When:** Wait 10 minutes after first course

**First:** Clear first course, including all other small bowls on the table

**Then:** Immediately begin to serve soup

**Each Bowl Should Have:**
- A matzah ball
- A carrot

---

#### Buffet Service

**After Soup:**
- Clear soup bowls and spoons
- Open the buffet

**Buffet Items:**
1. Roast
2. Chicken
3. Kugel
4. Ratatouille
5. Sweet potato
6. 2 bowls of Caesar salad

**Ensure:** Everything has a serving spoon

---

#### Dessert Service

**Prepare Dessert:**

**Each Plate Should Have:**
- Fruit salad
- 2 ice cream cubes
- A teaspoon

**Then:**
- Serve dessert
- Clear dessert

---

### End of Service

**Final Tasks:**
1. Clear tables completely
2. Wash dishes if you have time

---

## For Shluchim: Planning Community Seder Service

### Staffing Considerations

**This Document Shows:**
- Need for dedicated waitress position
- Clear role differentiation from waiters
- Specific responsibilities for food preparation
- Timeline coordination essential

**Compare With:**
- File 1118: Waiter instructions (room setup, traditions, main timeline)
- File 1120: Overall service timeline (coordination between roles)

---

### Service Flow Design

**Key Elements:**

**1. Advance Preparation:**
- First course plated early
- Items prepared "upon arrival"
- Ready before guests enter

**2. Staggered Cooking:**
- 8:30 PM: Oven
- 9:30 PM: Sternos
- Allows for timing adjustments

**3. Sequential Service:**
- Lettuce/horseradish/apple first
- Wait for cue
- First course
- 10-minute wait
- Clear, then soup immediately
- Buffet opens after soup cleared
- Dessert after buffet

**4. Continuous Maintenance:**
- Bottles replenished throughout
- Washing stations reset after first washing
- Spoons added before serving

---

### Menu Revealed

**From This Document:**

**First Course:**
- Spring mix salad
- Fish with carrot topping
- Basil dressing
- Half boiled egg

**Soup:**
- Matzah ball soup
- With carrot

**Main Course (Buffet):**
- Roast
- Chicken
- Kugel
- Ratatouille
- Sweet potato
- Caesar salad (2 bowls)

**Dessert:**
- Fruit salad
- Ice cream cubes

**Traditional Items:**
- Whole lettuce leaves
- Horseradish
- Apple mixture
- Salt water

---

### Timing Analysis

**From Schedule:**
- 8:30 PM: Food to oven
- 9:30 PM: Light sternos
- First course: "On cue" (after lettuce service)
- Soup: 10 minutes after first course
- Buffet: Immediately after soup cleared
- Dessert: After buffet
- End: Tables cleared completely

**Estimated Duration:**
- Approximately 1.5-2 hours for full service
- Multiple courses with gaps for Seder rituals
- Coordination with Seder leader essential

---

### Staff Training Points

**What Waitress Needs to Know:**

**1. Seder Ritual Integration:**
- Understand hand washing tradition (twice)
- Know what "on cue" means
- Coordinate with Seder progression
- Don't rush ritual elements

**2. Food Safety:**
- Covering plated food
- Refrigeration timing
- Hot food temperature management
- Sterno safety ("only light one fire if food is hot")

**3. Quality Standards:**
- Each plate identical
- Basil dressing "drizzled"
- Spoons added before serving
- Everything has serving utensil

**4. Flexibility:**
- "On cue" service (not clock-based)
- "If you have time" dish washing
- Continuous bottle monitoring

---

### Comparison with Waiter Instructions

**Waitress Focus:**
- Food preparation and plating
- Course sequencing
- Buffet management
- Dessert service
- Ongoing maintenance (bottles, washing stations)

**Waiter Focus (from File 1118):**
- Room setup
- Table setting
- Traditional item placement
- Seder plate preparation
- Major transitions

**Overlap:**
- Washing station maintenance
- Traditional items service
- Timing coordination

---

### Pre-Event Checklist from This Document

**Before Guests Arrive:**
- [ ] Horseradish in small bowls
- [ ] Apple mixture in small bowls
- [ ] Salt water prepared (bowls with water and salt)
- [ ] Lettuce in long bowls
- [ ] First course plated, covered, refrigerated
- [ ] Pineapple cut up
- [ ] Soup bowls on tray ready
- [ ] Buffet items ready to heat
- [ ] Dessert plates prepared
- [ ] All serving spoons available

**During Service:**
- [ ] 8:30 - Food in oven
- [ ] 9:30 - Light sternos, food on sternos
- [ ] Monitor and replenish bottles continuously
- [ ] Reset washing stations after first use
- [ ] Add spoons before serving each item
- [ ] 10-minute timing between courses
- [ ] Clear completely before next course
- [ ] Final table clearing
- [ ] Dishes if time permits

---

### Scalability Considerations

**This Setup Suggests:**
- Multi-table event (mentions "2 bowls of Caesar salad")
- Buffet-style main course
- Plated appetizers and desserts
- Professional service standards

**For Smaller Events:**
- Reduce advance plating
- Family-style instead of buffet
- Simplified timing
- Fewer staff

**For Larger Events:**
- Multiple waitresses
- Assembly line plating
- Larger buffet
- More washing stations
- Additional coordination

---

### Equipment Implied

**From Instructions:**
- Refrigeration for plated first course
- Oven capacity for all food
- Sternos (multiple)
- Trays for soup bowls
- Serving bowls (multiple sizes)
- Small bowls (for horseradish, apple, salt water, eggs)
- Long bowls (for lettuce)
- Dispensers for water at washing stations
- Tubs (for backyard emptying)
- Paper towel supplies

---

## Related Resources

**In This Collection:**
- **File 1118**: Detailed waiter instructions Friday April 3 (complementary role)
- **File 1120**: Overall service timeline (coordination document)
- **File 1116**: Community Seder tips (planning considerations)
- **File 1115**: "Unfold" Seder guide (ritual understanding for staff)
- **File 1110**: "Let My People Know" Seder seminar (educational content)

---

**Bottom Line:**

Waitress instructions for community Passover Seder with general responsibilities (throughout meal remove empty bottles and replenish with new ones for water/wine/grape juice; guests wash hands twice during meal - after first washing replenish water in dispensers/empty tubs in backyard/clear used paper towels/replace with new paper towels). **Schedule:** Upon arrival put horseradish and apple mixture in small bowls/prepare salt water (little bowls with water and salt)/put lettuce in long bowls; 8:30 put all food in oven; 9:30 light sternos and put food on sternos (if food is hot only light one fire). **First course preparation:** plate each with spring mix/1 slice fish topped with sliced carrot/drizzle basil dressing over salad/half a boiled egg, cover and place in fridge; cut up pineapple. **Service sequence:** (1) As soon as people sit down from washing hands bring out LETTUCE (not salad only whole lettuce leaves)/APPLE MIXTURE (add spoon before serving)/HORSERADISH (add spoon before serving); (2) On cue serve first course then prepare soup bowls on tray; (3) Wait 10 minutes then clear first course including all other small bowls on table, immediately begin to serve soup (each bowl should have matzah ball and carrot); (4) Clear soup bowls and spoons then open buffet (roast/chicken/kugel/ratatouille/sweet potato/2 bowls Caesar salad) ensuring everything has serving spoon; (5) Prepare dessert (small plate with fruit salad and 2 ice cream cubes, each plate should have teaspoon) then serve dessert; (6) Clear dessert then clear tables completely, wash dishes if you have time. **For Shluchim:** Shows need for dedicated waitress position with clear role differentiation from waiters (waitress focus: food preparation and plating/course sequencing/buffet management/dessert service/ongoing maintenance bottles and washing stations; waiter focus: room setup/table setting/traditional item placement/Seder plate preparation/major transitions); service flow design with advance preparation/staggered cooking/sequential service/continuous maintenance; menu revealed (first course: spring mix salad/fish with carrot topping/basil dressing/half boiled egg; soup: matzah ball with carrot; buffet: roast/chicken/kugel/ratatouille/sweet potato/Caesar salad; dessert: fruit salad/ice cream cubes; traditional items: whole lettuce leaves/horseradish/apple mixture/salt water); timing analysis approximately 1.5-2 hours full service with multiple courses and gaps for Seder rituals requiring coordination with Seder leader; staff training points: understand hand washing tradition/know what "on cue" means/coordinate with Seder progression/don't rush ritual elements/food safety/quality standards/flexibility. ## For Shluchim: Using This Timeline

### Master Coordination Document

**This Timeline Shows:**
- Integration of three service documents (1118, 1119, 1120)
- Complete view from 7:40 PM to 9:05 PM
- Exact quantities for 8-table event
- Critical timing intervals

**Purpose:**
- Coordinate multiple staff members
- Ensure nothing missed
- Maintain service pace
- Respect Seder ritual timing

---

### Critical Timing Patterns

**Pattern Analysis:**

**Service Intervals:**
- 8:00 - Traditional items (lettuce, horseradish, apple)
- 8:12 - Eggs (+12 minutes)
- 8:15 - First course (+3 minutes / wait for cue)
- 8:25 - Clear (+10 minutes)
- 8:30 - Second course (immediately after clear)
- 8:45 - Clear (+15 minutes)
- 8:50 - Dessert (immediately after clear)
- 9:00 - Clear dessert (+10 minutes)
- 9:05 - Final table clearing (+5 minutes)

**Pattern:**
- Traditional items → 12 min → Eggs → 3 min → First course
- 10-minute eating interval
- Immediate clear and serve
- 15-minute eating interval for main course
- 10-minute dessert interval
- 5 minutes final clearing

**Total Service Time:** 1 hour 25 minutes (7:40 PM prep to 9:05 PM complete)

---

### Scaling This Model

**For 8 Tables (As Written):**
- 16 bowls/platters for items with "2 per table"
- 8 platters for items with "1 per table"
- Total traditional item bowls: 48 (16+16+16)
- Total course platters/bowls: 8-16 per course

**To Scale Up:**
- Multiply platters/bowls per table added
- Add staff proportionally (1 waiter per 3-4 tables)
- Consider multiple sterno stations
- May need staggered service

**To Scale Down:**
- Fewer total items
- Single server possible for 4 tables
- Simplified timing
- Family-style instead of individual table service

---

### Integration with Seder Ritual

**Why These Timings:**

**8:00 - Traditional Items:**
- Corresponds to karpas (vegetable dipping)
- People just washed hands (urchatz)

**8:12 - Eggs:**
- Part of traditional Seder plate items
- Used during Maggid

**8:15 - First Course (wait for cue):**
- Not clock-based but ritual-based
- Flexible for Seder progression
- "Cue" from Seder leader

**8:30 - Main Course:**
- Corresponds to Shulchan Orech (meal)
- After all Maggid/rituals complete
- Longer interval (15 min) reflects main meal

**8:50 - Dessert:**
- Before afikoman
- Or after afikoman depending on custom
- Keeps evening flowing

---

### Pre-Event Setup Critical Path

**Friday AM (Morning):**
- All cold food preparation
- Table setup
- Washing station setup
- Seder plate assembly

**Advantages:**
- Less stress day-of
- Quality control time
- Can test layouts
- Fix any issues

**Must Remember Friday AM:**
- Delicate items (eggs, cake) need careful handling
- Refrigeration for prepared salads
- Covered storage
- Transport logistics if off-site prep

---

**Sterno Setup Reveals:**
- Hot food service model
- Racks, fuel, pans needed
- Safety equipment (matches)
- Keep food temperature controlled

**Multiple Plate Sizes:**
- 6" plates (x3) - likely for dessert/appetizers
- 10" plates - main course
- Specialized plates for fish, dessert, lettuce

**Serving Infrastructure:**
- "Little bowls" for traditional items
- "Bowls for veggies" (8 needed)
- "Platters for main course" (2 types)
- Abundance of serving spoons

**Beverage Program:**
- Wine and grape juice (four cups)
- Water (continuous availability)
- Kiddush cups separate from regular cups

---

### Venue Considerations

**"Bring to OVCC":**
- Off-site venue
- Everything must be transported
- Nothing can be assumed on-site
- Comprehensive packing list essential

- Use this as template

### Staff Coordination Points

**Multiple People Need This Timeline:**

**Kitchen Staff:**
- 7:40 PM plating deadline
- Hot food management
- Portion control (10 pieces kugel per tray, 8 pieces chicken, etc.)

**Service Staff:**
- Exact timing for delivery
- "Add forks/spoons before serving" reminders

**Seder Leader:**
- Knows "cue" timing for first course
- Can adjust if Seder running fast/slow
- Coordinates with service staff

---

### Quality Control Standards

**From This Document:**

**Portion Specifications:**
- "10 pieces per tray" (kugel)
- "About 8 pieces per tray" (chicken)
- "About 10 slices per tray" (meat)
- Consistency across all 8 tables

**Presentation Standards:**
- "Add forks before serving"
- "Add spoon before serving"
- Remove from sterno first
- Arrange on platters (not serve in pans)

**Service Standards:**
- "Immediately" clearing and serving
- Complete table clearing at end
- All small bowls removed with courses

- Meat: 10 slices × 8 platters = 80 slices
- Kugel: 10 pieces × 8 platters = 80 pieces

- 8 tables

- Total: 64-96 guests
- This matches portion calculations

## For Shluchim: Pesach Masterchef Program

### Program Overview

**From These Materials:**

**Program Name:** Pesach Masterchef

**Target Audience:** Children/families

**Format:** Cooking competition or activity

**Materials Provided:**
- Marketing flyer
- Completion diplomas
- Branded water bottles
- Event backdrop
- Educational Kahoot game

---

### Implementation Guide

**Pre-Event:**

**Marketing:**
- Download and customize flyer from Canva link
- Add your Chabad House details
- Include date, time, location
- Registration information
- Print and distribute or share digitally

**Preparation:**
- Print diplomas (one per participant)
- Order water bottle labels (or print on sticker paper)
- Print backdrop (large format at copy shop like FedEx)
- Test Kahoot link and familiarize with questions

---

**During Event:**

**Setup:**
- Display backdrop prominently
- Arrange cooking stations
- Distribute branded water bottles
- Have diplomas ready

**Activities:**
- Cooking competition/demonstration
- Passover learning (via Kahoot)
- Photo opportunities with backdrop
- Diploma ceremony at end

---

**Post-Event:**
- Photos with backdrop for social media
- Follow-up with participants
- Collect feedback for next year

---

### Customization Options

**Canva Links Are Shareable:**
- These links allow viewing
- To edit: May need Canva account
- Can duplicate and customize
- Maintain branding consistency

**What to Customize:**
- Your Chabad House name and logo
- Event date and time
- Location details
- Contact information
- Any specific program details

**Keep Standard:**
- "Pesach Masterchef" branding
- Overall design aesthetic
- Educational content (Kahoot)

---

### Program Variations

**Competition Format:**
- Teams compete to make best dish
- Judging by panel or attendees
- Categories: Presentation, taste, creativity
- Awards for different categories

**Workshop Format:**
- Demonstration by chef/Shlucha
- Hands-on participation
- Everyone makes same recipe
- Educational component about Passover

**Family Format:**
- Parent-child teams
- Age-appropriate tasks
- Focus on fun and learning
- Everyone wins diploma

---

### Integration with Passover Programming

**Timing Options:**

**Pre-Pesach:**
- Week before Passover
- Learn about Passover foods
- Practice recipes for Seder
- Build excitement

**During Pesach:**
- Chol Hamoed activity
- Day program for families
- Camp activity
- Community event

**Educational Integration:**
- Kahoot teaches Passover facts
- While cooking, discuss symbolism
- Why matzah? Why maror?
- Connect food to freedom story

---

### Recipe Selection

**For Children's Program:**
- Simple, age-appropriate recipes
- Passover-friendly (obviously)
- Limited sharp knives
- Mostly no-cook or simple baking
- Visible results quickly

**Popular Options:**
- Charoset variations
- Matzah pizza
- Fruit salads
- Simple desserts (see File 1128 for recipes)
- Decorated matzah

**Safety:**
- Adult supervision for all stations
- Pre-chop ingredients if needed
- Electric mixers supervised
- Oven use by adults only

---

### Budget Considerations

**Design Materials:**
- Canva designs: Free (already created)
- Printing flyer: Minimal cost
- Printing diplomas: $1-2 each
- Water bottle labels: $0.50-1 each
- Backdrop: $50-150 (reusable)

**Event Costs:**
- Ingredients for cooking
- Disposable supplies
- Prizes (optional)
- Marketing
- Venue (if off-site)

**Revenue:**
- Registration fees (optional)
- Sponsor the event
- Free to community

---

### Marketing Strategy

**Using the Flyer:**

**Digital:**
- Social media posts
- Email blast
- WhatsApp groups
- Website/blog
- Online registration link

**Physical:**
- Post in Jewish businesses
- Hand out at Hebrew school
- Include in Purim packages
- Mail to families with children

**Messaging:**
- Fun, hands-on activity
- Learn while cooking
- Passover preparation
- Family bonding
- Certificate of completion

---

### Diploma Ceremony

**End Event on High Note:**

**Presentation:**
- Call each child by name
- Brief comment about their work
- Hand diploma with handshake
- Photo opportunity
- Applause from group

**What Diplomas Can Say:**
- "Certified Pesach Masterchef"
- Child's name
- Date of completion
- Signature line (Rabbi/Rebbetzin)
- Official-looking design

**Added Value:**
- Children feel accomplished
- Parents appreciate recognition
- Nice memento to keep
- Incentive for participation

---

### Kahoot Game Tips

**If Unfamiliar with Kahoot:**
- Free online quiz platform
- Students answer on their devices
- Questions appear on main screen
- Competitive and engaging
- Tracks scores automatically

**Using Pesach Kahoot:**
- Access link before event
- Review questions
- Ensure WiFi adequate
- Test on your devices
- Prepare prizes for winners

**When to Use:**
- Opening icebreaker
- Between cooking activities
- While waiting for baking/cooking
- Educational break
- Closing activity

**Age Considerations:**
- Very young: May need parent help
- Elementary: Perfect age
- Teens: May need more challenging version
- Mixed ages: Team format

---

### Photo Opportunities

**Using the Backdrop:**

**Setup:**
- Well-lit area
- Stable mounting
- Clear space in front
- Props available (chef hats, utensils)

**Photo Types:**
- Individual with diploma
- Group shot of all participants
- Action shots while cooking
- Display of finished dishes
- Candid moments

**Sharing:**
- Social media (with permission)
- Email to parents
- Community newsletter
- Website gallery
- Next year's marketing

---

### Reusability

**Save for Future Years:**
- Backdrop is reusable
- Water bottle design template
- Diploma template (update date)
- Kahoot can be reused
- Flyer (update dates)

**Build on Success:**
- Collect photos
- Document recipes used
- Note what worked well
- Improve for next year
- Create tradition

---

**In This Collection:**
- **File 1128**: Pesach Recipes 5777 (massive recipe collection for selecting Masterchef recipes)
- **File 1124/1133**: Menu amounts for 45 people (quantity guidance)

- **File 1116**: Community Seder tips (Maggid activities adaptable for kids)

**Canva Links:**
- May expire over time
- May require login
- May have access restrictions

**Solutions:**
- Create own designs in Canva
- Use these as inspiration
- Search "Passover Masterchef" templates
- Commission designer
- Simple Word/PowerPoint versions

**Essential Elements:**
- "Pesach Masterchef" title
- Colorful, kid-friendly design
- Clear information
- Professional appearance
- Passover imagery (matzah, Seder plate, etc.)

# [Misc > For Writer > _5 Chanukah > General] Passover Menu Amounts for 45 People - Shopping List

## Note: Passover Content (Not Chanukah)

**Resource Type:** Shopping list with quantities

**Purpose:** Ingredient planning for community Passover Seder or event

**Serves:** 45 people

**Format:** Itemized grocery list with specific quantities

**Related:** File 1133 (exact duplicate of this file)

---

## Complete Shopping List

### Vegetables

**Root Vegetables:**
- **8 beetroots**
- **15 carrots** (note: appears twice in list, may need 15+8=23 total)
- **15 potatoes**
- **30 red potatoes**
- **22 sweet potatoes**
- **2 butternut squash**

**Leafy Greens:**
- **2 red leaf lettuce**
- **2 green leaf lettuce**

**Squash:**
- **20 zucchini** (note: appears twice, may need 20+5=25 total)
- **20 yellow squash** (note: appears twice, may need 20+5=25 total)

**Peppers:**
- **8 red peppers**
- **8 yellow peppers**

**Other Vegetables:**
- **5 pickles**
- **2 jicama**
- **1 red onion**
- **10 onions** (for mock liver)
- **2 onions** (for roast beef)
- **1 head garlic**
- **Celery stalks**

---

### Fruits

- **8 oranges**
- **20 apples** (plus **5 apples** for kugel = 25 total)
- **6 avocados**
- **2 small pineapple**
- **KLP raisins, if you can get**

---

### Eggs

- **30 eggs**

---

### Canned Goods

- **2 cans cranberry sauce**
- **Tomato sauce** (2 cans implied)
- **1.5 can crushed pineapple**

---

### Additional Items

- **Additional fruit juice** (for kugel)
- **2-3 lemons** for lemon juice

---

## For Shluchim: Using This Shopping List

### Understanding This List

**Scale:** 45 people

**Type of Meal:** Appears to be full Seder or festive meal

**Implied Menu:**
- Multiple salads (beet, lettuce-based, Israeli, jicama)
- Mock chopped liver appetizer
- Roast beef main course
- Multiple kugels (potato, sweet potato, apple)
- Vegetable side dishes

---

### Adjusting Quantities

**For Different Group Sizes:**

**For 30 People (Divide by 1.5):**
- 5 beetroots
- 10 carrots
- 10 potatoes
- 20 eggs
- Etc.

**For 60 People (Multiply by 1.33):**
- 11 beetroots
- 20 carrots
- 20 potatoes
- 40 eggs
- Etc.

**For 100 People (Multiply by 2.22):**
- 18 beetroots
- 33 carrots
- 33 potatoes
- 67 eggs
- Etc.

---

### Clarifying Duplicate Items

**Items Listed Twice:**

**Carrots:**
- "15 carrots" (early in list)
- "8 carrots" (later in list)
- **Likely:** Different uses (salad vs. soup vs. side dish)
- **Recommendation:** Buy 23 carrots total or round up to 25

**Zucchini:**
- "20 zucchini" (early)
- "5 zucchinis" (later)
- **Total:** 25 zucchini
- **Uses:** Likely for different recipes

**Yellow Squash:**
- "20 yellow squash" (early)
- "5 yellow squash" (later)
- **Total:** 25 yellow squash

**Apples:**
- "20 apples" (general)
- "5 apples (kugel)" (specific)
- **Total:** 25 apples

**Onions:**
- "10 onions (for mock liver)" (specific use)
- "2 onions (roast beef)" (specific use)
- "1 red onion" (specific variety)
- **Total:** 10-12 regular onions + 1 red onion

---

### Shopping Strategy

**Where to Buy:**

**Produce:**
- Farmers market (fresh, bulk pricing)
- Costco/Sam's Club (bulk quantities)
- Regular grocery (fill in gaps)
- Restaurant supply store (some items)

**Specialty Items:**
- **KLP raisins:** Jewish grocery or online
- **Jicama:** May need Hispanic market or specialty store
- **Butternut squash:** Seasonal availability

---

### Storage Considerations

**How Much Refrigerator Space:**

**High Volume Items:**
- 30 eggs (2.5 cartons)
- 4 heads lettuce
- 45 zucchini and squash combined
- 30+ potatoes
- Multiple other vegetables

**Recommendation:**
- Start shopping 1 week before
- Items that keep: potatoes, onions, beetroots, squash, oranges, apples
- Buy 2-3 days before: lettuce, avocados, jicama
- Buy day before: herbs, delicate items

**Storage Tips:**
- Potatoes: Cool, dark place (not fridge)
- Onions: Cool, dry place (not with potatoes)
- Lettuce: Wash, dry, refrigerate in container
- Avocados: Buy at varying ripeness stages
- Eggs: Refrigerate immediately

---

### Cost Estimation

**Approximate Costs (May vary by location):**

**Vegetables:**
- Root vegetables & potatoes: $30-40
- Leafy greens: $10-12
- Squash: $35-45
- Peppers: $15-20
- Other vegetables: $15-20
- **Subtotal: $105-137**

**Fruits:**
- Oranges: $8-10
- Apples: $20-25
- Avocados: $10-12
- Pineapples: $8-10
- **Subtotal: $46-57**

**Eggs:**
- 30 eggs: $10-15

**Canned Goods:**
- Canned items: $10-15

**TOTAL ESTIMATED: $171-224**

**Per Person Cost:** $3.80-4.98 (produce/eggs only)

---

### Missing from This List

**Items Not Included (May Need):**

**Seder Plate Items:**
- Matzah
- Maror (horseradish)
- Charoset ingredients (beyond listed apples)
- Karpas (unless using listed potatoes/celery)
- Z'roa (shankbone)
- Beitzah (hard-boiled egg from 30 listed)

**Proteins:**
- Only "2 onions (roast beef)" implies roast beef needed
- Quantity not specified
- **For 45 people:** Need approximately 15-20 lbs roast beef

**Beverages:**
- Wine/grape juice for four cups
- Water
- Other drinks

**Staples:**
- Oil
- Salt
- Sugar/sugar water
- Spices
- Potato starch (for recipes)
- Nuts (for mock liver, kugels)

**Serving Supplies:**
- Plates, cups, utensils
- Serving platters
- Napkins

---

### Recipe Cross-Reference

**Implied Recipes (Based on Quantities):**

**Mock Chopped Liver:**
- 10 onions specified
- Needs eggs (from 30), nuts, oil
- See File 1128 for recipe

**Roast Beef:**
- 2 onions specified
- Need roast beef quantity
- Wine, sugar, OJ for sauce
- See File 1128 for recipes

**Kugels:**
- Apples (5 for kugel)
- Sweet potatoes (22 - likely for kugel)
- Red potatoes (30 - likely for kugel)
- Crushed pineapple (1.5 cans)
- Additional fruit juice
- See File 1128 for multiple kugel recipes

**Salads:**
- Beets (8) - beet salad
- Lettuce (4 heads) - multiple salads
- Jicama (2) - jicama salad
- Oranges, avocados - fruit/avocado salads
- See File 1128 and 1135 for salad recipes and dressings

**Side Dishes:**
- Zucchini & yellow squash (25 each) - roasted veggies or zucchini kugel
- Peppers (16) - roasted or pepper salad
- Carrots (23) - multiple uses
- Butternut squash (2) - soup or side
- See File 1128 for recipes

---

### Prep Timeline

**1 Week Before:**
- Shop for non-perishables and sturdy produce
- Potatoes, onions, beetroots, squash, oranges, apples

**3 Days Before:**
- Shop for remaining produce
- Lettuce, avocados, jicama, peppers
- Eggs, canned goods

**2 Days Before:**
- Wash and prep vegetables that can be prepped
- Cook beetroots (3 hours!)
- Make any kugels that freeze well

**1 Day Before:**
- Finish vegetable prep
- Cook any dishes that improve overnight
- Roast beef, some kugels

**Day Of:**
- Final cooking
- Assembly
- Plating

---

### Quality Control

**Selecting Produce:**

**Beetroots:**
- Firm, smooth skin
- No soft spots
- Smaller ones cook faster

**Potatoes:**
- Firm, no green tinge
- No eyes or sprouts
- Even sizes for uniform cooking

**Lettuce:**
- Crisp, no wilting
- No brown edges
- Heavy for size (more moisture)

**Peppers:**
- Firm, glossy
- No wrinkles
- Heavy for size

**Avocados:**
- Buy at varying stages
- Some hard (for later)
- Some yielding (for soon)
- No dark soft spots

---

### Waste Reduction

**Using All Parts:**

**Lettuce:**
- Outer leaves: Soup or smoothies
- Cores: Compost or discard

**Carrots:**
- Tops: Make vegetable stock
- Peels: Stock or compost

**Onions:**
- Skins: Save for stock
- Scraps: Stock

**Celery:**
- Leaves: Add to soup/salad
- Ends: Stock

**Make Stock:**
- Save all vegetable scraps
- Boil with water, strain
- Freeze for later use

---

### Substitutions

**If Can't Find Certain Items:**

**Jicama:**
- Substitute: Water chestnuts, daikon radish, or crisp apple
- Or: Omit and increase other salad vegetables

**KLP Raisins:**
- Check if really need KLP (depends on your custom)
- Substitute: Other dried fruit if allowed

**Butternut Squash:**
- Substitute: Other winter squash (acorn, kabocha)
- Or: Sweet potatoes

**Red/Yellow Peppers:**
- Can use all one color
- Or mix with green peppers (less expensive)

---

**In This Collection:**
- **File 1128**: Pesach Recipes 5777 (complete recipe collection for using these ingredients)
- **File 1133**: Duplicate of this file (same shopping list)
