# Shluchim Forum: Community Seder Menu Standards - Machine vs Shmurah Matzah

**Type**: Shluchim Exchange Forum Discussion
**Topic**: Standards for food served at community Seders in Chabad houses
**Date**: March 2015
**Source**: http://www.shluchimexchange.com/en/forum/viewtopic.php?t=478224
**Key Question**: Can/should Chabad houses serve machine matzah and lower food standards at public Seders?

## Original Question - Moshe Stiefel, Almere, Netherlands

**Context**: In past years, the shliach made a community Seder in the shul, serving food "not on our standards" - machine matzah, food not cooked in his own kitchen, gebrokts, etc. (His family ate a different menu.) This year, they've recently opened their Chabad house (the community shul closed down).

**Dilemma**: "In a way I feel that our bais Chabad is like our own house which we of course do not allow machine matzah etc., but perhaps we could allow it, as it isn't our private house...."

**Request**: "What do other shluchim do which arrange a seder in their Chabad houses? Please advise or at least tell me what you do."

**Urgency**: "Of course, this issue needs a quick answer, as we are in the midst of preparations..."

## Response #1: Yechiel S Levitansky, Sumy, Ukraine

**Position**: Maintains high standards despite cost

"Although I know many shluchim here in ukraine who serve machine matzah at the public sedarim etc. 'mekublani mebais avi' [I received from my father's house] that we serve only Shmurah and anything we serve in our CH is what we would serve in our house (at least to the kids)....so yes, it gets expensive and the menu is less colorful but people appreciate it and the Rebbe blaibt nisht kein baal chov! [the Rebbe doesn't remain indebted!]"

**Principle**: Whatever is served in the Chabad House must meet the standards they would maintain in their own home, particularly for their children.

**Acknowledgment**: Admits this approach is expensive and limits menu options ("less colorful")

**Results**: "People appreciate it" and trust in the Rebbe's blessing that the investment will be rewarded

**Contact**: chabadsumy@gmail.com

## Response #2: Yankie Denburg, Coral Springs, FL

**Position**: Received rabbinic guidance against machine matzah

"Several years ago I was told by my Rov not to serve machine matzah in my shul at all - not only not at the Seder but not during any time of pesach..."

**Follow-Up Question**: "In the Rebbe's shitah, if someone ended up eating machine matzah for the seder, are they yotzei the mitzvah, or since the matzos need to be made lshem mitzvas matzah which a machine can't do they would still need to eat shmurah matzah (with another bracha)?"

**Context**: Discussing whether machine matzah can fulfill the mitzvah d'oraysa of matzas mitzvah, given the requirement for "l'shem mitzvas matzah" (intention for the mitzvah) which a machine cannot have.

## Response #3: Levi Brashevitzky, Norfolk, VA

**Position**: Serve only what they personally eat

"We have been doing Seders and all meals during pesach for all that need at the Chabad house and serve only what we eat."

**What They Buy Ready-Made**:
- Prepared kugels (from Crown Heights community - some family members eat, some don't due to machmir standards)
- Oil
- Wine and grape juice
- Salt
- Balsamic vinegar
- Matzah (hand-made shmura only)
- Raw meat
- Raw gefilte fish
- Coffee and tea (which they don't personally use but have available for guests)

**Everything Else**: "All made in our kitchen"

**Standard**: "Anything we buy is what I would eat myself (other than what I buy for the kids which I will serve my kids)"

**Cost Acknowledgment**: "It is very pricey but we fundraise for it"

**Contact**: Cell: 757-513-3663

## Response #4: Shraga Sherman, Merion Station, PA

**Historical Story - The Rebbe Rashab**:

Tells a story (requesting confirmation/correction) that the Joint Distribution sent machine-made matzah (possibly to Rostov) for Pesach. The Yeshiva didn't use it on Pesach but used it after Pesach. Some bochurim wouldn't eat it as "chometz she'avar alav haPesach" (chometz that passed over Pesach). When the Rebbe Rashab heard this, he was upset and said "matza upon which many many (thousands and thousands?) Jews were mekayim mitzvas matzah is not Chometz."

**Interpretation**: "With that said, I understood the Rebbe Rashab's answer as a b'deved b'deved [post-facto, emergency situation] and melamed zechus [finding merit], not at all how we should conduct ourselves, etc."

**The Rebbe's Mivtza**: "I understood the Rebbe's mivtza (the first mivtza?) to be promoting Shmurah Matzah as opposed to a campaign against machine matzah."

**The Rebbe's Statement**: "The Rebbe said (see last week's hiskashrus) that it is better to give children shruya [soaked matzah - which some don't eat] than machine matzah."

## Response #5: Shlomo Uminer, Palm City, FL

**Strong Position on Standards**:

"Dont mix the two things. Being mehader in cooking is nice and you can do it but you can get food from a caterer that does not have every hidur you have."

**But on Shmurah Matzah - No Compromise**:

"Rabbi shtifel you absolutley do not have to mutche [trouble] your wife to cook everthing. shmurah matzah is diffrent its an inyan of the rebbe that the rebbe shturemt [pushed strongly] that we should give all our baalei batim and even not for the seder, there is no place whatsoever fo non shmurah matzah in our chabad house at all no matter what, other then the seder itself better they eat kartofel [potatoes]. This is part of our misssion to give and teach the world about this, its the febbes [Rebbe's] mivtza."

**On Gebrokts**: "Gebroks is not on the same level but its not somthing we should do unless you have shas hadchak [pressing circumstances] circumstances which needs a yishuv hadas [settlement of mind] and a rav."

**Includes Sicha Quote**: Pastes a sicha from Vayakhel-Pekudei 5732 (in Yiddish) about the Rebbe's push for shmurah matzah distribution.

**Translation of Sicha Excerpt**:

The Rebbe emphasized seeing that as many Jews as possible should have shmurah matzah for Pesach - give them matzah for the whole Pesach, or at minimum for the Seder (six matzos as they used to say "a gang matzos"), or at minimum a whole matzah (the middle matzah), or at minimum for the k'zayis matzah.

And this should be done "b'chayus uvemaratz hachi gadol" (with the greatest enthusiasm and energy), seeing that as many Jews as possible should have matzah, reaching another Jew and another Jew, and specifically hand matzah, and specifically round [not square], with all the hiddurim, up to the manner of "ushmartem es hamatzos" (you shall guard the matzos) according to the simple interpretation - guarding the matzos, and also the second interpretation "mamtinim umetzah" - that a Jew looks and waits for when the time will come that he can eat matzah, which is "michla d'asvasa" and "michla d'mehemnusa" (food of healing and food of faith), as stated in the Zohar.

**Contact**: rabbi@chabadmsl.com

**Closing**: "We should see the rebbe immidiatley and celebrate yud alef nissan together. Shlomo uminer"

## Response #6: Yosef Levertov, Austin, TX

**Additional Rebbe Instruction**:

"If I remember correctly, The Rebbe instructed Ezras Achim to send to Russia Shmurah Matza only."

**Significance**: Reinforces that even for outreach to Jews in Russia during Soviet times, the Rebbe insisted on shmurah matzah only, not machine matzah.

## Response #7: Yankie Denburg (Follow-Up Question)

**Clarification Sought**:

"Of course, ch"v [chas v'shalom - G-d forbid] we should say that someone who eats machine matzah is eating chametz."

**The Real Question**: "My question is: would it be a correct or false statement to tell someone that in order to be mekayim the MITZVAH DORAYSA [Torah commandment] of eating matzah, they can not use machine matzah and MUST use shmurah matzah to fulfill the mitzvah."

**Real-Life Context**: "(I actually had this conversation with a lady who very nicely refused to take matzah because she didn't like the taste of the matzah I gave her last year ... :-)"

**Contact**: Rabbi Yankie Denburg, Chabad Southwest Coral Springs

## Response #8: Joseph Korf, Hollywood, FL

**Clear Answer**: "Totally incorrect to say that to another Jew and is factually incorrect."

**Implication**: One cannot tell someone they're halachically required to use only shmurah matzah. Machine matzah fulfills the mitzvah d'oraysa, even if shmurah is preferred or the Chabad standard.

**Contact**: HCS-Chabad Lubavitch of Hollywood, 305.761.0607, Rabbihcs@gmail.com

## Response #9: Yaakov Saacks, Dix Hills, NY

**Reinterpretation of Rebbe Rashab Story**:

"Sharaga I understand the Rebbe Rashab's answer as very practical and pragmatic and not simply this is a b'dieved. This matza is kosher. PERIOD. Not for us and not for Jews at the Seder."

**Key Point**: The matzah is kosher, but "not for us and not for Jews at the Seder" - meaning it's not appropriate for the Seder even though it's kosher.

**Leadership Philosophy** (signature quote):
"A true leader does not seek followers; he wants to teach others how to be leaders. He does not want to control; he wants the truth. He does not impose his leadership on others, nor does he take away anyone's autonomy. He inspires by love, not coercion. When it comes time to take credit, he makes himself invisible; but is the first to arrive in the time of need, and he will never shrink away in fear. He is so passionate about your welfare that when you consult him for guidance, it is like coming face to face with yourself for the first time."

**Contact**: 631-351-8672, WWW.TheChaiCenter.com

## Response #10: Berel Levertov, Santa Fe, NM

**Clarifying the Question**:

"Rabbi Denburg is asking about someone being yotzei matzas mitzvah with Machine matzah that cannot have in mind 'lshem matzas mitzvah.' Can/should you tell/argue with someone that they are not yotzei with machine matzah?"

**Key Issue**: The halachic question is whether a machine (which cannot have intention) can produce matzah that fulfills "matzas mitzvah" given the requirement for "l'shem matzas matzah."

## Response #11: Menachem Lazar, Rome, Italy

**Practical Note**: "Lechuro [in actuality] they say leshem matzas mitzvah when they turn on the machibe [machine]"

**Implication**: Machine matzah bakeries do have intention when they start the machine, potentially addressing the "l'shem" requirement.

## Response #12: Berel Levertov (Follow-Up)

**Question Remains**: "Hence the question: Is that enough?"

**Core Issue**: Even if intention is stated when starting the machine, is that sufficient for the halachic requirement of "l'shem matzas mitzvah," or must each individual matzah be made with active, ongoing intention?

## For Shluchim: Navigating Community Standards vs. Halachic Requirements

### The Core Tension

This discussion reveals a fundamental tension Shluchim face: balancing **Chabad standards and the Rebbe's directives** with **halachic requirements**, **community accessibility**, and **resource constraints**.

**Three Positions Emerge**:

1. **Maintain Full Home Standards** (Levitansky, Brashevitzky): Whatever is served in the Chabad House must meet the standards you'd maintain for your own family. Expensive, limited menu, but people appreciate it and trust in the Rebbe's blessings.

2. **Shmurah Matzah Non-Negotiable, Other Hiddurim Flexible** (Uminer, Denburg's Rov): Distinguish between shmurah matzah (which is the Rebbe's mivtza and non-negotiable) versus other chumros like gebrokts or home-cooked food (which can be relaxed with rabbinic consultation in pressing circumstances).

3. **Practical Halachic Approach** (Korf, Saacks): Recognize that machine matzah is kosher and fulfills the mitzvah d'oraysa. While Chabad promotes shmurah, one cannot tell others they're halachically required to use it or haven't fulfilled the mitzvah without it.

### Practical Implementation Guidelines

**On Shmurah Matzah**:
- **Consensus**: Every respondent agrees that Chabad houses should serve only shmurah matzah, not machine matzah, at Seders and throughout Pesach
- **Rationale**: This is "the Rebbe's mivtza," part of Chabad's mission to teach about this
- **Historical Precedent**: The Rebbe instructed Ezras Achim to send only shmurah matzah to Russia
- **The Rebbe's Statement**: Better to give children shruya (which some don't eat due to gebrokts concerns) than machine matzah
- **Sicha Source**: Vayakhel-Pekudei 5732 - extensive push for distributing shmurah matzah with "greatest enthusiasm and energy"

**On Other Food Standards**:
- **Spectrum of Practice**: From everything home-cooked to using caterers/prepared foods with reliable supervision
- **Key Principle** (Uminer): "Being mehader in cooking is nice... but shmurah matzah is different"
- **Gebrokts**: Can potentially be permitted in "shas hadchak" (pressing circumstances) with rabbinic consultation, unlike machine matzah which has "no place whatsoever"
- **Budget Reality**: Maintaining high standards "gets expensive" and requires active fundraising

**On Halachic Communication**:
- **Critical Mistake**: Never tell someone machine matzah doesn't fulfill the mitzvah or is chametz - this is "factually incorrect"
- **Proper Approach**: Promote shmurah matzah as the preferred, more mehudar (enhanced) option without delegitimizing machine matzah
- **The Rebbe Rashab's Teaching**: Matzah upon which thousands of Jews fulfilled mitzvas matzah is not chometz - showing respect for others' observance even while maintaining higher personal standards
- **Nuance**: Machine matzah is "kosher PERIOD" but still "not for us and not for Jews at the Seder" - it's about what we aspire to, not what's minimally acceptable

### For New Chabad Houses

**The Transition Question**: The original questioner faced a common scenario - previously renting space (shul) where lower standards felt acceptable, now in their own Chabad house which "feels like our own house."

**Consensus Guidance**:
1. **Set Standards Early**: The Chabad house sets the tone from the beginning. What you establish initially becomes your known standard.
2. **Communicate Mission**: Frame it as educational - teaching the community about shmurah matzah, not looking down on other practices
3. **Budget Proactively**: Factor the cost of higher standards into fundraising from the start, not as an afterthought
4. **Distinguish Levels**: Shmurah matzah is non-negotiable (Rebbe's mivtza); other hiddurim can be evaluated case-by-case with rabbinic guidance

### Fundraising Messaging

**The "Pricey but Worth It" Approach** (Brashevitzky model):
- Be transparent: "It is very pricey"
- Active solution: "But we fundraise for it"
- Frame as investment in quality Jewish experience
- Trust: "The Rebbe blaibt nisht kein baal chov" - the Rebbe doesn't remain indebted

**Donor Appeal**:
- Sponsor shmurah matzah for community Seder: ~$5-10 per person
- Sponsor full elevated menu: ~$40-60 per person
- "Your support ensures everyone at our Seder experiences Passover the Chabad way - with hand-made shmurah matzah and the highest standards"

### Addressing Pushback

**"I Don't Like the Taste"** (Denburg's scenario):

- Acknowledge: "I know it's different from what many are used to"
- Educate: "This is the traditional way matzah was made for thousands of years - the same way our ancestors ate in Egypt"
- Experience: "Give it another chance - many people find they acquire a taste, and it's only for the Seder itself"
- Benefits: "It's actually more digestible than machine matzah" (anecdotal)
- Mission: "Part of what makes the Chabad Seder special is connecting to this authentic tradition"

**"Why So Strict?"**:

- Frame positively: "We're not being strict - we're being authentic"
- Historical: "This is how the Rebbe asked us to do it"
- Universal: "We want everyone to experience Pesach at the highest level, not just our own family"
- Standards: "Just like we wouldn't serve non-kosher food, we also want to ensure the matzah meets the highest kosher standards"

### The L'shem Mitzvas Matzah Question

**The Unresolved Halachic Issue**:

The discussion leaves open whether machine matzah can truly fulfill "l'shem mitzvas matzah" if the machine itself cannot have intention, even if intention is stated when starting the machine.

**Practical Shliach Response**:
- Don't engage in this debate with community members
- Simply promote: "We use hand-made shmurah matzah because it's made with personal attention and intention at every step"
- If pressed on whether machine is kosher: "Yes, it's kosher. We just choose to enhance the mitzvah with shmurah"

### Contact Information Network

This discussion demonstrates the value of the Shluchim Exchange network - multiple experienced Shluchim from diverse locations (Ukraine, Florida, Virginia, Pennsylvania, New York, Illinois, Connecticut, New Mexico, Texas, Rome) sharing practical guidance, halachic sources, and real-world experience, allowing newer Shluchim to learn from veterans' successes and challenges.

## Bottom Line

This March 2015 Shluchim Exchange forum discussion (http://www.shluchimexchange.com/en/forum/viewtopic.php?t=478224) addresses a fundamental dilemma for Chabad houses: what food standards to maintain at community Seders, sparked by Moshe Stiefel (Almere, Netherlands) who previously ran Seders in rented shul space serving "food not on our standards" (machine matzah, not home-cooked, gebrokts) while his family ate differently, but now with a new Chabad house feels it's "like our own house" and questions whether to maintain home standards or allow lower standards since "it isn't our private house," urgently seeking guidance from fellow Shluchim. The responses reveal three main positions: (1) Yechiel Levitansky (Sumy, Ukraine) and Levi Brashevitzky (Norfolk, VA) maintain full home standards at their Chabad houses serving "only what we eat" and "what we would serve in our house (at least to the kids)" using only shmurah matzah and everything meeting their personal kashrut standards, acknowledging "it gets expensive and the menu is less colorful" and "very pricey" but "people appreciate it," they "fundraise for it," and trust "the Rebbe blaibt nisht kein baal chov" (doesn't remain indebted); (2) Shlomo Uminer (Palm City, FL) and Yankie Denburg's Rov (Coral Springs, FL) distinguish between shmurah matzah which is "an inyan of the rebbe that the rebbe shturemt" (pushed strongly) as "part of our mission" with "no place whatsoever for non shmurah matzah in our chabad house at all no matter what" (better to serve potatoes) versus other hiddurim like gebrokts or home-cooking which "is nice and you can do it but you can get food from a caterer," with Uminer quoting a sicha from Vayakhel-Pekudei 5732 about promoting shmurah matzah distribution "with greatest enthusiasm and energy" and Denburg's Rov forbidding machine matzah "not only not at the Seder but not during any time of pesach"; and (3) Joseph Korf (Hollywood, FL) and Yaakov Saacks (Dix Hills, NY) emphasize halachic accuracy that while Chabad promotes shmurah, telling someone machine matzah doesn't fulfill the mitzvah d'oraysa is "totally incorrect" and "factually incorrect," with Saacks interpreting the Rebbe Rashab's teaching that "matza upon which many many Jews were mekayim mitzvas matzah is not Chometz" as "very practical and pragmatic" meaning machine matzah "is kosher PERIOD" though still "not for us and not for Jews at the Seder," while Shraga Sherman (Merion Station, PA) reports "the Rebbe said it is better to give children shruya than machine matzah" and Yosef Levertov (Austin, TX) notes "the Rebbe instructed Ezras Achim to send to Russia Shmurah Matza only." The discussion also addresses the unresolved halachic question raised by Denburg about whether machine matzah can fulfill "l'shem mitzvas matzah" since machines cannot have intention, with Berel Levertov (Santa Fe, NM) clarifying this as the core question and Menachem Lazar (Rome, Italy) noting "they say leshem matzas mitzvah when they turn on the machibe" though Levertov questions "is that enough?" For Shluchim implementation, this reveals: shmurah matzah is universally considered non-negotiable in Chabad houses as the Rebbe's first mivtza and central mission, distinguishing it from other chumros that can be evaluated case-by-case with rabbinic consultation; cost reality requires proactive fundraising framed as investment in quality Jewish experience; new Chabad houses should set standards early as they establish their identity; communication must promote shmurah positively (preferred, more mehudar, authentic tradition) without delegitimizing machine matzah halachically (which remains kosher and fulfills the mitzvah even if not Chabad's standard); practical donor appeals can offer sponsorship tiers (shmurah matzah $5-10/person, full elevated menu $40-60/person); addressing pushback requires education about tradition and authenticity rather than strictness; Brashevitzky's detailed shopping list provides template (buy ready: prepared Crown Heights kugels with family eating selectively, oil, wine/grape juice, salt, balsamic vinegar, hand shmurah matzah, raw meat, raw gefilte fish, coffee/tea; make everything else in own kitchen); and the Shluchim Exchange network demonstrates invaluable peer support with experienced Shluchim from Ukraine, multiple Florida locations, Virginia, Pennsylvania, New York, Illinois, Connecticut, New Mexico, Texas, and Rome sharing practical guidance, halachic sources (the Vayakhel-Pekudei 5732 sicha, last week's Hiskashrus, Rebbe Rashab story about Joint Distribution matzah), real-world experience, contact information, and philosophical frameworks ultimately establishing that while standards vary on other matters, the consensus is clear that Chabad houses serve exclusively shmurah matzah as expression of the Rebbe's mission to teach the world about this practice, balancing authentic Chabad identity with halachic accuracy, communal accessibility, and fiscal sustainability through dedicated fundraising and clear mission-driven messaging that elevates rather than condemns.

# Shluchim Forum: Shipping Matzah to 500 Households - Logistics and Cost Solutions

**Type**: Shluchim Exchange Forum Discussion
**Topic**: Most economical methods for mailing matzah gift boxes
**Date**: March 2017
**Source**: http://www.shluchimexchange.com/en/forum/viewtopic.php?t=514914
**Key Question**: "What is the best / most economical way to mail matzah gift boxes to approximately 500 households?"

## Original Question

**Challenge**: Shliach needs to mail matzah gift boxes to approximately 500 households

**Request**: Looking for best/most economical shipping method

## Unrelated Initial Response (Facebook RSVP Context)

**Note**: The document contains an apparently unrelated response about Facebook event RSVPs that doesn't address the shipping question:

"I've often found that the actual RSVPs are a good indicator of about how many people will come to an event - if not the actual list of who will come. I try very hard to push people to RSVP on a different service to actually claim their seat - using the FB event mainly for promotion. Messaging each person who said maybe is a good way to actually get them to respond if they plan on coming or not ... but is time consuming."

**Context**: This appears to be from a different thread mistakenly included in the document.

## Response #1: Daniel Sanoff, Poughkeepsie, NY (March 8, 2017)

### First Class Mail Solution

**Weight Limit**: If less than 13 ounces, can send First Class mail

**Commercial Rate Advantage**:
- Using stamps.com or similar: $3.47 for 13oz (commercial rate)
- Retail rate: $4.11
- **Savings**: $0.64 per package (14% discount)

### Packaging Selection

**Tested Multiple Envelopes**, settled on:
- **Product**: Bubble mailer from Uline
- **Model**: S-7550
- **Description**: Uline Bubble-Lined Polyolefin Mailers 7 1/4 x 20
- **Link**: http://www.uline.com/Product/Detail/S-7550/Poly-Mailers/Uline-Bubble-Lined-Polyolefin-Mailers-7-14-1-4-x-20?keywords=s-7550
- **Weight**: Just over 1 oz

**Total Package Weight**:
- Matzah + bubble mailer + letter/brochure = 11 oz

**Strategy**: "Because of slight variations in the weight of the matzo, and not wanting to individually weigh each piece, we just paid the 13oz rate for each package."

**Rationale**: Easier to pay slightly more and guarantee First Class eligibility than risk packages going over 13oz limit

### Label Recommendation

**Strong Preference**: "I would HIGHLY recommend paying the extra for AVERY products as they peel off easily while the cheaper versions can be a hassle to deal with."

**Product**: amazon.com/Avery-Shipping (specific product link truncated in document)

**Reasoning**: Time savings and frustration reduction worth the premium when processing 500 packages

### Bottom Line Costs

**Per Package**:
- Packaging (Uline bubble mailer): ~$0.83 (estimated based on typical Uline pricing for this product)
- Postage (13oz First Class with tracking): $3.47
- **Total**: ~$4.30 + cost of actual matzah

**Benefits**:
- Includes tracking
- Works anywhere in the country (no zone pricing)
- First Class speed (2-5 business days typically)

### Important Warning

**Weight Considerations for Printed Materials**:

"Keep in mind: If you're going to add printed material to the package, many pesach guides and other brochures can weigh a lot, and push you over the 13 oz limit, which forces you to pay priority mail rates."

**Implication**: If adding heavy brochures/Haggadahs, may need to:
- Use lighter paper stock
- Reduce number of pages
- Switch to Priority Mail pricing
- Weigh samples before committing to full run

## Response #2: Yitzi Hein, Pittsford, NY (March 8, 2017)

**Alternative Suggestion**: "I believe a medium sized priority mail fits a shmura matzah box"

**Implication**:
- Priority Mail Flat Rate Medium Box might work
- Flat Rate advantage: One price regardless of weight (up to 70 lbs)
- 2017 rate was approximately $13.65 for Medium Flat Rate
- Trade-off: Higher cost per package but no weight concerns

## Response #3: Bulk Mail Suggestion (Date/Author unclear from document)

**Method**: "we send our matzos thru the non profit bulk mail"

**Product**: "buy hard matzah boxes from eisenbach and you can mail them bulk mail"

**Advantages of Bulk Mail**:
- Significantly cheaper per piece (potentially $0.50-1.00 each)
- Non-profit postal rate eligibility for Chabad houses (501(c)(3))

**Disadvantages**:
- Requires bulk mail permit
- Minimum quantities (typically 200 pieces)
- Slower delivery (2-3 weeks)
- More complex sorting/preparation requirements
- Must meet USPS bulk mail standards for addressing, bundling, etc.

**Hard Matzah Boxes**: Mention of purchasing from Eisenbach suggests these are protective boxes specifically designed for mailing, preventing breakage

## Response #4: Shlomo Uminer, Palm City, FL (March 13, 2017)

**Question**: "Is there a link or a phone number to obtain these hard matza boxes?"

**Context**: Interested in the Eisenbach hard boxes mentioned for bulk mail but needs contact information

## Response #5: Yossi Brackman, Chicago, IL (March 13, 2017)

**Humorous Suggestion**: "Get the really thick matzah, you can probably mail it in a poly bag. ;-)"

**Context**: Joke about using extra-thick/sturdy matzah that wouldn't need protective packaging (but not practical advice)

**Implication**: Acknowledges the fragility concern - regular hand shmurah matzah is quite breakable and needs protective packaging

## Response #6: Yisroel Eliyahu Wilansky, Ponte Vedra Beach, FL (March 16, 2017)

**Comment**: "Mivtza Matza :)"

**Context**: Expressing support/enthusiasm for the matzah mailing project, comparing it to a "Mivtza" (Chabad outreach campaign)

## Response #7: Joseph Eisenbach, Litchfield, CT (March 25, 2017)

**Solution**: "BH www.thematzahbox.org"

**Significance**: Eisenbach (likely the manufacturer mentioned earlier) provides direct source

**The MatzahBox.org**:
- Appears to be dedicated service/product for shipping matzah
- Likely offers both boxes and potentially full shipping solutions
- Eisenbach family has been in matzah business for generations
- Provides "hard matzah boxes" designed specifically for mailing

## For Shluchim: Comprehensive Shipping Decision Framework

### Method Comparison

**Option 1: First Class Mail (Sanoff Method)**
- **Best for**: 50-1000 packages, quality presentation, tracking needed
- **Cost**: ~$4.30 + matzah
- **Pros**: Tracking, reasonable speed, national flat rate, professional appearance
- **Cons**: More expensive than bulk, weight limits restrictive
- **Prep time**: Moderate (labels, stuffing envelopes)

**Option 2: Priority Mail Flat Rate (Hein Method)**
- **Best for**: Heavier packages, including substantial printed materials
- **Cost**: ~$13.65 per medium flat rate box (2017 rate)
- **Pros**: No weight concerns up to 70 lbs, tracking included, faster delivery
- **Cons**: Significantly more expensive, box size may be excessive for just matzah
- **Prep time**: Low (just seal boxes)

**Option 3: Non-Profit Bulk Mail**
- **Best for**: 500+ packages, advance planning, budget-conscious
- **Cost**: ~$0.50-1.00 per piece
- **Pros**: Dramatically cheaper at scale, non-profit rates
- **Cons**: Requires permit ($240/year), slow (2-3 weeks), complex preparation, minimum quantities
- **Prep time**: High (sorting, bundling, paperwork)

**Option 4: Commercial Matzah Box Solutions (Eisenbach/MatzahBox.org)**
- **Best for**: Simplicity, protective packaging, professional appearance
- **Cost**: Variable (boxes + chosen shipping method)
- **Pros**: Purpose-designed protection, professional, may offer turnkey solutions
- **Cons**: Box cost adds to expense
- **Prep time**: Low to moderate depending on service level

### Cost Analysis for 500 Packages

**First Class Mail (Sanoff Method)**:
- Packaging: $415 (500 × $0.83)
- Postage: $1,735 (500 × $3.47)
- Labels: $20 (Avery shipping labels)
- Matzah: $1,000-2,500 (500 × $2-5 per matzah depending on source/size)
- **Total**: $3,170-4,670
- **Per package**: $6.34-9.34

**Priority Flat Rate (Hein Method)**:
- Boxes: Free (USPS supplies)
- Postage: $6,825 (500 × $13.65)
- Matzah: $1,000-2,500
- **Total**: $7,825-9,325
- **Per package**: $15.65-18.65

**Bulk Mail Method**:
- Boxes (Eisenbach): $250-500 (estimated $0.50-1.00 per box)
- Bulk mail permit: $240 (annual)
- Postage: $250-500 (500 × $0.50-1.00 non-profit rate)
- Matzah: $1,000-2,500
- **Total**: $1,740-3,740 (first year including permit), $1,500-3,500 (subsequent years)
- **Per package**: $3.00-7.00

**Savings Analysis**:
- Bulk Mail vs. First Class: Save $1,430-$1,930 (42-52% savings)
- Bulk Mail vs. Priority: Save $6,085-$5,585 (78% savings)
- **But**: Bulk requires advance planning (3+ weeks before Pesach for delivery)

### Implementation Recommendations

**For First-Time Matzah Mailing**:
1. Start with First Class (Sanoff method)
2. Learn logistics, breakage rates, recipient feedback
3. Evaluate whether worth bulk mail investment next year

**For Established Annual Program (500+)**:
1. Invest in bulk mail permit
2. Use Eisenbach hard boxes
3. Mail 4 weeks before Pesach
4. Save $1,500-2,000 annually to reinvest in more matzah or recipients

**For Premium Presentation**:
1. Use Priority Flat Rate
2. Include substantial printed materials (Haggadah, Pesach guide, etc.)
3. Position as high-value gift justifying higher cost
4. Target major donors or VIPs

**For Maximum Reach with Limited Budget**:
1. Bulk mail to maximize number of recipients
2. Simple packaging
3. Focus resources on matzah quality rather than shipping speed

### Practical Tips from the Discussion

**Packaging Materials**:
- **Bubble mailers**: Uline S-7550 proven effective
- **Hard boxes**: Eisenbach/MatzahBox.org for better protection
- **Labels**: Invest in Avery brand - time savings worth premium when doing 500 packages

**Weight Management**:
- Test package weight before bulk ordering materials
- Account for variations in matzah weight
- Round up to next postage tier to avoid individual weighing (Sanoff's strategy)
- Remember printed materials add significant weight

**Workflow Efficiency**:
- Production line approach: One station stuffing, one labeling, one sealing
- Recruit volunteers - make it a community event ("Mivtza Matza" party)
- Allow 2-3 days for 500 packages with volunteer team
- Schedule 3-4 weeks before Pesach to allow shipping time

**Tracking Considerations**:
- First Class and Priority include tracking
- Bulk mail typically does not
- For major donors, consider upgrading to tracked service even if using bulk for others
- Tracking allows proactive follow-up if packages delayed

### Resources Mentioned

**Shipping Services**:
- Stamps.com - Commercial postage rates, print labels at home
- USPS.com - Bulk mail information, Click-N-Ship for Priority

**Packaging Suppliers**:
- Uline.com - Bubble mailers (S-7550), shipping supplies
- USPS - Free Priority Mail boxes
- Eisenbach/MatzahBox.org - Purpose-built matzah shipping boxes

**Label Products**:
- Avery shipping labels on Amazon - Premium quality, easy peel

**Matzah Sources** (from companion document 1166):
- matzah.biz
- shlichusmarket.com
- shluchim.jewfadz.com
- Shapiro: 718-774-0999

### Mailing List Considerations

**Quality Over Quantity**:
- 500 households is significant expense ($1,500-9,000 depending on method)
- Ensure addresses are current
- Consider segmentation: Core community vs. peripheral contacts
- May be more impactful to send fewer packages with personal notes than mass mailing

**Compliance**:
- Non-profit bulk mail requires statement of ownership
- Can't use bulk mail for commercial purposes
- Ensure Chabad house has current 501(c)(3) status
- Keep records for audit purposes

**Follow-Up Strategy**:
- Include note with matzah explaining how to use for Seder
- Add contact information for Pesach questions or Seder invitation
- Consider including response card or QR code to confirm receipt and gather feedback
- Use mailing as touchpoint for Pesach invitation or other engagement

### Timing Considerations

**First Class**: Mail 1-2 weeks before Pesach
- Arrives in 2-5 business days
- Buffer for delays
- Fresh arrival creates excitement

**Priority**: Mail 10 days-2 weeks before
- Faster delivery (1-3 days)
- Can mail closer to holiday

**Bulk**: Mail 4 weeks minimum before Pesach
- Slow processing (2-3 weeks)
- Must factor in postal service delays
- Risk of late arrival if mailed too close

## Bottom Line

This March 2017 Shluchim Exchange forum discussion (http://www.shluchimexchange.com/en/forum/viewtopic.php?t=514914) addresses the practical logistics of economically mailing matzah gift boxes to approximately 500 households, with Daniel Sanoff (Poughkeepsie, NY) providing the most detailed response recommending First Class mail for packages under 13 ounces using bubble mailers from Uline (model S-7550, measuring 7¼ x 20 inches weighing just over 1 oz) with commercial postage rates through stamps.com ($3.47 for 13oz vs. $4.11 retail saving $0.64 per package or 14%), packaging the matzah with bubble mailer and letter/brochure totaling 11 oz but paying the 13oz rate to avoid individual weighing given slight matzah weight variations, strongly recommending premium AVERY label products despite higher cost because "they peel off easily while the cheaper versions can be a hassle" when processing hundreds of packages, yielding bottom line cost of approximately $4.30 per package (packaging plus postage) plus matzah cost with tracking included and delivery anywhere in the country, while warning that adding printed materials like Pesach guides or brochures can push packages over the 13oz limit forcing more expensive Priority Mail rates. Alternative approaches presented include Yitzi Hein (Pittsford, NY) suggesting Priority Mail medium flat rate boxes which fit shmura matzah boxes at approximately $13.65 each (2017 rate) eliminating weight concerns but significantly increasing cost; an unnamed contributor recommending non-profit bulk mail using "hard matzah boxes from eisenbach" allowing much cheaper postage (~$0.50-1.00 per piece) though requiring bulk mail permit ($240/year), minimum quantities (typically 200+ pieces), slower delivery (2-3 weeks), and complex USPS preparation requirements for sorting and bundling; and Joseph Eisenbach (Litchfield, CT) providing the direct solution website www.thematzahbox.org offering purpose-designed protective packaging for mailing matzah. For Shluchim implementation, cost analysis for 500 packages reveals First Class totaling $3,170-4,670 ($6.34-9.34 per package), Priority totaling $7,825-9,325 ($15.65-18.65 per package), and Bulk Mail totaling $1,740-3,740 first year or $1,500-3,500 subsequently ($3.00-7.00 per package), demonstrating bulk mail saves 42-52% versus First Class and 78% versus Priority but requires 3+ weeks advance planning, leading to recommendations that first-time programs start with First Class to learn logistics and evaluate bulk mail investment for next year, while established annual programs serving 500+ recipients should invest in bulk mail permit using Eisenbach hard boxes mailed 4 weeks before Pesach saving $1,500-2,000 annually to reinvest in reaching more recipients or higher quality matzah, premium presentations can justify Priority Flat Rate when including substantial printed materials (Haggadah, comprehensive Pesach guide) positioned as high-value gift for major donors or VIPs, and maximum reach with limited budget requires bulk mail to redirect savings from shipping toward more recipients. Practical tips emphasize packaging material testing before bulk ordering, accounting for matzah weight variations by rounding up to next postage tier avoiding individual weighing (Sanoff's proven strategy), remembering printed materials add significant weight potentially exceeding limits, implementing production line workflow with volunteer teams completing 500 packages in 2-3 days when scheduled as community event ("Mivtza Matza" party per Wilansky's enthusiastic characterization), allowing 3-4 weeks before Pesach for preparation and shipping, considering tracking capabilities (included with First Class and Priority but not bulk mail) for donor relations and problem resolution, ensuring mailing list quality given significant expense ($1,500-9,000 depending on method) by confirming current addresses and potentially segmenting core community versus peripheral contacts rather than indiscriminate mass mailing, maintaining non-profit bulk mail compliance requiring statement of ownership and current 501(c)(3) status with audit records, including follow-up strategy with explanatory notes about Seder use plus contact information and response mechanisms (cards or QR codes) transforming mailing into engagement touchpoint for Pesach invitations or ongoing connection, and adhering to timing guidelines of 1-2 weeks for First Class (2-5 day delivery), 10 days-2 weeks for Priority (1-3 day delivery), and minimum 4 weeks for bulk mail (2-3 week processing) with appropriate buffers preventing late arrival disappointment, ultimately providing Shluchim with comprehensive decision framework balancing cost efficiency, delivery reliability, presentation quality, and logistical complexity when implementing large-scale matzah distribution programs that extend Pesach outreach to hundreds of households through tangible gift demonstrating care and enabling mitzvah observance even for those not attending community Seders.

# Matzah Gift Letter Template - Shmurah Matzah Distribution

**Type**: Sample Letter/Template
**Purpose**: Accompany shmurah matzah gift packages sent to community members
**Tone**: Educational, warm, mitzvah-focused
**Recipient**: [REDACTED-NAME] (placeholder for personalization)

## Letter Text

Dear [REDACTED-NAME],

On the threshold of the joyous Holiday of Passover, we are pleased to share with you and your family with Shmura Matzot.

Shmura Matzah is quite unique. The word "Shmura" means watched and is an apt description of this Matzah. From the moment of harvest, through the milling, sifting and packaging, continuous supervision guarantees that no water comes in contact with the grain and flour. Any such contact would cause leavening and disqualify it from use on Pesach. The Matzah is then kneaded, shaped and baked completely by hand, guaranteeing that it will never fall beyond immediate personal supervision.

The message of exodus is ever present in today's modern world, the Hebrew word for Egypt can also be translated as limitations, the flat Matzah bread represents humility, and by being humble one can lift himself from his limitations to unseen heights.

We are cognizant of the relative unavailability of Shmura Matzot to the general public, and deem it a privilege to present them to you. It's our honor and pleasure to share the spirit of the holiday with you and your family. Please enjoy them Monday nught April 10th and Tuesday night April 11th after sunset to fulfill the special Mitzvah of eating Matzah on Passover.

With best wishes for a happy, healthy and joyous Pesach to you and your entire family.

[Signature line not specified]

## Letter Analysis

### Opening

**"On the threshold of the joyous Holiday of Passover, we are pleased to share with you and your family with Shmura Matzot."**

- Sets joyful, anticipatory tone
- "Threshold" creates sense of special moment approaching
- "Share with you and your family" emphasizes community and inclusion
- Uses proper term "Shmura Matzot" (plural of Shmurah Matzah) immediately establishing what's being gifted

**Note**: Grammar issue in original ("share with you and your family with") likely should be "share with you and your family" - may want to correct in actual use

### Educational Section - What is Shmurah Matzah?

**Three-Part Explanation**:

1. **Etymology**: "The word 'Shmura' means watched and is an apt description"
   - Accessible Hebrew word definition
   - "Apt description" implies it's not just a name but accurately describes the process

2. **Production Process**: "From the moment of harvest, through the milling, sifting and packaging, continuous supervision guarantees that no water comes in contact with the grain and flour."
   - Complete timeline: harvest → milling → sifting → packaging
   - Key requirement: continuous supervision
   - Critical standard: no water contact (prevents leavening)
   - Consequence: "Any such contact would cause leavening and disqualify it from use on Pesach"

3. **Handmade Element**: "The Matzah is then kneaded, shaped and baked completely by hand, guaranteeing that it will never fall beyond immediate personal supervision."
   - Entirely manual process
   - Rationale: ensures constant personal oversight
   - Contrast to machine-made (implied, not stated negatively)

### Spiritual/Philosophical Message

**Modern Relevance**:
"The message of exodus is ever present in today's modern world, the Hebrew word for Egypt can also be translated as limitations, the flat Matzah bread represents humility, and by being humble one can lift himself from his limitations to unseen heights."

**Three Connected Ideas**:

1. **Exodus is Contemporary**: Not ancient history but relevant today
2. **Egypt = Mitzrayim = Limitations**: Classic Chassidic interpretation making Exodus personally applicable
3. **Matzah = Humility**: Flat bread (no rising/ego) → Humility → Transcending limitations

**Pedagogy**: Transforms ritual food into spiritual practice with contemporary application

### Positioning the Gift

**Addressing Availability**:
"We are cognizant of the relative unavailability of Shmura Matzot to the general public, and deem it a privilege to present them to you."

- Acknowledges shmurah matzah isn't commonly available in regular stores
- "Cognizant" = we understand your challenge in obtaining this
- "Deem it a privilege" = elevates the giving as honor, not charity
- Creates value: This is special/hard to get, and we're providing it

**Framing as Sharing**:
"It's our honor and pleasure to share the spirit of the holiday with you and your family."

- "Honor and pleasure" = reciprocal gift, not one-way charity
- "Share the spirit" = not just physical matzah but spiritual experience
- Maintains dignity of recipients

### Specific Usage Instructions

**Date-Specific Guidance**:
"Please enjoy them Monday nught April 10th and Tuesday night April 11th after sunset to fulfill the special Mitzvah of eating Matzah on Passover."

**Elements**:
- **When**: Specific dates and times (Monday night April 10th, Tuesday night April 11th)
- **Timing**: "After sunset" = precise halachic requirement
- **Purpose**: "To fulfill the special Mitzvah of eating Matzah on Passover"
- **Verb**: "Enjoy" = makes mitzvah pleasurable, not burdensome

**Note**: "nught" appears to be typo for "night" in original

**Customization Needed**: Dates must be updated annually for current year's Pesach

### Closing

**"With best wishes for a happy, healthy and joyous Pesach to you and your entire family."**

- Triple blessing: happy, healthy, joyous
- "Entire family" = inclusive, multigenerational
- Uses "Pesach" (Hebrew) assuming some Jewish literacy, though letter otherwise uses "Passover" (English)

## For Shluchim: Implementation and Customization

### Personalization Requirements

**Essential Updates**:
1. **Recipient name**: Replace [REDACTED-NAME] with actual names
2. **Dates**: Update "Monday night April 10th and Tuesday night April 11th" to current year's first two Seder nights
3. **Signature**: Add Shliach and Rebbetzin names, Chabad house name
4. **Optional**: Add contact information (phone, email, website) for follow-up

**Mail Merge Capability**:
- Letter structure allows easy mail merge for 500+ recipients
- Keep greeting format consistent: "Dear [First Name]," for warmth
- Consider "Dear [First Name] and [Spouse Name]," if both names known

### Tone and Messaging Strengths

**Educational Without Condescending**:
- Explains "Shmura" meaning without assuming ignorance
- Provides enough detail to appreciate the gift without overwhelming

**Accessible Spirituality**:
- Egypt/Mitzrayim/limitations teaching is accessible Chassidic concept
- Humility → transcendence is universal message beyond denominational lines

**Gift Framing**:
- "Honor and pleasure" + "privilege" language prevents charity stigma
- Positions Chabad as giving something valuable/rare
- Creates gratitude rather than obligation

### Areas for Enhancement

**Grammatical Corrections Needed**:
- "share with you and your family with" → "share with you and your family"
- "nught" → "night"

**Potential Additions**:
- Quantity specification: "Enclosed you will find [2 or 6] hand-made Shmurah Matzos"
- Storage instructions: "Please keep in a dry place until use"
- Amount guidance: "Each person should eat at least 1 oz (approximately half of one matzah) at the Seder"
- Invitation: "If you need a place for the Seder or have Pesach questions, please contact us at [phone/email]"
- Website reference: "Learn more about Passover at [website]"

**Alternative Spiritual Messages**:
- Could emphasize matzah as "bread of faith" and "bread of healing" (Zohar)
- Could mention matzah our ancestors ate leaving Egypt (connecting to tradition)
- Could include brief story or teaching

### Production Considerations

**Printing**:
- Quality paper stock reflects gift value
- Letter-size on letterhead more formal than note card
- Consider Chabad house logo/branding at top
- Leave space for signature (handwritten or printed)

**Timing**:
- Print/stuff 2-4 weeks before Pesach depending on distribution method
- If hand-delivering, can print closer to holiday
- If mailing, factor in shipping time (see file 1170 for shipping logistics)

### Inclusion with Matzah Package

**Folding/Placement**:
- Tri-fold fits well in bubble mailer with matzah
- Place on top so visible when package opened
- Consider clear protective sleeve if matzah might shed crumbs on letter

**Additional Enclosures**:
- Pesach guide/brochure (but watch weight limits for shipping - see file 1170)
- Chabad house event calendar
- Donation envelope (subtle, optional)
- Recipe card for charoset or other Pesach dish

### Alternative Versions for Different Audiences

**For Less Affiliated**:
- Add more background on Passover story
- Explain Seder briefly
- Include invitation to community Seder more prominently

**For More Knowledgeable**:
- Can assume more Hebrew/Jewish literacy
- Could reference specific sources (Zohar, etc.)
- Might include deeper Chassidic teaching

**For Major Donors**:
- More personal handwritten note in addition to printed letter
- Perhaps reference their support: "As a valued supporter of [Chabad house], we wanted to ensure..."
- Upgrade to premium presentation

### Follow-Up Strategy

**After Pesach**:
- Thank you note/email: "We hope you enjoyed the Shmurah Matzah we sent"
- Feedback request: "Did you use it at your Seder?"
- Connection maintenance: "Looking forward to seeing you at [next event]"
- Story sharing: "We distributed [X] matzos to [Y] families this year thanks to supporters like you"

### Cost Context

**Per Package**:
- Matzah: $2-5 (depending on source, see file 1166)
- Letter: $0.05-0.20 (paper, printing, depending on quality)
- Envelope/packaging: $0.50-1.00 (see file 1170)
- Postage: $0.50-13.65 (depending on method, see file 1170)
- **Total**: $3-20 per household

**For 500 Households**: $1,500-10,000 total

### Integration with Other Files

**This Letter Complements**:
- **File 1166**: Matzah procurement and distribution ideas
- **File 1170**: Shipping logistics for large-scale distribution
- **Files 1172-1173**: Alternative letter templates from other Chabad houses for comparison

## Bottom Line

This sample matzah gift letter template provides a warm, educational framework for Shluchim distributing shmurah matzah to community members, opening with "On the threshold of the joyous Holiday of Passover, we are pleased to share with you and your family" establishing anticipatory and inclusive tone, then offering three-part explanation of shmurah matzah starting with etymology ("Shmura means watched"), detailing production process emphasizing continuous supervision from harvest through milling, sifting, and packaging preventing water contact that would cause leavening, and highlighting handmade nature guaranteeing it "never falls beyond immediate personal supervision," contrasting implicitly with machine production. # Matzah Gift Letter - Chabad of Maple, Ontario

**Source**: Chabad of Maple
**Location**: Maple, Ontario
**Date**: Nissan 3, 5776 (April 11, 2016)
**Authors**: Rabbi Chezky & Shaina Deren
**Type**: Personalized matzah gift letter template

## Full Letter Text

Nissan 3, 5776
April 11, 2016
Maple, Ontario

Dear Friends,

Greetings & Blessings,

One of the beautiful Mitzvahs of Pesach is eating the Matzah commemorating the unleavened bread that our ancestors ate when leaving Egypt. The Zohar teaches us that Matzah on Pesach is a "food of faith" as well as a "food of good health". This precious Mitzvah is one that has been cherished by our people throughout history; even under the most difficult circumstances.

Matzah – The Poor Man's Bread- teaches us an important lesson in humility. As high as we rise and as far as we reach we must never forget our humble beginnings. In every generation and every day we must remember that we in fact were slaves in Egypt and never take for granted G-d's gift of 'Freedom'. The simplicity of the Matzahs remind us never to forget about those less fortunate than we are.

Although this Mitzvah can be performed by eating any plain Kosher for Pesach Matzah, this cherished Mitzvah is best done at the Seder by eating handmade "Matzot Shmurot". While a machine can make a perfect Matzah; it lacks 'soul-Kavanah'. When it comes to a Mitzvah intentions absolutely do count! The ingredients of these Matzahs are only flour, water and three and half thousand years of human heart and soul.

These delicious handmade in Israel Matzahs are our gift to you. In order to do the Mitzvah properly please be sure to eat at least one half of a Round Shmurah Matzah during each of your Pesach Seders (after dark).

Enjoy!

Our best wishes to you and your family for a Kosher, Joyous, and stress free Passover!

Rabbi Chezky & Shaina Deren
Chabad of Maple

Please see the Sale of Chametz form on the reverse side of this page.

## Bottom Line

This April 2016 matzah gift letter from Rabbi Chezky & Shaina Deren of Chabad of Maple, Ontario, provides a more developed spiritual and practical framework than the basic template (file 1171), emphasizing matzah as both "food of faith" and "food of good health" (Zohar teaching), presenting "Matzah - The Poor Man's Bread" as humility lesson that "as high as we rise and as far as we reach we must never forget our humble beginnings" and must "remember that we in fact were slaves in Egypt and never take for granted G-d's gift of 'Freedom'" with the matzah's simplicity reminding us "never to forget about those less fortunate," distinguishing between halachically acceptable "any plain Kosher for Pesach Matzah" versus ideal "handmade Matzot Shmurot" by noting "while a machine can make a perfect Matzah; it lacks 'soul-Kavanah'" and "when it comes to a Mitzvah intentions absolutely do count," poetically describing the matzah's ingredients as "only flour, water and three and half thousand years of human heart and soul," specifying these are "handmade in Israel Matzahs" as "our gift to you," providing clear usage instruction to "eat at least one half of a Round Shmurah Matzah during each of your Pesach Seders (after dark)," closing warmly with wishes for "Kosher, Joyous, and stress free Passover" (notably adding "stress free" acknowledging Pesach preparation challenges), and efficiently including "Sale of Chametz form on the reverse side of this page" combining matzah gift with essential pre-Pesach service in single mailing, offering Shluchim a model balancing deeper spiritual content (Zohar source, kavanah concept, soul/heart language, humility/freedom/responsibility themes), practical halachic distinction (kosher is acceptable, shmurah is ideal), clear quantity guidance (half matzah per Seder), geographical specificity (made in Israel adds authenticity), relatable closing (stress-free acknowledgment), and operational efficiency (dual-purpose mailing with chametz sale form maximizing touchpoint value).

# Matzah Gift Letter - Chabad Lubavitch of Idaho

**Source**: Chabad Lubavitch of Idaho
**Location**: Boise, Idaho
**Date**: 10 Nissan, 5779 (April 15, 2019)
**Authors**: Rabbi Mendel & Esther Lifshitz
**Type**: Personalized matzah gift letter with contemporary relevance and existential themes

## Full Letter Text

10 Nissan, 5779
April 15, 2019

Dear Friend,

Friday night, April 19, 2019 will be the 3331st anniversary of our ancestors' emancipation! When we eat matzah on the first night of Passover, we are connecting to generations of Jews. We are intimately bound with the taste of freedom. And, we are connecting to the very essence of our being and our Creator. Surely this is an opportunity not to miss!

So, this is how we need to celebrate. On April 19 after nightfall, which is at 9:04pm in Boise, sit down and eat 1 oz of the enclosed Shmurah Matzah. That's about ½ of a large size matzah. As you're doing so, envision your great grandparents leaving Egypt 3330 years ago. Envision them eating the exact same handmade matzah (no Manischewitz yet!). Even if you are having an 'early' Seder, save this matzah for Afikoman or dessert and eat it after nightfall, so you can connect with the spirit of Passover.

I have a question for you, though. How can I repeat the same rituals each year and still feel like it's important and inspiring?

The Chassidic Masters explain that the Hebrew word for Egypt, Mitzrayim, means limitations. We too, must transcend the limitations of our own lives; the complacency we have grown accustomed to; the voice of despair in our own head. We too, must leave Egypt every year – and every day. Freedom, it turns out, is a relative term. Yesterday's freedom might be today's enslavement.

The Exodus isn't a story for the history books. It can – and must – be our story as well. On Passover we each can break free from whatever may be hindering us. We too can leave Egypt – our Egypt. As you bite into this traditional matzah, think about why G-d has commanded us to recount and relive the Exodus each year. Think of your current personal bondage and liberation.

Please accept our heartfelt wishes and blessings to you and yours for a happy and kosher Passover. May it be truly liberating!

Sincerely,

Rabbi Mendel & Esther Lifshitz
Chabad Lubavitch of Idaho

P.S. If you need a place for the Seder, need to sell your chametz or any other Passover needs, please call our office and we will be happy to help you, or visit www.jewishidaho.com.

## Bottom Line

This April 2019 matzah gift letter from Rabbi Mendel & Esther Lifshitz of Chabad Lubavitch of Idaho stands out for its existential depth, contemporary relevance, and sophisticated engagement style, opening dramatically with "Friday night, April 19, 2019 will be the 3331st anniversary of our ancestors' emancipation" providing specific historical timeline that "when we eat matzah on the first night of Passover, we are connecting to generations of Jews" being "intimately bound with the taste of freedom" and "connecting to the very essence of our being and our Creator" positioning participation as "opportunity not to miss," then offering remarkably specific instructions: "On April 19 after nightfall, which is at 9:04pm in Boise" (exact local nightfall time showing attention to halachic detail and geographical specificity) "sit down and eat 1 oz of the enclosed Shmurah Matzah" (½ large matzah) while envisioning "your great grandparents leaving Egypt 3330 years ago" eating "the exact same handmade matzah (no Manischewitz yet!)" with humor acknowledging commercial alternatives, crucially addressing early Seders by instructing "even if you are having an 'early' Seder, save this matzah for Afikoman or dessert and eat it after nightfall, so you can connect with the spirit of Passover" solving timing conflict pragmatically. The letter's philosophical core addresses reader skepticism directly: "I have a question for you, though. How can I repeat the same rituals each year and still feel like it's important and inspiring?" then answering through Chassidic teaching that "Mitzrayim means limitations" so "we too, must transcend the limitations of our own lives; the complacency we have grown accustomed to; the voice of despair in our own head" needing to "leave Egypt every year – and every day" because "Freedom, it turns out, is a relative term. Yesterday's freedom might be today's enslavement," making Exodus urgently contemporary: "The Exodus isn't a story for the history books. It can – and must – be our story as well" challenging readers to "think about why G-d has commanded us to recount and relive the Exodus each year. Think of your current personal bondage and liberation" as they "bite into this traditional matzah," closing with wishes for "truly liberating" Passover and practical P.S. offering Seder hosting, chametz sale, and comprehensive Passover assistance via office call or www.jewishidaho.com, providing Shluchim with model for addressing modern Jewish ambivalence toward ritual repetition through existential reframing (ritual as personal liberation opportunity), engaging skepticism head-on rather than avoiding it, using precise local detail (9:04pm Boise nightfall) demonstrating care and halachic seriousness, solving early Seder conflict with creative afikoman/dessert solution maintaining halachic integrity, employing gentle humor (Manischewitz reference) building rapport, crafting philosophically sophisticated message about ongoing personal exodus from internal limitations/complacency/despair that positions annual observance as psychological/spiritual necessity rather than historical commemoration, and integrating comprehensive service offerings (Seder invitation, chametz sale, general assistance) in postscript maintaining letter's inspirational focus while providing practical onramp for engagement.

# Model Matzah Bakery - "Back to the Exodus" Full Production Guide

**Type**: Event Production Script and Props List
**Program**: Interactive Model Matzah Bakery Show
**Theme**: "Back to the Exodus" - immersive Pesach story experience before participants make matzah
**Format**: Multi-act theatrical presentation followed by hands-on matzah baking
**Audience**: Children and families (pre-Pesach programming)

## Program Overview

This is an interactive Model Matzah Bake show—a full experience that immerses participants in the Pesach story before they actually make their own matzah. The document provides organized breakdown of props and items needed for each act.

**Most Common Format**: Showing wheat stalks → milling them → making the dough → allowing each participant to make their own matzah

## Resource Links

### Where to Buy Materials

**JewishYouthPrograms.com**
- All materials needed for the show
- **Note**: "on the pricier side"
- Best source for authentic wheat stalks with kernels (hard to find elsewhere online)

**webstaurantstore.com**
- Affordable utensils and baking equipment
- Commercial kitchen supplies

**Local Matzah Bakeries** (NY area or nearby)
- Free rolling pins
- Free paper (often discarded by bakeries)
- Build relationship with local bakery for ongoing materials

**Amazon**
- Backdrops (ready-made):
  - Splitting of the Sea
  - Wheat Field
  - Egyptian Pyramids
- Wheat kernels

### Equipment Considerations

**Manual Grain Mill**
- Stone mills can be quite expensive
- Alternative: Budget-friendly mill

**Backdrops**
- Ready-made options available on Amazon (listed above)
- Or create custom from Sukkah Depot or similar

## Matzah Recipe Options

**Option 1:**
- 2 cups regular flour
- 1 cup whole wheat flour
- 1 cup water

**Option 2:**
- 3 1/4 cups white flour
- 3/4 cups whole wheat flour
- 1 1/3 cups water

## Matzah Rolling Paper

- Large rolls of thick parchment paper are ideal

## Aprons & Hats

- Can get these with the Matzah Bakery logo from Shluchim selling websites

## Oven Considerations

### Portable Oven Option

**Requirements**:
- Portable oven that plugs into 110 outlet needed to bake matzah
- **Challenges**:
  - Can be expensive
  - Take long time to bake matzah even with stone placed at bottom to speed up
  - Often trigger smoke alarms

**Recommendation**: "If you're using a venue's kitchen, it's best to let them manage the oven"

### Toaster Oven Option

- High-quality toaster oven with tile placed at bottom
- Helps bake matzah faster
- Smaller commercial ovens (typically ~$100) can work well

### Portable Stove Top Option

- Use portable stove top to bake matzah directly on it
- **Important**: Be sure to tovel (immerse in mikvah) the stove top before use

## Additional Elements

**Kemach + Mayim Station**
- Hands-on experience station
- Backdrop can be purchased online (e.g., Sukkah Depot)
- Can add booths or other themed props to enhance experience

**Model Matzah Presentation Video**
- Link provided for inspiration (specific URL in original)

## Act-by-Act Props List

### Act 1: Introduction/Egypt Theme

**Technology**:
- Jcrafts wristbands
- Speakers
- All soundtracks
- Large button
- Large hammer
- Smoke machine
- Bubble machine
- Flashing lights
- Red flashing lights

**Set Design**:
- Backdrop of "Back to the Exodus" / Egypt
- Stand to hold backdrop

**Costumes**:
- Scientist costume (jacket, hat, glasses)

### Act 2: Slavery and Exodus Story

**Props**:
- Foam bricks (representing slavery labor)
- Whip (representing Egyptian taskmasters)
- Sneh (small tree on flashing light - burning bush)
- Martini glass cup
- Water
- Pitcher
- Red food coloring (for blood plague)
- Plastic frogs (frog plague)
- Bottle sprayers (for plagues effects)

**Costumes**:
- Ancient Jew costume
- Ancient Egyptian costume
- Moses costume
- Moses stick (staff)

### Act 3: Wheat/Flour Preparation

**Materials**:
- Wheat stalks (order from JewishYouthPrograms.com for ones with actual kernels)
- Barley kernels
- Wheat mill grinder
- Wheat bowl
- Sifter
- Large bowl to mix dough
- Flour
- Pitcher
- Water

**Costumes**:
- Farmer costume (overalls and hat)

**Theme**: Kemach + Mayim station concept

### Act 4: Actual Matzah Baking

**Safety/Hygiene**:
- Aprons
- Hats
- Gloves
- Pins (likely for securing aprons/hats)

**Equipment**:
- Oven
- Paper bags to roll matzah on
- Pizza server to take matzah out of oven

## For Shluchim: Production and Implementation Guide

### Budget Planning

**Startup Costs** (First Year):
- Props/costumes: $500-1,500 (depending on quality and sourcing)
- Backdrops: $100-300
- Wheat stalks/grains: $50-100
- Equipment (mill, oven): $100-500
- Aprons/hats (custom logo): $200-400 for 50 sets
- Flour/baking supplies: $50-100
- **Total First Year**: $1,000-3,000

**Recurring Costs** (Subsequent Years):
- Wheat stalks/grains: $50-100
- Flour/baking supplies: $50-100
- Replacement items: $50-150
- **Total Recurring**: $150-350

**Revenue Potential**:
- Charge $15-25 per child
- 50 participants = $750-1,250
- Can cover recurring costs and contribute to amortizing startup

### Venue Requirements

**Space Needs**:
- Performance area for Acts 1-3 (theatrical presentation)
- Tables/workspace for Act 4 (matzah making)
- Oven access (kitchen or portable)
- Seating for audience/participants
- **Minimum**: 1,000-1,500 sq ft
- **Ideal**: 2,000+ sq ft

**Kitchen Access**:
- If venue has kitchen with oven: Coordinate usage, test temperature
- If using portable: Ensure adequate electrical (110V outlets), test smoke alarm sensitivity
- Ventilation important (ovens and smoke effects)

### Staffing

**Minimum Team**:
- Lead presenter/actor (often Shliach or experienced educator)
- Assistant for tech (lights, sound, smoke/bubble machines)
- 2-3 volunteers for Act 4 (helping kids roll matzah, managing oven)

**Optional**:
- Actors for different roles (Moses, Egyptian, farmer) - can be older kids/teens
- Photographer/videographer for marketing future events

### Timeline and Logistics

**Pre-Event** (2-3 months before):
- Book venue
- Order custom aprons/hats if needed
- Acquire reusable props (costumes, backdrops, equipment)

**Pre-Event** (2-4 weeks before):
- Order wheat stalks (fresh for show)
- Finalize registration (capacity planning)
- Recruit volunteers
- Test all tech (sound, lights, machines)

**Pre-Event** (1 week before):
- Purchase flour, water (fresh)
- Prepare dough if doing demo first
- Set up backdrops if venue allows early access

**Day Of**:
- Arrive 2-3 hours early for setup
- Test oven temperature
- Lay out workspace for Act 4
- Sound check
- Brief volunteers

**Event Duration**:
- Acts 1-3: 30-45 minutes
- Act 4 (matzah making): 30-45 minutes
- Total: 60-90 minutes

### Age Considerations

**Preschool (3-5)**:
- Shorter Acts 1-3 (20-30 min)
- More hands-on, less lecture
- Adult helpers for each child in Act 4
- Safety critical (oven kept far from kids)

**Elementary (6-12)**:
- Full program works well
- Can handle more story detail
- Some independence in Act 4
- Older kids can help younger

**Family Program (All Ages)**:
- Parents participate with younger children
- Entertainment value in Acts 1-3 for adults too
- Family teams for matzah making

### Safety Protocols

**Oven Safety**:
- Adult-only oven operation
- Oven mitt stations
- Clear oven perimeter (rope/tape marking)
- Fire extinguisher accessible

**Food Allergies**:
- Pre-registration asks about wheat/gluten allergies
- Alternative activity for allergic children (observing, helping with non-flour tasks)

**Tech Safety**:
- Smoke machines: Check venue fire alarm sensitivity, inform venue management
- Bubble machines: Non-slip solution, mop spills immediately
- Electrical: No exposed cords, tape down cables, GFCI outlets for water-near areas

### Enhancement Ideas

**Act Integration**:
- QR codes on wristbands linking to Pesach resources
- "Scientist" theme could explore "science" of keeping flour dry, timing under 18 minutes
- Ten Plagues could be more elaborate with additional effects
- Burning bush (Sneh) could have voice recording of calling Moshe

**Takeaways**:
- Kids take home their matzah (package immediately after baking)
- Certificate of participation
- Recipe card for making at home
- Mini Haggadah or Pesach coloring book

**Marketing**:
- Video clip from previous year
- Photos of kids in aprons/hats
- "Make your own matzah!" headline
- Early bird discount
- Sibling discount

### Model Variations

**Express Version** (30-45 minutes total):
- Skip elaborate Acts 1-2
- Quick story overview
- Focus on wheat-to-matzah (Act 3-4)
- Good for school visits with time limits

**Deluxe Version** (2+ hours):
- All four acts fully developed
- Sit-down Seder simulation with matzah they made
- Full meal (simple: matzah ball soup, salad)
- Parents invited for last 30 minutes

**School Assembly Version**:
- Performance focus (Acts 1-3)
- Demo matzah making (one volunteer makes, all watch)
- Take-home: Store-bought shmurah matzah for each child
- 45 minutes total

**Traveling Program**:
- Portable setup (lightweight backdrops, collapsible props)
- Battery-powered equipment where possible
- Partner with schools/JCCs
- No oven (demo only or cold "pretend" matzah)

## Bottom Line

This comprehensive production guide for "Back to the Exodus" interactive Model Matzah Bakery show provides complete act-by-act breakdown of props, equipment, and materials needed to create immersive Pesach educational experience where participants engage with Exodus story through theatrical presentation before making their own matzah, organized in four acts: (1) Introduction/Egypt theme using technology (speakers, soundtracks, large button, hammer, smoke/bubble/flashing light machines), set design (backdrop and stand), and scientist costume establishing theatrical environment; (2) Slavery and Exodus story using props (foam bricks for slavery labor, whip for taskmasters, sneh/small tree with flashing light for burning bush, martini glass/pitcher/water/red food coloring for blood plague, plastic frogs, bottle sprayers for plague effects) and costumes (Ancient Jew, Egyptian, Moses with staff) dramatizing liberation narrative; (3) Wheat/flour preparation demonstrating matzah-making process using wheat stalks from JewishYouthPrograms.com (only source with actual kernels), barley kernels, wheat mill grinder, wheat bowl, sifter, large mixing bowl, flour, pitcher, water, and farmer costume (overalls/hat) creating "Kemach + Mayim station" hands-on learning; and (4) Actual baking with safety/hygiene items (aprons, hats, gloves, pins) and equipment (oven, paper bags for rolling, pizza server) allowing each participant to create their own matzah. Resource guidance directs to JewishYouthPrograms.com for complete materials ("on the pricier side"), webstaurantstore.com for affordable utensils/equipment, local matzah bakeries (NY area) for free discarded rolling pins and paper, and Amazon for ready-made backdrops (Splitting of Sea, Wheat Field, Egyptian Pyramids) and wheat kernels, while providing two recipe options (Option 1: 2 cups regular/1 cup whole wheat flour with 1 cup water; Option 2: 3¼ cups white/¾ cup whole wheat with 1⅓ cups water), recommending large rolls of thick parchment paper for rolling, custom-logo aprons/hats from Shluchim websites, and addressing oven challenges noting portable ovens plugging into 110 outlets are expensive, slow even with bottom stone, and trigger smoke alarms so "best to let venue manage the oven," with alternatives being high-quality toaster oven with tile at bottom or portable stove top (must tovel before use) or smaller commercial ovens (~$100). For Shluchim implementation, budget planning shows $1,000-3,000 first-year startup (props/costumes $500-1,500, backdrops $100-300, wheat $50-100, equipment $100-500, custom aprons $200-400, flour/supplies $50-100) with $150-350 recurring costs and revenue potential of $750-1,250 from 50 participants at $15-25 each covering recurring costs and amortizing startup; venue requirements include 1,000-1,500 sq ft minimum (2,000+ ideal) with performance area, tables/workspace, oven access, seating, and kitchen coordination or portable electrical setup with ventilation and smoke alarm sensitivity testing; staffing needs minimum lead presenter, tech assistant, and 2-3 Act 4 volunteers with optional additional actors and photographer; timeline spans 2-3 months advance (venue, orders, props), 2-4 weeks (wheat, registration, volunteers, tech testing), 1 week (fresh flour/water purchase, dough prep, setup), day-of 2-3 hours early arrival for setup/testing with 60-90 minute total event (30-45 min Acts 1-3, 30-45 min Act 4); age adaptations from preschool (shorter/simpler, adult helpers, critical safety) through elementary (full program, some independence) to family (parents participate, entertainment for all ages); safety protocols covering adult-only oven operation with mitts/clear perimeter/fire extinguisher, pre-registration allergy screening with alternatives for wheat/gluten allergic children, and tech safety including smoke machine venue coordination, bubble solution slip prevention, and electrical cord management with GFCI; enhancement ideas including integrated QR codes, elaborate plague effects, voice-recorded burning bush, takeaways (packaged matzah, certificates, recipe cards, mini Haggadahs), and marketing with video clips, photos, discounts; and program variations from Express (30-45 min wheat-to-matzah focus for school visits) through Deluxe (2+ hours with Seder simulation and full meal) to School Assembly (performance with demo, take-home store matzah, 45 min) and Traveling (portable lightweight setup, battery power, no oven) allowing customization for different contexts, budgets, and audiences while maintaining core educational mission of immersing participants in Pesach story through multi-sensory theatrical experience before hands-on mitzvah participation creating lasting memories and meaningful pre-Pesach engagement for children and families.
